Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 1:

Page 184

(Surat al-Ra'd)
Madaniyyah (Medinan), and its verses number 43. It was revealed after Surat Muhammad.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful) ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Book. And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe﴾

Surat al-Ra'd

It has forty-three verses. It is Makkan, except for His the Exalted's words: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve for what they have done﴾ (al-Ra'd: 31) and His words: ﴿And those who have knowledge of the Book﴾ (al-Ra'd: 43). Al-Asamm said: it is Madani by consensus, except for His the Exalted's words: ﴿And if only a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved﴾ (al-Ra'd: 31).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Book. And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe﴾

Know that we have already discussed these letters. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: its meaning is: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing." In a narration from 'Ata', he said: "I am Allah, the King, the Most Gracious." Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i and others imala (inclined) them, while a group, including 'Asim, pronounced them with emphasis (tafkhim). His words ﴿These﴾ refer to the verses of the surah named after (Alif Lam Mim Ra). Then He said: they are the verses of the Book, meaning this Book which He gave to Muhammad, by sending it down to him and making it remain for all time.

His words ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ are the subject (mubtada'), and His words ﴿the truth﴾ are its predicate (khabar). Some people have held to this verse in denying qiyas (analogical reasoning). They said: a ruling derived by qiyas is not sent down from Allah, for otherwise whoever did not judge by it would be a disbeliever, by His the Exalted's words: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, those are the disbelievers﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 44), and by consensus one does not become a disbeliever for this. Thus it is established that a ruling affirmed by qiyas is not sent down from Allah.

If that is the case, it must not be true, because His words ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ imply that there is no truth except what Allah has sent down. So whatever Allah has not sent down must not be true, and if it is not true it must be false, by His the Exalted's words: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ (Yunus: 32). The proponents of qiyas answer this by saying that a ruling affirmed by qiyas is also sent down from Allah, because

Page 185

when He commanded acting upon qiyas, the ruling indicated by qiyas became sent down from Allah.
And when He, the Exalted, mentioned that what was sent down to Muhammad ﷺ is the truth, He made clear that most people do not believe in it, as a rebuke and a warning.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see. Then He established Himself over the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He arranges the affair and explains the signs in detail, that you may be certain of meeting your Lord.﴾

He, may He be exalted, when He mentioned that most people do not believe, followed it with what proves the soundness of tawhid (the oneness of God) and ma'ad (the return and resurrection). This is the verse, and concerning it there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Allah" is the subject (mubtada') and "who raised the heavens" is its predicate (khabar), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾ (al-Ra'd: 3).

It is also permissible for "who raised the heavens" to be an attribute (sifah), and His saying ﴿He arranges the affair, explains the signs﴾ to be a second predicate.

Al-Wahidi said: *al-'amad* means the pillars (al-asatin), and it is the plural of * 'imad*. It is said: *'imad* and *'umud*, like *ihab* and *uhub*. Al-Farra' said: *al-'amad* and *al-'umud* are plurals of *al-'amud* (pillar), like *adim* and *adam* and *udum*, and *qadim* and *qadam* and *qudum*. *Al-'imad* and *al-'amud* are that by which a thing is supported. From this it is said: "So-and-so is the 'amad of his people" when they rely upon him among themselves.

**The second issue:** Know that He, may He be exalted, argued from the conditions of the heavens, the conditions of the sun and moon, the conditions of the earth, and the conditions of plants.

As for the argument from the conditions of the heavens, "without pillars that you can see," the meaning is that these great bodies remain standing in the high atmosphere. It is impossible that their remaining there is due to their own essences and selves, for two reasons:

The first: bodies are equal in their complete quiddity (mahiyyah). If it were necessary for one body to be located in a specific place, it would be necessary for every body to be located in that place.

The second: the void (al-khala') has no end, and the spaces that extend through that pure void are infinite and all equal. If it were necessary for a body to be located in a specific space, it would be necessary for it to be located in all spaces, since all spaces are alike. Thus it is established that the location of the celestial bodies in their spaces and directions is not a necessity of their essences. Rather, there must be a specifier (mukhassis) and a preponderator (murajjih). It is not permissible to say that they remain by a chain above them or a pillar below them, for then the discussion would return to that holder, and it would lead to an infinite regress, which is impossible. Therefore it is established that one should say: the celestial bodies are in their high spaces because the Manager of the world, may He be exalted and sanctified, has stationed them there.

This is a decisive proof of the existence of the Almighty, the All-Powerful God. It also indicates that God is not a body, nor confined to a space. For if He were located in a specific space, His being in that space could not be due to His essence and self, since we have shown that all spaces are equal. Therefore it is impossible that His being in a specific space be due to His essence. It must then be by the specification of a specifier. Whatever comes about through a free, chosen agent is originated (muhdath). So His being specified to a particular space is originated, and His essence does not separate from that specification. Whatever does not separate from the originated is itself originated. Thus it is established that if He were located in a specific space, He would be originated, and that is impossible. So it is established that He, may He be exalted, is above space and direction.

Also: whatever is "sama" (above) you is "sama" (a heaven). So if God, may He be exalted, existed in a direction above another direction, He would be among the heavens, and would fall under His saying: ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾.

[Page 186]

Therefore whatever is specified to a direction above another direction is in need of God's preservation by the ruling of this verse. So it is obligatory that God be transcendent above the direction of "above."

As for His saying ﴿that you can see﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: it is a new, independent statement, and the meaning is: He raised the heavens without pillars. Then He said ﴿that you can see﴾, meaning: while you see them, i.e., raised without support.

The second: al-Hasan said, in explaining the verse, that there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its intended sense being: He raised the heavens, which you can see, without pillars.

Know that when the statement can be taken in its apparent sense, resorting to inversion is not permissible.

The third: that His saying ﴿that you can see﴾ is an attribute of the pillars, and the meaning is: without visible pillars. That is, the heavens have pillars, but we do not see them. They said: they have pillars on Mount Qaf, which is a mountain of emerald encircling the world. But you do not see them.

This interpretation is extremely weak, because He, may He be exalted, mentioned this statement only to serve as proof of the existence of the All-Powerful God. Had the intended meaning been what they mentioned, the proof would not be established, for it would be said: since the heavens are fixed upon Mount Qaf, what indication is there in their stability for the existence of God? In my view there is another opinion better than all of these, which is that *al-'imad* is that upon which one relies. We have shown that these bodies remain standing in the high atmosphere only by the power of God, the Exalted. In that case their pillar is the power of God, the Exalted. Thus it follows that it is said: He raised the heaven without pillars that you can see, meaning: there is in reality a pillar for them, but that pillar is the power of God, His preservation, His management, and His keeping them in the high atmosphere. And they do not see that management, nor do they know the mode of that holding.

\* \* \*

As for His saying ﴿then He established Himself over the Throne﴾, know that its meaning is not His being settled upon the Throne. For the purpose of this verse is to mention what indicates the existence of the Creator, and that thing must be observed and known. And no one has seen that He, may He be exalted, has settled upon the Throne, so how could one argue from it to Him? Furthermore, even if His being settled upon the Throne were observed, that would not indicate the perfection of His state or the extent of His majesty, but rather would indicate His need for place and space. Moreover, this would indicate that He was not in this state and then came to be in this state, and that entails change.

Also, *al-istiwa'* is the opposite of crookedness. The apparent wording of the verse would indicate that He was crooked and disordered, then became straight. All of that is impossible for God. Therefore it is established that the intended meaning is His establishment over the world of bodies by subjugation, power, management, and preservation. That is, from what is above the Throne to what is beneath the earth is under His preservation, His management, and in need of Him.

As for the argument from the conditions of the sun and moon, it is His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿and He subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term﴾.

Know that this statement contains two kinds of evidence:

The first kind: His saying ﴿and He subjected the sun and the moon﴾. Its essence returns to an argument for the existence of the Creator, the All-Powerful, the Subjugator, through the movements of these bodies. This is because bodies are alike, so these celestial bodies are capable of motion and rest. Their being specified to continuous motion rather than rest requires a specifier.

Also, each of those motions is specified to a definite manner of slowness and speed, so there must also be a specifier, especially according to those who say that slow motion means motions mixed with pauses. This necessitates acknowledging that they move in some spaces and rest in others. So the occurrence of motion in that specific space and rest in the other space also requires a preponderator.

The third aspect: the determination of those motions and rests by specific measures in a manner whereby their returns and cycles are equal in duration is a wondrous state, so there must be a determiner (muqaddir).

[Page 187]

The fourth aspect: some of those motions are eastward, some westward, some inclined toward the north, and some inclined toward the south. This too can only be accomplished through complete management and far-reaching wisdom.

The second kind of proof mentioned in this verse is His saying ﴿each running for a specified term﴾. On this there are two opinions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: the sun has one hundred and eighty stations (manazil), each day it has a station, and this is completed in six months. Then it returns once more to one of them in another six months. Likewise the moon has twenty-eight stations. So the meaning of His saying ﴿each running for a specified term﴾ is this.

Its verification is that He, may He be exalted, determined for each one of these stars a particular course toward a particular direction with a particular measure of speed and slowness. And when that is the case, it necessarily follows that for each moment and instant it has a state different from what it had before.

The second opinion: the intended meaning is that the two are moving until the Day of Resurrection. When that day comes, these motions will cease and these courses will be voided, as God, may He be exalted, described in His saying: ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾ ﴿and when the stars fall﴾ (al-Takwir: 1, 2) ﴿when the sky is split open﴾ (al-Inshiqaq: 1) ﴿when the sky is cleft asunder﴾ (al-Infitar: 1) ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾ (al-Qiyamah: 9). This is like His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him﴾ (al-An'am: 2).

Then, when He, may He be exalted, mentioned these proofs, He said: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾. Each of the exegetes took this to refer to the management of another kind of the world's conditions. The better view is to take it as referring to the whole. So He manages them by bringing into existence and annihilating, by giving life and causing death, by enriching and impoverishing, and this includes sending down revelation, sending the messengers, and imposing obligations upon the servants. In this there is a wondrous proof of perfect power and mercy. This is because this known world, from the heights of the Throne to what is beneath the earth, consists of kinds and species that none encompasses except God, may He be exalted.

The argument mentioned indicates that the specification of each of them to its position, its place, its attribute, its nature, and its form is from God alone. It is known that whoever is occupied with managing one thing cannot manage anything else except the Creator, glorified and exalted is He, for no matter distracts Him from another matter. As for the intelligent person, when he reflects upon this verse, he knows that He, may He be exalted, manages the world of bodies and the world of spirits, manages the great as He manages the small. No matter distracts Him from another matter, and no management prevents Him from another management. That indicates that He, may He be exalted, in His essence, attributes, knowledge, and power, is not similar to originated and contingent things.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿He explains the signs﴾. On this there are two opinions:

The first: He, may He be exalted, made clear the signs that indicate His divinity, knowledge, and wisdom.

The second: the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator are of two kinds:

One: the existing, enduring, everlasting things, such as the spheres, the sun, the moon, and the stars. This kind of proof is the one mentioned earlier.

The second: the existing, originated, changing things, namely death after life, poverty after wealth, old age after health, the fool living in the most comfortable life, and the intelligent, clever person in the most difficult conditions. This kind of existing things and conditions indicates clearly and manifestly the existence of the Wise Creator.

His saying ﴿He explains the signs﴾ indicates that some of them come after others in a sequence of distinction and detail.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿that you may be certain of meeting your Lord﴾. Know that the proofs mentioned, just as they indicate the existence of the Wise Creator, also indicate the soundness of the doctrine of gathering and resurrection (al-hashr wa al-nashr). For whoever is capable of creating these things and managing them, with their greatness and multiplicity, is all the more capable of gathering and resurrecting.

It is related that a man said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: "How does He, may He be exalted, call the creatures to account all at once?" He said: "As He provides for them all at once now, and as He hears their calls and answers their supplications all at once now."

The gist of the matter is that just as He, exalted is He, is able to keep the celestial bodies and the luminous stars in the high atmosphere, even though creation is incapable of doing so, and just as He can govern everything from above the Throne down to what lies beneath the earth in such a way that one affair does not preoccupy Him from another, so likewise He reckons with creation in such a way that one affair does not preoccupy Him from another. Among the companions (al-Ashab) there are those who held fast to the word "liqa'" (meeting) as evidence for the vision of God, exalted is He; and its explanation has already been set out in this book many times and in various places.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth and placed therein firmly set mountains and rivers, and of all fruits He made therein two mates, two. He covers the night with the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, established the celestial proofs, He followed them with establishing the terrestrial proofs, so He said: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾.

Know that the argument from His creation of the earth and its conditions comes in several aspects:

The first: when the body and quantity of a thing increase, that body and quantity come to be as if they were extended. So His saying ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾ indicates that Allah, glorified is He, is the One who made the earth specific to that determined quantity which it has, neither more nor less. The evidence for this is that the earth being greater in quantity than it is now, or less than it is, is something possible and conceivable in itself. Therefore its being specific to that determined quantity must come from the specification and determination of a determiner.

The second: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "Madd (extension) is spreading out to an extent whose limit cannot be perceived." So His saying ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾ suggests that He, exalted is He, made the volume of the earth a great volume, whose limit the eye does not reach. For if the earth were smaller in volume than it is now, its benefit would not be complete.

The third: some people said: "The earth was round, so He extended it and spread it out from Makkah, beneath the House, and it went such and such." Others said: "It was gathered at the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Muqaddas), and He said to it: 'Go such and such.'"

Know that this saying is only complete if we say the earth is flat, not a sphere. The proponents of this view argued for it with His saying: ﴿And after that He spread it out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30]. And this view is problematic from two aspects:

The first: it has been established by proofs that the earth is a sphere, so how can one insist otherwise?

If they say: "His saying ﴿spread out the earth﴾ contradicts its being a sphere, so how can it be spread out?"

We reply: We do not grant that the earth is a body of great size. When a sphere is extremely large, every piece of it is seen like a surface, and the difference between it and a surface does not arise except in the knowledge of Allah. Do you not see that He said: ﴿And the mountains as pegs﴾ [al-Naba': 7], making them pegs although the people of the world settle upon them? So likewise here.

The second: this verse was mentioned so that it could be used as evidence for the existence of the Creator, and the condition for that is that the matter be observed and known, so that the argument for the existence of the Creator from it is valid. But that the earth is gathered beneath the House is not something observed or perceived, so it cannot be used as evidence for the existence of the Creator. Thus it is established that the true interpretation is what we have mentioned.

* * *

The second type of proofs: the argument from the conditions of the mountains, to which He refers in His saying ﴿and placed therein firmly set mountains﴾, meaning, from above it, fixed, enduring in their places, not moving from their positions. It is said: "This peg stood firm (rasa) and I made it stand firm (arsaytuhu)." And the intended meaning is what we have mentioned.

Know that the argument for the existence of the Creator, the Powerful, the Wise, from the existence of the mountains comes in several aspects:

The first: the nature of the earth is one, so the existence of a mountain in some of its regions and not others must be by the creation of the Powerful, the Wise. The philosophers said: "These mountains came into being because the seas were, in this side of the world, and so in the sea a sticky clay was generated; then the influence of the sun strengthens upon it, and it turns into stone, as is observed in a foam-bottle (kūz al-fiqā'). Then the water would recede and diminish, and what remained would harden into stone. For this reason these mountains came into being. They said: 'The seas were in this side of the world because the apogee (awj) and perigee (hadīd) of the sun are moving. In the most ancient age the perigee of the sun was on the northern side, and whenever the sun is at its perigee it is closer to the earth, so heating is stronger, and intense heat causes moisture to be attracted. So when the perigee was on the northern side, the seas were on the northern side. Now, as the apogee has moved to the northern side and the perigee to the southern side, the seas have moved to the southern side, and these mountains remained on the northern side.'" This is the sum of their discourse on this matter, and it is weak in several respects:

The first: the occurrence of clay in the sea is a general matter, and the sun's falling upon it is a general matter. So why would this mountain join in some regions and not others?

The second: we observe in some mountains that those rocks are placed in layers upon layers, as if the structure were many bricks placed one upon another. It is far-fetched that such a composition would come about from the cause they mention.

The third: the apogee of the sun now is near the beginning of al-Saratān (Cancer). Accordingly, since the time when the apogee of the sun moved to the northern side, about nine thousand years have passed. By this reckoning, the mountains during this long period would have been crumbling, so that no stone should remain. But that is not the case. So we know that the cause they mention is weak.

The second aspect of the argument from the conditions of the mountains for the existence of the Creator, Possessor of majesty: what arises in them of the mines of the seven base metals (fiddhiz) and the places of precious jewels; and there arise in them mines of vitriols (zājāt) and salts, and there arise in them mines of naphtha, pitch and sulphur. So the earth being one in nature, the mountain being one in its disposition, and the influence of the sun being one upon all of them, clearly indicates that the whole is by the decree of a Powerful, Dominating Creator, exalted above resemblance to created and contingent things.

The third aspect of the argument from the conditions of the mountains: that by means of them rivers are generated upon the surface of the earth. That is because stone is a solid body. When vapours rise from the depths of the earth and reach the mountain, they are held back there and continue to accumulate, so that vast waters form beneath the mountain. Then, because of their abundance and force, they break through and flow out upon the surface of the earth. Thus the benefit of mountains in generating rivers is from this aspect. For this reason, in most cases wherever Allah mentions the mountains He joins with them the mention of rivers, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And We placed therein lofty firm mountains, and We gave you sweet water to drink﴾ [al-Mursalat: 27].

* * *

[Page 5]

The third type of the proofs mentioned in this verse: the argument from the wondrous creation of plants, to which He refers in His saying ﴿and of all fruits He made therein two mates, two﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: when a seed is placed in the earth and the moisture of the earth affects it, it swells and grows, and by this its top and bottom split. From the upper split emerges the tree rising into the air, and from the lower split emerge the roots plunging into the depths of the earth. This is among the wonders, because the nature of that seed is one, and the influence of the natures, the spheres and the stars upon it is one. Then from the upper side of that seed there comes forth a body rising into the air, and from its lower side a body sinking into the earth. It is impossible that two opposite natures should arise from one nature. So we know that this came about by the disposal of the Wise Administrator and the Ancient Determiner, not by the cause of nature and property. Then the tree that springs from that seed: some of it becomes wood, some of it becomes blossom, and some of it becomes fruit. Then that fruit too contains bodies of differing natures. The walnut has four kinds of shells: the outer shell, beneath it the woody shell, beneath that the shell enclosing the kernel, and beneath that shell another shell of extreme thinness, which is distinguished from what is above it while the walnut is fresh. Also, in a single fruit there may be differing natures: the citron (utruj) — its rind is hot and dry, its flesh is hot and moist, its juice (humad) is cold and dry, its seed is hot and dry, and its blossom is hot and dry. Likewise the grape — its skin and its pip are both cold and dry, while its flesh and its water are both hot and moist. So the generation of these differing natures from one seed, with the influences of the natures and of the stars and spheres being equal, must be due to the arrangement of the Wise, Powerful, Ancient One.

The second issue: the meaning of "two mates, two" is: two kinds, two. The difference may be in respect of taste, such as sweet and sour; or in nature, such as hot and cold; or in colour, such as white and black.

If it is said: "A pair must necessarily be two; so what is the point of His saying ﴿two mates, two﴾?"

We reply: It has been said that when Allah first created the world and created trees in it, He created from each kind only two, no more. Had He said "He created two mates," it would not have been known whether the intended meaning was the type or the individual. But when He said "two," we know that Allah, when He first created from each thing, created two, no fewer and no more. The summary is that the people now are many, but when they began from two mates, the individuals Adam and Eve, so likewise is the case with all trees and crops. And Allah knows best.

The fourth type of the proofs mentioned in this verse: the argument from the conditions of night and day, to which He refers in His saying ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾. The intended meaning is that the favour is not complete except by night and day and their succession, as He said: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day to give sight﴾ [al-Isra': 12], and from it His saying: ﴿He covers the night with the day, which pursues it swiftly﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. The full exposition of this has already passed earlier in this book.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read [yughashshi] with the doubled shin and a fatḥa on the ghayn; the rest read it without doubling.

Then, when He mentioned these luminous proofs and compelling decisive signs, He said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾.

Know that wherever He mentions proofs existing in the lower world, He usually mentions after them: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾, or something close to it in meaning. The reason is that the philosophers attribute the events of the lower world to the variations occurring in the stellar configurations. So unless proof is established to repel this objection, the intended purpose is not complete. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾, as if He, exalted is He, were saying: "The field of reflection remains open; after this position there must be reflection and contemplation for the argument to be complete."

Know that the answer to this objection is in two aspects:

The first: We say, suppose you attribute the events of the lower world to celestial conditions and stellar connections. Nevertheless, we have established a decisive proof that the particular attributes of each of the celestial bodies, its nature, its position and its property, must come by the specification of the Ancient Determiner and the Wise Administrator. Thus this objection falls away. This answer has been established by Allah, exalted is He, in this context, for He began with mentioning the celestial proofs, and we have shown how they indicate the existence of the Creator, and then He followed them with the terrestrial proofs.

If someone says: "Why could these terrestrial events not be due to the celestial conditions?" our answer is: Suppose the matter is so; nevertheless, we have shown earlier the dependence of the celestial bodies upon the Wise Creator. Then this objection does not undermine our purpose.

The second part of the answer: we shall establish the proof that it is not possible for the occurrence of terrestrial events to be due to celestial conjunctions (al-ittisalat al-falakiyya). This is what is mentioned in the verse that comes after this verse. Whoever reflects upon these subtleties and comprehends them will know that this Book includes the sciences of the first and the last (ʿulum al-awwalin wa-l-akhirin).

﴿وفِي الأرْضِ قِطَعٌ مُتَجاوِراتٌ وجَنّاتٌ مِن أعْنابٍ وزَرْعٌ ونَخِيلٌ صِنْوانٌ وغَيْرُ صِنْوانٍ يُسْقى بِماءٍ واحِدٍ ونُفَضِّلُ بَعْضَها عَلى بَعْضٍ في الأُكُلِ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾.

Issues in the verse:

First issue: The aim of this verse is to establish the proof that the occurrence of events in this world cannot be due to celestial conjunctions (al-ittisalat al-falakiyyah) and planetary movements (al-harakat al-kawkabiyyah). The argument is presented in two ways.

The first: On the earth there are plots of land that differ in their nature and essence, yet they are adjacent to one another. Some are saline (sabakhah, salt-laden), some are loose, some are hard, some are fertile, some are stony or sandy, and some are sticky clay. Yet they are adjacent, and the influence of the sun and of the rest of the stars upon these plots is the same. This shows that their differing qualities are by the decree of the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful.

The second: A single plot of land is watered with one water, so the influence of the sun upon it is uniform, yet the fruits that come forth differ in taste, colour, nature and property. Indeed, you may take a cluster of grapes in which all the berries are sweet and ripe except a single berry, which has remained sour and dry. We know by necessity that the relation of natures and spheres to all of them is the same. Indeed, we may say that there is something even more wondrous than this: in some varieties of rose, one of its two faces is intensely red while the other is intensely black, although that rose is extremely thin and delicate. It is inconceivable to say that the influence of the sun reached one of its edges and not the other. This clearly indicates, with certainty, that the whole is by the arrangement of the free and choosing Agent, not by the cause of celestial conjunctions. This is what is meant by His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿يُسْقى بِماءٍ واحِدٍ ونُفَضِّلُ بَعْضَها عَلى بَعْضٍ في الأُكُلِ﴾. This is the complete discussion of the explanation, elucidation and clarification of this proof.

Know that with the mention of this answer the proof is complete. These lower events necessarily have an agent (mu'aththir). We have demonstrated that this agent is not the stars, the spheres, or the natures. At this point it must be affirmed with certainty that there is necessarily another agent apart from these things. Here the argument is complete, and no room for further reflection remains after it. For this reason He says here: ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, because there is no way to dispute this proof except by saying that these lower events came into being without any agent whatsoever. That would impair the perfection of the intellect, since knowledge of the contingent's need for a originator (muhdith), being a necessary knowledge (ilm darури), means that the failure to attain this knowledge is a defect in the perfection of the intellect. Therefore He says: ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, and in the preceding verse He said: ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾. These subtleties are precious secrets of the science of the Qur'an, and we ask the Mighty God to make understanding them a means of attaining mercy and forgiveness.

Second issue: His words ﴿وفِي الأرْضِ قِطَعٌ مُتَجاوِراتٌ﴾. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: A land close to another land is one good land, and another is saline, another is a harrah (volcanic stony ground), another is sandy, another is gravelly, another is red, and another is black. In sum, the variation of the regions of the earth in elevation and depression, in natures and properties, is a known matter. In some codices it reads [قِطَعًا مُتَجاوِراتٍ], and the implied meaning is: "He placed in it firm mountains and placed on the earth adjacent plots."

As for His words ﴿وجَنّاتٌ مِن أعْنابٍ وزَرْعٌ ونَخِيلٌ﴾, we say: the jannah (garden) is the orchard in which there are palm trees, vines and crops, and those trees surround it. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿جَعَلْنا لِأحَدِهِما جَنَّتَيْنِ مِن أعْنابٍ وحَفَفْناهُما بِنَخْلٍ وجَعَلْنا بَيْنَهُما زَرْعًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 32].

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿وزَرْعٌ ونَخِيلٌ صِنْوانٌ وغَيْرُ صِنْوانٍ﴾ all in the nominative (raf'), as a conjunction to His words [وجَنّاتٌ]. The rest read them in the genitive (jarr), as a conjunction to "al-a'nab" (grapes). Hafs from 'Asim, in the transmission of al-Qawwas, reads [صُنْوانٍ] with a damma on the sad, while the rest read it with a kasra. Both are dialectal variants. Al-sinwan is the plural of sinw, like qinwan and qinw; it is also pluralised as asna', like ism and asma'. When they become numerous it is called al-sinniy, and al-sinniy may be pronounced with a kasra or fatha on the sad. The sinw is when the root is one and two or three or more palm trees grow from it; each one is a sinw. Tha'lab reported from Ibn al-A'rabi: al-sinw means "the like," and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Verily, a man's paternal uncle is the sinw of his father," meaning his equal.

Having understood this, we say: if we explain sinw by the first explanation, the meaning is: among palm trees are those that grow from one root, two or more trees, and among them are those that do not. If we explain it by the second explanation, the meaning is: palm trees may be similar and alike, and they may not be so.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿يُسْقى بِماءٍ واحِدٍ﴾. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read [يُسْقى] with the ya', on the presumption of "yusqa kulluhu" (all of it is watered), or to give precedence to the masculine over the feminine. The rest read it with the ta', in agreement with His words [جَنّاتٍ]. Abu 'Amr said: What bears witness to the feminine is His saying: ﴿ونُفَضِّلُ بَعْضَها عَلى بَعْضٍ في الأُكُلِ﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read [يُفَضِّلُ] with the ya', as a conjunction to His words [يُدَبِّرُ، ويُفَصِّلُ، ويُغْشِي]. The rest read it with the nun, on the presumption of "wa-nahnu nufaddilu" (and We favour).

As for ﴿فِي الأُكُلِ﴾, there are two views, related by al-Wahidi. He related from al-Zajjaj that al-ukul is the fruit that is eaten, and he related from others that al-ukul is what is prepared for eating. I say: the latter is more appropriate, because of His words, exalted be He, describing the Garden: ﴿أُكُلُها دائِمٌ﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], which is general to all edibles. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read "al-ukl" with a sukun on the kaf throughout the Qur'an, while the rest read it with a damma on the kaf. Both are dialectal variants.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 13, verse 5:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; those have shackles around their necks; and those are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein forever.﴾

There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the compelling proofs for what is needed in knowing the Originator, He then mentioned the matter of the Return, saying: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾. On this there are several views:

The first view: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "If you are amazed at their denying you, after they had judged that you are truthful, then that is amazing."

The second: "If you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their worshipping what can neither benefit them nor harm them, after they have recognized the proofs indicating Tawhid (the oneness of Allah), then that is amazing."

The third: The sense of the statement is: "If you are amazed, O Muhammad, then you are amazed at a point deserving of amazement. For when they acknowledged that He, exalted is He, is the Governor of the heavens and the earth and the Creator of all creatures, and that He is the One who raised the heavens without pillars, who subjected the sun and the moon to the benefit of the servants, and who manifested in the world all kinds of wonders and marvels, then whoever has power sufficient for these great things, how could his power not be sufficient for returning a human being after his death? For the one who is capable of the stronger and more perfect is more fitting to be capable of the weaker and lesser. This is the explanation of the point of amazement."

Then, after He, exalted is He, related this statement, He passed three judgments upon them:

First: His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord﴾. This indicates that everyone who denies the Resurrection and the Last Day is a disbeliever. The denial of the Resurrection necessarily entails disbelief in their Lord, because denying the Resurrection is not complete except by denying power, knowledge, and truthfulness. As for denying power: this is like saying that the God of the world is a necessitating cause by its essence and not an agent by choice, so He is not able to restore; or it is said that although He is capable, He is not fully capable, so He cannot create living beings except through the two parents and the influences of natures and spheres. As for denying knowledge: this is like saying that He, exalted is He, does not know particulars, so He cannot distinguish this obedient one from the disobedient. As for denying truthfulness: this is like saying that although He gives information about it, He will not do it, because lying is permissible for Him. Since all of these are disbelief, it is established that denying the Resurrection is disbelief in Allah.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿And those have shackles around their necks﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "What is meant by the shackles is their disbelief, their humiliation, and their submission to the idols. Its parallel is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8]. The poet said:

*For them, away from right guidance, are shackles and fetters.*

And it is said of a man: 'This is a shackle around your neck for the bad deed,' meaning: it is binding upon you and you will be recompensed for it with punishment." The judge (al-Qadi) said: "Although this is possible, taking the words in their literal sense is more appropriate." I say: The view of al-Asamm can be supported by the fact that [p. 9] the apparent meaning of the verse requires that the shackles be in their necks at present, and that is not the case. You take the wording to mean that this meaning will occur, while we take it to mean that it is occurring now, except that what is meant by the shackles is what we have mentioned. So each of us departs from the literal meaning in some respect. Why, then, is your view more appropriate than ours?

The second view: What is meant is that Allah, exalted is He, will place the shackles around their necks on the Day of Resurrection. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks and the chains; they will be dragged, into the boiling water, then in the Fire they will be kindled﴾ [Ghafir: 71–72].

The third attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein forever﴾. What is meant by it is a warning of punishment that is everlasting and perpetual. Our companions, may Allah have mercy on them, used this verse as evidence that everlasting punishment is only for the disbelievers. They said: His saying ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾ indicates that they are the ones described as abiding forever, and no one else; and that indicates that the people of major sins will not abide forever in the Fire.

**The second issue:** The theologians (al-Mutakallimun) said: amazement is that whose cause is not known, and that is impossible with respect to Allah, exalted is He. So the meaning is: "And if you are amazed, then it is amazing in your view."

One may say: Some read the other verse by attributing amazement to Allah Himself, exalted is He. In that case it must be interpreted, and we have explained that such expressions must be purified of the beginnings of accidents (a'rad) and interpreted in terms of their ultimate ends. For when a human being is amazed at something, he denies it, so this is understood as denial.

**The third issue:** The readers differed regarding His saying: ﴿Shall we, when we are dust, indeed be in a new creation?﴾ and similar expressions, when they take the form of interrogation in the first and second parts. Some combine the two interrogatives in both words, and they are Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Hamzah. Then these differed: Ibn Kathir uses a single interrogative hamzah but does not prolong it; Abu 'Amr uses an elongated interrogative hamzah in which he prolongs; and Hamzah and 'Asim use two hamzahs throughout the Qur'an. Others do not combine the two interrogatives. Then they differed: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Kisa'i use the interrogative in the first and read it as a statement in the second; Ibn 'Amir reads it as a statement in the first and an interrogative in the second. Then these differed from another angle: Nafi' uses a non-elongated hamzah, while Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i use two hamzahs. As for Nafi', he does the same except in al-Saffat; and likewise Ibn 'Amir, except in al-Waqi'ah; and likewise al-Kisa'i, except in al-'Ankabut and al-Saffat.

**The fourth issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The governing element in ﴿Shall we, when we are dust﴾ is omitted, its estimated sense being: "Shall we, when we are dust, be raised?" and what follows indicates the omitted element.

[Page 10]

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them. Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾

Know that he (ﷺ) used to threaten them sometimes with the punishment of the Resurrection and sometimes with the punishment of this world. Whenever he threatened them with the punishment of the Resurrection, the people denied the Resurrection, the raising, the gathering and the scattering, which is what was mentioned earlier in the first verse. Whenever he threatened them with the punishment of this world, they would say to him: "Then bring this punishment," and they demanded that he make it appear and descend, by way of mocking it and showing that what he said had no basis. For this reason, Allah related about them that they ask the Messenger to hasten the evil before the good. By "the evil" here is meant the descent of punishment upon them, as Allah, the Exalted, said about them: ﴿Then rain down upon us stones﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and in His words: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ (al-Isra: 90), up to His words: ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ (al-Isra: 92). They only said that out of mockery toward what the Messenger had mentioned. He (ﷺ) used to promise them, for belief, reward in the Hereafter and the attainment of victory and triumph in this world. The people asked him for the descent of punishment and did not ask him for the attainment of victory and triumph. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾. Some commentators interpreted "the good" here as respite and delay. They called the punishment "evil" only because it harms them and afflicts them.

As for His words: ﴿though exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾, know that the Arabs say: "al-'uqubah is mathulah and mathlah, like ṣadqah and ṣadqah." The first form (mathulah) is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the second (mathlah) is the dialect of Tamim. Whoever says mathulah, its plural is mathulat, and whoever says mathlah, its plural is mathlat and muthlath with the letter thā' sukun. This is what al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj related. Ibn al-Anbari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: al-muthlah is a punishment that is clearly manifested upon the one punished, a change by which the form remains ugly, and it comes from the saying of the people: "Fulan mathhala by Fulan" when he disfigured his form, whether by cutting off his ear or his nose, or by gouging out his eyes, or by splitting open his belly. This is the original meaning. Then the lasting shame and the enduring disgrace are also called muthlah.

Al-Wahidi said: The origin of this word is from al-mithl, which is resemblance. Since the original purpose of punishment is that it should resemble and match the one punished, it was necessarily named by this name. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read as [al-muthulat] with two ḍammahs, by assimilating the fā' to the 'ayn, and [al-mathlat] with a fatḥah on the mīm and sukun on the thā', as one says al-samurah (with a ḍammah), and [al-muthlat] with a ḍammah on the mīm and sukun on the thā' is a lightened form of al-muthulat with two ḍammahs. Al-muthlat is the plural of muthlah, like rukbah and rukbat.

Having known this, we say: the meaning of the verse is: "They ask you to hasten the punishment which We have not hastened upon them, though they know what Our punishments descended upon the past nations, yet they did not take heed from them." It would have been fitting for the fear of that to deter them from disbelief, by taking a lesson from the condition of those who came before.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾, know that our companions (the Ash'aris) held fast to this verse as proof that Allah, the Exalted, may pardon the one who commits a major sin (kabirah) before repentance (tawbah). The way of deriving evidence from it is that His words: ﴿full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ mean "while they are engaged in wrongdoing," just as one says: "I saw the amir while (ʿalā) his eating," meaning while he was engaged in eating. This requires that Allah, the Exalted, forgives mankind while they are engaged in wrongdoing. It is known that the state of a person engaged in wrongdoing is not a state of repentance. Thus this shows that Allah, the Exalted, may forgive a sin before the person engages in repentance. Then we say: this proof was set aside regarding the people of disbelief, so it must remain applicable regarding the people of major sins, which is what was sought. Or we say: Allah, the Exalted, did not limit Himself to His words ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾, but mentioned with it His words ﴿and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾. Therefore the first must be understood as referring to the people of major sins, and the second must be understood as referring to the states of the disbelievers.

[Page 11]

If it is said: Why could it not be that the intended meaning is: "full of forgiveness for the people of minor sins (ṣaghirah), because their punishment is expiating"? Then we say: why could it not be that the intended meaning is: "Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness when they repent, and He, the Exalted, only delays punishment to give them respite to come to repentance; so if they repent, He is full of forgiveness for them, and from this forgiveness is the postponement of the punishment until the Hereafter." Indeed, we say: it is obligatory to interpret the wording this way, because when the people asked for the hastening of punishment, the answer given in it must be understood as the postponement of punishment, so that the answer matches the question. Then we say: why could it not be that the intended meaning is: "Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness," meaning that He, the Exalted, only delays the punishment to give them respite to come to repentance; so if they repent, He is full of forgiveness, and even if their wrongdoing is great and they do not repent, He is severe in punishment?

As for the answer to the first objection: the postponement of punishment is not called forgiveness, for otherwise it would have to be said that all the disbelievers are forgiven because Allah postponed their punishment until the Hereafter. As for the second: He, the Exalted, praised Himself with this, and praise is only attained through grace (tafaḍḍul), whereas by the performance of an obligation there is no praise in it; and according to you, the forgiveness of minor sins is obligatory. As for the third: we have shown that the apparent meaning of the verse requires the attainment of forgiveness during the state of wrongdoing, and we have shown that the state of wrongdoing prevents the attainment of repentance. Thus these objections fall away, and what we have mentioned is correct.

**The Qur'an:** ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related that the disbelievers attacked his prophethood first by denying resurrection and gathering. Second, they attacked his prophethood by disputing the truth of what he warned them of, namely the descent of the punishment of annihilation (*isti'sal*). Third, they attacked his prophethood by demanding from him a miracle and a clear proof, and this is what is mentioned in this verse.

Know that the reason for this is that they denied that the Qur'an belongs to the category of miracles. They said: "This is a book like other books. A person producing a particular composition and a particular book is not a miracle at all. A miracle is only something like the miracles of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both."

Know that some people claimed that no miracle other than the Qur'an appeared as proof of the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. They said: "This statement is valid only if they challenged the Qur'an being a miracle, yet no other kind of miracle appeared through him. For if another kind of miracle had appeared at his hand, they could not have said: ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ This shows that he, peace be upon him, had no miracle other than the Qur'an."

Know that the answer to this is in two respects:

The first: Perhaps what they meant was a demand for miracles other than those they had witnessed from him, peace and blessings be upon him, such as the trunk of the palm tree moaning, water gushing from between his fingers, and feeding a large crowd with a little food. So they demanded from him compelling miracles other than these, such as splitting the sea with a staff and turning a staff into a serpent.

If it is asked: "What is the reason that Allah, exalted is He, withheld them and did not give them what they asked for?"

We say: When He displayed one miracle, the purpose was accomplished, so demanding the rest would be arbitrary. Moreover, the Qur'an is itself a miracle, so there was no need for all the other miracles. Furthermore, perhaps Allah, exalted is He, knew that they would persist in obstinacy even after those demanded miracles appeared, and that they would then deserve the punishment of annihilation. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, did not give them what they asked for. Allah, exalted is He, has explained this in His saying: ﴿Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And had He made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse﴾ [al-Anfal: 23]. This shows that He did not give them what they asked for because He knew they would not benefit from it. Also, opening this door leads to endless consequences: whenever he brought a miracle, another person would come and demand from him yet another miracle, and this would entail the invalidation of the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, which is false.

The second answer: Perhaps the disbelievers made this statement before witnessing the other miracles. Then, when He, exalted is He, related the disbelievers' statement, He said: ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The reciters agreed on the tanwin (nunation) in His saying ﴿hadin﴾ (a guide) and on deleting the *ya'* in connected speech (*wasl*), but they differed regarding pausing (*waqf*). Ibn Kathir recited with pausing on the *ya'*, while the rest recited without the *ya'*. This is the transmission of Ibn Fulayh from Ibn Kathir, for ease of pronunciation.

The second issue: There are several interpretations of this verse:

The first: The meaning is that the Messenger, peace be upon him, is a warner to his people and a clarifier for them, and that for every people before him there was a guide, a warner, and a caller. He, exalted is He, equalized all of them in displaying a miracle, but each people had a particular path, for which they deserved that particular miracle. When the prevailing concern in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, was magic, he made his miracle something closer to their way. When the prevailing concern in the time of Jesus, peace be upon him, was medicine, he made his miracle something of the same kind as that field, namely bringing the dead to life and healing the blind and the leper. When the prevailing concern in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, was eloquence and rhetoric, he made his miracle something suitable for that time, namely the eloquence of the Qur'an. Since the Arabs did not believe in this miracle even though it was most suited to their natures, they would be even less likely to believe when other miracles were displayed. This is what al-Qadi established, and it is the correct interpretation, the one with which the statement remains coherent.

The second: The meaning is that they do not deny that the Qur'an is a miracle, so do not let your heart be constricted because of them. "You are only a warner"; so your duty is only to warn until faith enters their hearts, and you have no power over them. "And for every people there is a guide," who is capable of guiding them by creating guidance in them, and He is Allah, glorified and exalted. So the meaning is: you have only warning, while guidance is from Allah, exalted is He.

Know that the literalist exegetes (*ahl al-zahir*) mentioned several opinions here:

The first: "The warner" and "the guide" are one and the same thing. The meaning is: "You are only a warner, and for every people there is a separate warner," and the miracle of each one of them is different from the miracle of the other.

The second: The warner is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and the guide is Allah, exalted is He. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak.

The third: The warner is the Prophet, and the guide is Ali. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, placed his hand on his chest and said: 'I am the warner.' Then he pointed to the shoulder of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: 'You are the guide, O Ali. Through you those who are guided will be guided after me.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 8–10:

Page 13

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is in measure.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾ ﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals speech or speaks it aloud, and whether one hides by night or goes forth freely by day.﴾

In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the connection of the verse (wajh al-nazm), there are several opinions.

The first: when He, exalted is He, related about them that they asked for other signs besides what the Messenger (ﷺ) had brought, He made clear that He is knowing of all things known. He knows from their state whether they asked for the other sign for guidance and seeking clarification, or for the sake of obstinacy and stubbornness; and whether they would benefit from the appearance of those signs, or their insistence and arrogance would increase. So if Allah, exalted is He, knew that they asked for that for the sake of guidance, seeking clarification and greater benefit, He would have manifested it and not withheld it from them. But since He, exalted is He, knew that they said that only for the sake of pure stubbornness, He undoubtedly withheld it from them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ [Yunus: 20] and His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the signs are only with Allah."﴾ [al-An'am: 109].

The second: the connection of the verse is that when He said: ﴿But if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾ regarding the denial of resurrection, that is because they denied resurrection on the basis that the parts of the bodies of living beings, when they are scattered and crumbled, mix with one another and distinction is not preserved. So He made clear that the distinction is not preserved only with respect to one who does not know all things known; but as for one who knows all things known, He preserves those parts such that some of them are distinguished from others. Then He argued for His being knowing of all things known by saying that He knows what every female bears and what the wombs diminish.

The third: this is connected to His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾, and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is knowing of all things known, so He sends down punishment only according to what He knows to be beneficial. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: the word "mā" in His saying: ﴿what every female bears and what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾ is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) or a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah). If it is a relative pronoun, the meaning is: He knows what she bears of offspring, of which category it is: whether male or female, complete or incomplete, good or bad, tall or short, and other states present in it or awaited.

Then He said: ﴿and what the wombs diminish﴾. The ghayḍ (diminishing) is decrease, whether intransitive or transitive. It is said: ghāḍa al-mā' (the water decreased) and ghiḍtuhu anā (I decreased it). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the water was made to subside﴾ [Hud: 44]. The meaning of the verse is "what the wombs diminish of it," but the returning pronoun has been omitted. And His saying: ﴿and what they increase﴾ means what they take as an increase. You say: "I took my right from him and I took from him such-and-such extra."
