Thus this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is described by complete knowledge and perfect power, and is exalted above everything unbefitting, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable of the resurrection they denied, of the signs they demanded, and of the punishment they hastened; and that He only delays that according to the divine will in the view of some, and according to wisdom in the view of others. Ibn Kathir read [al-Mutaʿālī] with the yā' affirmed in both pause and continuation, following the original form, while the rest omitted the yā' in both states for lightness.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, emphasized the explanation of His being knowing of all known things, saying: ﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals speech or speaks it aloud, and whether one hides by night or goes forth freely by day﴾. In this there are issues:

The first issue: the word [sawāʾun] requires two things; you say: "Zayd and ʿAmr are equal (sawāʾun)." Then there are two opinions:

The first: that sawāʾ is a verbal noun, and the meaning is "possessor of equality," as you say: "Zayd and ʿAmr are just (ʿadl)," meaning possessors of justice.

The second: that sawāʾ is in the sense of "equal" (mustawin). According to this reading, there is no need for an implied element, except that Sibawayh disliked saying "equal Zayd and ʿAmr," because when active participles are indefinite they are not begun with.

One may say: rather this view is preferable, because interpreting the statement this way avoids the need for an implied element, which is contrary to the basic principle.

The second issue: concerning the one who hides (al-mustakhfī) and the one who goes forth (al-sārib), there are two opinions:

The first opinion: it is said: akhfaytu al-shay' ukhfīhi ikhfā'an, so khafiya and istakhfā fulān min fulān, meaning he hid and concealed himself. As for His saying: ﴿and one who goes forth freely by day﴾, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: he is apparent by day in his sarb, that is, his path. It is said: khalā lahu sarbuhu, meaning his path was clear for him. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs say sarabat al-ibil yasrubu saraban, meaning the camels went on the earth openly wherever they wished. When you know this, the meaning of the verse is: whether a person is hidden in darknesses or is visible on the roads, Allah's knowledge encompasses all of it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is the same whether what hearts conceal or what tongues express. Mujahid said: it is the same whether one who commits abominations in the darkness of nights or one who does them openly in broad daylight in succession.

The second opinion: al-Wahidi transmitted from al-Akhfash and Qutrub that he said: al-mustakhfī is the manifest one, and al-sārib is the one who is hidden. From this it is said: khafaytu al-shay' and akhfaytuhu, meaning I brought it out (into the open). And ikhtafaytu al-shay' means I extracted it. The grave-robber is called al-mustakhfī, and the one who hides is called al-sārib, and from this one who enters is called sarab, and the sarab are wild animals when they enter the sirb, that is, their hiding place. Al-Wahidi said: this opinion is sound in the language, but the preferred one is the first, due to the consensus of most exegetes upon it; and also, night indicates concealment, while day indicates manifestness and spreading.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For him there are successive angels before and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah. Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah wills misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector besides Him.﴾

Know that the pronoun in "lahu" (for him) refers back to "man" in His saying: ﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals speech or declares it openly﴾. It has also been said that it refers to the name of Allah in ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The meaning is: for Allah there are successive angels (mu'aqqibat). As for the word mu'aqqibat, its original form may be mu'taqibat, with the taa' assimilated into the qaf, as in His saying: ﴿And those who make excuses (al-mu'adhdhirun) among the Bedouins came﴾ [al-Tawbah: 90], where what is meant is al-mu'tadhirun (those who make excuses). It may also be derived from "a'qabahu", when one comes after another's heels; the name al-mu'aqqib of everything is that which follows and comes after what preceded it. The meaning in both readings is one.

Having understood this, we say: concerning what is meant by the mu'aqqibat there are two opinions.

The first, which is the well-known one held by the majority, is that what is meant by them is the guarding angels (al-hafazah). Their being described as mu'aqqibat is either because the angels of the night follow the angels of the day and vice versa, or because they follow the deeds of the servants, guarding and recording them after them. Anyone who performs an action and then returns to it has "'aqqaba". On this view, what is meant by the mu'aqqibat is the angels of the night and the angels of the day. It is narrated from Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about the servant: how many angels are with him?" He (ﷺ) said: "There is an angel on your right who records the good deeds, and he is the trustworthy one over the one on the left. When you do a good deed, it is recorded as ten. When you do a bad deed, the one on the left says to the companion on the right: 'Shall I record?' He says: 'No, perhaps he will repent.' When he says it three times, he says: 'Yes, record it. May Allah relieve us of him! Evil is the companion who has so little regard for Allah the Exalted and so little shame before us.' And there are two angels before you and behind you, and this is His saying: ﴿For him there are successive angels before and behind him﴾. And there is an angel holding your forelock: if you humble yourself before your Lord, He raises you, and if you become arrogant, He breaks you. And there are two angels on your lips guarding for you the prayers upon me. And an angel over your mouth who does not leave off preventing the serpent from entering your mouth. And two angels over your eyes. These are ten angels over every son of Adam. The angels of the night are replaced by the angels of the day, so there are twenty angels over every son of Adam." And from him (ﷺ): "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Fajr prayer and the 'Asr prayer." This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And the recitation at dawn; indeed the recitation at dawn is witnessed﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. It was said: the angels of the night ascend, and they are ten, and the angels of the day descend. Ibn Jurayj said: this is like His saying: ﴿One seated on the right and one on the left﴾ [Qaf: 17]: the companion on the right records the good deeds, and the one on the left records the bad deeds. Mujahid said: there is no servant but that he has an angel guarding him from the jinn, mankind and the vermin, in his sleep and in his waking.

There are questions concerning the verse.

The first question: angels are male, so why did He use the feminine plural form mu'aqqibat for them?

The answer: there are two opinions.

The first: al-Farra' said: the mu'aqqibat are males, being the plural of mu'aqqibah (feminine) of angels, and then mu'aqqibah was made plural as mu'aqqibat, just as it is said: "ibna'wat Sa'd" and "rijalat Bakr", the plural of rijal. What indicates the masculine is His saying: ﴿who guard him﴾ (yahfazunahu).

The second, which is the view of al-Akhfash: it is feminine only because of the frequency of this from them, like: nassabah (one who is very skilled in genealogy) and 'allamah (very learned), and it is masculine.

The second question: what is meant by those mu'aqqibat being before him and behind him?

The answer: the one who hides by night and the one who walks openly by day is surrounded by these mu'aqqibat, who count his deeds and words in their entirety, and not a single one of those deeds and words escapes their guarding at all. Some have said: rather, what is meant is that they guard him from all ruin, from before him and from behind him, because the one who walks openly by day, when he strives in his affairs, is only wary of what is before him and behind him.

The third question: what is meant by His saying: ﴿by the command of Allah﴾?

The answer: al-Farra' mentioned two opinions concerning it.

The first opinion: it is by way of inversion, and the sense is: for him there are mu'aqqibat from the command of Allah, guarding him.

The second opinion: there is an ellipsis in it, i.e., that guarding is from the command of Allah, i.e., from what Allah has commanded, so the subject is omitted and its predicate kept, as "two thousand" is written on a bag, meaning the contents of which are two thousand.

The third opinion: mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, that the word "min" (from) has the meaning of "bi" (by), and the sense is: they guard him by the command of Allah and by His help. The proof that one must come to this view is that the angels, and no one of creation, have no power to guard anyone from the command of Allah and from what He has decreed for him.

The fourth question: what is the benefit in appointing these angels to be entrusted with us?

The answer: this statement is not far-fetched, because the astrologers agree that the management of each day belongs to a separate planet, and likewise for each night. Undoubtedly those planets have spirits according to them, so those different managements are in reality for those spirits. The same applies to the management of the Moon, the hayyaj and the kadkhuda, according to what the astrologers say. As for the practitioners of talismans, this statement is well known on their tongues, and for this reason you find them saying: "The complete natural spirit informed me." By "the complete natural spirit" they mean that every human has a celestial spirit that takes charge of the proper handling of his affairs and the repelling of his calamities and afflictions. And if this is agreed upon among the early philosophers and the practitioners of judgments, how can its coming through the Shari'ah be considered unlikely? The full verification of this is that human spirits differ in their substances and natures: some are good, some are evil, some are honored, some are abased, some are strong in domination and authority, and some are weak and contemptible. Just as the matter is so with human spirits, so it is with celestial spirits. Undoubtedly celestial spirits are stronger than human spirits in every respect and every attribute. Each group of human spirits shares a particular nature and a specific attribute, because they are nurtured by a celestial spirit resembling it in nature and property, and those human spirits are as if they were children of that celestial spirit. Whenever this is the case, that celestial spirit helps them in their affairs, guides them to their interests, and protects them from kinds of afflictions. This is a statement mentioned by the verifying philosophers. And if the matter is so, we know that what the Shari'ah has brought is accepted by all, so how can it be denied from the Shari'ah? Furthermore, in the singling out of these angels and their dominion over the children of Adam there are many benefits beyond those previously mentioned.

The first: the devils call to evils and sins, while these angels call to good deeds and acts of obedience.

The second: Mujahid said: there is no servant but that he has with him an angel guarding him from the jinn, mankind and the vermin, in his sleep and in his waking.

The third: we see that a person may have a strong motive arise in his heart without any cause, and then it becomes clear in the end that the arising of that motive in his heart was a cause of his interests and goods; and it may also become clear in the end that it was a cause of his falling into calamity or sin. So it becomes evident that the caller to the first matter was desiring good and ease, and the caller to the second was desiring corruption and trial. The first is the guiding angel, and the second is the misleading devil.

The fourth: when a person knows that the angels record his deeds, he is closer to beware of sins, because whoever believes in the sublimity of the angels and the loftiness of their ranks, when he attempts to commit a sin and believes they are witnessing it, shame before them restrains him from undertaking it, just as it restrains him when a human preacher is present to admonish him. And when he knows that the angels count those deeds against him, that too is a deterrent from them; and when he knows that the angels are writing them down, the deterrence is more complete.

The fifth question: what is the benefit in the recording of the servants' deeds? We say here there are stages:

The first stage: the interpretation of "recording" in its well-known sense of writing. The speculative theologians said: the benefit in those pages is their weighing, so that it may be known which of the two pans outweighs the other. For if the pan of good deeds outweighs, it becomes apparent to the creatures that he is among the people of Paradise, and if it is the opposite, then the opposite. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is far-fetched, because the proofs indicate that each person, before his death, at the moment of witnessing, knows whether he is among the blessed or among the wretched, so the attainment of that knowledge does not depend on the scale. Then the judge answered this objection and said: it is also not impossible, for what we have related, that by reason of his joy at the great character, it is related to his gladness at the moment of the great character that he is among the friends of Allah in Paradise; and the opposite of that concerns the enemies of Allah.

The second stage: the statement of the sages of Islam that writing is a reference to specific markings established by convention to indicate specific meanings. So if we assume that those markings indicate those meanings by their very essences and beings, that writing would be stronger and more perfect.

Having established this, we say: when a person performs an action of the actions many times and repeatedly in succession, there arises in his soul, because of the repetition, a strong and firmly established disposition. If that disposition is one that delights in beneficial actions for spiritual felicities, his joy in them greatly increases after death; and if that disposition is one that harms in spiritual states, his harm from it greatly increases after death.

Having established this, we say: since the great repetition was a cause of the acquisition of that firmly established disposition, each of the repeated actions has an effect in the acquisition of that firmly established disposition. And although that effect is not perceptible, it is in reality present. Knowing this, it becomes clear that no glance, movement or stillness occurs to a person without there occurring in the essence of his soul an effect of the effects of happiness or the effects of wretchedness, be it little or much. This is what is meant by the recording of deeds according to these people. And Allah knows best the realities of matters.

All of this applies if we interpret His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For him there are successive angels before and behind him﴾ as referring to the angels.

The second opinion: this is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and was chosen by Abu Muslim al-Isfahani. The meaning is: that secret and open speech are equal in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, and so are the one who hides in the darkness of the night and the one who walks openly by day, relying on helpers and supporters, who are the kings and the commanders. Whoever takes refuge in the night, his affair will not escape Allah. And whoever goes about by day accompanied by the mu'aqqibat, who are the guards and the helpers who protect him, his guards will not save him from Allah the Exalted. The mu'aqqib is the helper, because when this one sees that one, that one must in turn see this one, so the insight of each of them becomes a successor to the insight of the other. These mu'aqqibat do not free anyone from the decree of Allah and His destiny, and if they think they can free their master from the command of Allah and His decree, they are absolutely unable to do so. The purpose of this statement is to rouse sultans, commanders and the great to seek deliverance from hardships through the protection and preservation of Allah, and not to rely in repelling them on helpers and supporters. For this reason, after it, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when Allah wills misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector besides Him.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 11 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves﴾, the words of all the exegetes indicate that the meaning is that He does not change the blessings they are in by sending down retribution, unless wickedness and corruption come from them. The judge (al-Qadi) said: The apparent meaning admits of nothing but this sense, because nothing that Allah, the Exalted, does apart from punishment does not begin in this world without a change proceeding from the servant beforehand, since He, the Exalted, initiates blessings, religious and worldly, and favours whom He wills over whom He wills. So what Allah the Exalted mentioned means change by destruction and punishment.

Then they differed. Some of them said that this statement refers back to His saying:
Page 19
﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾. So He, the Exalted, made clear that He does not send down the punishment of annihilation upon them except when it is known of them that they persist in disbelief and disobedience, to the point that they said: If it is known that among them there is someone who will believe, or among his descendants someone who will believe, then He, the Exalted, does not send down upon them the punishment of annihilation.

Others said: Rather, the statement runs on its general sense, and what is meant by it is that every people who have gone to extremes in corruption and altered their manner of displaying the worship of Allah the Exalted, then Allah removes blessings from them and sends down upon them kinds of punishment. Others said: The believer who is mixed among those peoples may, perhaps, be included in that punishment. It is related from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If people see the wrongdoer and do not take hold of his hands, it is about to happen that Allah the Exalted will encompass them all with punishment."

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi argued with this verse on two issues:

The first issue: that He, the Exalted, does not punish the children of polytheists for the sins of their fathers, because they have not changed the blessing that is in themselves, so that Allah would change their state from blessing to punishment.

The second issue: They said: The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of the Jabriyyah that He, the Exalted, begins the servant with misguidance and forsaking as soon as he reaches maturity, and that is greater than punishment, while there was no change from him.

The answer: The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that Allah's act of changing is posterior to the servant's act, but His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30] indicates that the servant's act is posterior to Allah's act, so a contradiction arises.

As for His saying: ﴿And when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back﴾, our companions (the Ash'aris) have argued with it that the servant is not independent in the act. They said: That is because if the servant disbelieves, there is no doubt that He, the Exalted, judges that he deserves blame in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. If the servant were independent in attaining faith, he would be able to turn back what Allah the Exalted has willed, and then His saying "there is no turning it back" would be invalid. Thus it is established that although the preceding verse suggests their doctrine, this verse is among the strongest proofs for our doctrine. Ad-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The successive angels did not avail anything." 'Ata' related from him: "There is no repeller of My punishment and no annuller of My judgment." ﴿And they have no protector other than Him﴾, meaning: they have no one besides Allah who would take charge of them and prevent Allah's decree from befalling them. The meaning is: they have no guardian who manages their affairs and prevents punishment from them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 12–13 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and who produces the heavy clouds.﴾ ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about Allah, and He is mighty in power.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, made His servants fear by sending down what cannot be turned back, He followed it with mention of these signs. They contain three matters, because they are indications of Allah's power and wisdom, and because they resemble blessings and kindness in some respects and resemble punishment and subjugation in other respects.

Page 20

Know also that He, the Exalted, mentions here four matters.

The first: the lightning, which is His saying: ﴿He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope.﴾ On this there are several issues.

First issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said, concerning the grammatical status (i'rab) of His saying ﴿as a fear and a hope﴾, there are several views:
The first: They cannot be objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for them, because they are not the act of the agent of the verb being explained, except on the assumption that a word has been omitted, i.e. "the desire of fear and hope," or in the sense of "causing fear and causing hope."
The second: They may be in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the lightning, as if it were itself fear and hope, the sense being "possessing fear and possessing hope," or in the sense of "causing fear and causing hope."
The third: That they are circumstantial states of the addressees, i.e. "fearful and hopeful."

Second issue: Concerning the lightning being fear and hope, there are several views:
The first: At the flashing of lightning, one fears the occurrence of thunderbolts and hopes for the descent of rain. Al-Mutanabbi said:
A youth like the dark cloud, who fears and hopes: he hopes for the rain from it and fears its thunderbolts.
The second: One who has harm from rain, such as a traveler, fears it, while dates and raisins are stored in his saddlebag; and one who has benefit from it hopes for it.
The third: Everything that occurs in this world is good for some people and bad for others. Likewise rain is good for one who needs it at its proper time, and bad for one whom it harms, either because of place or because of time.

Third issue: Know that the occurrence of lightning is a wondrous proof of Allah's power. Its explanation is that the cloud is undoubtedly a body composed of moist watery parts, and of airy and fiery parts. Undoubtedly the watery parts predominate in it, and water is a cold and moist body, while fire is a dry body. The appearance of an opposite from a complete opposite is contrary to reason, so there must be a choosing Creator who brings forth opposite from opposite.

If it is said: Why is it not possible to say that wind is enclosed within the body of the cloud, cold settles on its exterior so that its outer surface freezes, and then that wind tears it apart violently, so that from that violent tearing a fierce motion arises, and the fierce motion causes heat, which is the lightning?

The answer: All that you have mentioned is contrary to reason, and its explanation is in several respects:
The first: If the matter were as you say, it would necessarily follow that wherever lightning occurs, thunder—the sound produced by the tearing of the cloud—must occur as well. It is known that this is not the case, for strong lightning often occurs without any thunder.
The second: The heat produced by the strength of motion is opposed to the watery nature that causes cold. When this strong accident occurs, how does fire arise? Rather, we say: great fires are extinguished by pouring water on them, and the cloud is entirely water, so how can a weak fiery flame arise in it?
The third: According to your own doctrine, pure fire has no color at all. Suppose that fiery nature was produced through the strength of friction among the parts of the cloud; yet from where did that red color come? Thus it is established that the cause you mentioned is weak, and that the arising of fire within the body of the cloud, while it is pure water, is possible only by the power of the Powerful, the Wise.

* * *

The second type of the indications mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and He produces the heavy clouds.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Sahab" (cloud) is a collective noun whose singular is "sahabah," and "thiqal" is the plural of "thaqilah," because you say "sahabah thaqilah" and "sahab thiqal," just as you say "imra'ah karimah" and "nisa' kiram." It means laden with water.

Know that this too is one of the proofs of power and wisdom, because these watery parts either came into existence in the atmosphere of the air, or rose up from the surface of the earth. If the former, then their coming into being must be by the act of a wise, powerful originator, which is what is sought. If the latter, namely that those parts rose from the earth and, when they reached the cold layer of the air, grew cold and heavy and so returned to the earth, we say: this is false. The reason is that rains vary: sometimes the drops are large, sometimes small, sometimes close together, sometimes far apart; sometimes rain lasts a long time, sometimes briefly. The variation of rains in these attributes, while the nature of the earth is one and the nature of the sun that heats the vapors is one, necessarily requires the specification of a choosing agent. Moreover, experience has shown that supplication and humble entreaty have a great effect in the descent of rain, which is why the prayer for rain (salat al-istisqa') was legislated. Thus we know that the one who effects it is the power of the Agent, not nature and inherent property.

* * *

The third type of the indications mentioned in this verse is the thunder, which is His saying: ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him.﴾ On this there are several views.

The first view: The thunder is the name of an angel among the angels, and this audible sound is the sound of that angel glorifying and declaring God's oneness (tahlil). This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "The Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ about thunder, what is it? He said: 'It is an angel among the angels, entrusted with the clouds, with rods of fire with which he drives the clouds wherever Allah wills.' They said: 'What is the sound that we hear?' He said: 'His driving of the clouds.'" And from al-Hasan that it is a creation of Allah's creation, not an angel. According to this view, thunder is the angel entrusted with the clouds, and its sound is glorification of Allah the Exalted, and that sound is also called thunder. This is confirmed by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when he heard thunder he would say: "Glory be to the One whom it glorifies." And from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Allah produces the heavy clouds, and they speak the finest speech and laugh the finest laughter; their speech is the thunder and their laughter is the lightning."

Know that this view is not far-fetched, because according to the People of the Sunnah, bodily structure is not a condition for the occurrence of life. Therefore it is not far from Allah the Exalted to create life, knowledge, power, and speech in the parts of the cloud, so that this audible sound is an act of His. And how is that deemed unlikely when we see that the salamander arises in fire, frogs arise in cold water, and a great worm sometimes arises in ancient snows? Moreover, if the glorification of mountains in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, was not far-fetched, nor the glorification of pebbles in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, how is the glorification of clouds deemed unlikely? On this view, this thing called thunder is either an angel or not an angel, and there are two opinions on it:
One: that it is not an angel, because He joined the angels to it by saying: "and the angels, out of awe of Him," and the thing joined to is distinct from what it is joined to.
The second: that it is not far-fetched that it is of the kind of the angels, and its being mentioned separately is for the sake of honor, as in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98], and in His saying: ﴿and when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7].

The second view: The thunder is the name of this specific sound, and nevertheless the thunder glorifies Allah, the Glorified, because glorification (tasbih), sanctification (taqdis), and what is similar to them are nothing but the existence of an utterance indicating the occurrence of declaring Allah free of imperfection and sanctifying Him. Since the occurrence of this sound is a proof of the existence of a being exalted above deficiency and contingency, that is in reality glorification, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

Page 22

The third view: The meaning of the thunder being glorifying is that whoever hears the thunder glorifies Allah the Exalted, and for this reason this glorification is attributed to it.

The fourth view: From the sayings of the Sufis: the thunder is the swooning of the angels, the lightning is the sighs of their hearts, and the rain is their weeping.

If it is said: What is the reality of thunder?
We reply: We have fully discussed this in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, in His saying: ﴿therein are darknesses, and thunder, and lightning﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].

As for His saying: ﴿and the angels, out of awe of Him﴾, know that among the exegetes there are those who say: by these angels is meant the helpers of the thunder, for He, glorified is He, has appointed helpers for it. The meaning of His saying ﴿and the angels, out of awe of Him﴾ is: and the angels glorify out of fear and dread of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They fear Allah, not as the fear of the son of Adam; for one of them does not know who is on his right and who is on his left, and food, drink, or anything does not preoccupy him from the worship of Allah."

Know that the scholarly philosophers (muhaqqiqun min al-hukama') mention that these higher effects are accomplished only by spiritual celestial powers. So for the cloud there is a spirit from the celestial spirits that manages it; and likewise concerning the winds and all other higher effects. This is exactly what we related: that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies Allah. Thus what the exegetes expressed in this phrasing is what the investigating scholars cited from the philosophers. How then is it fitting for a sensible person to deny it?

* * *

The fourth type of the indications mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills.﴾ Know that we have already mentioned the meaning of thunderbolts (sawa'iq) in Surat al-Baqarah. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'ah. They came to the Prophet ﷺ, disputing with him and arguing with him, intending to kill him treacherously. Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'ah, said: "Tell us about our Lord: is He of brass or of iron?" Then when Arbad returned, He sent a thunderbolt upon him and it burned him, and He struck 'Amir with a boil like a camel's boil, and he died in the house of a woman of the Banu Salul.

Know that the matter of the thunderbolt is very wondrous, because sometimes it arises from the cloud, and when it descends from the cloud it may plunge into the sea and burn the fish in the depths of the ocean. The philosophers have exaggerated in describing its strength. The point of inference is that fire is hot and dry, and its nature is opposite to the nature of the cloud; therefore its heat and dryness should be weaker than the nature of the fires that arise among us by custom. But this is not the case, for it is the strongest fire of this world. Thus it is established that its specification with this extra strength must be due to the specification by a choosing agent.

Know that when He, the Exalted, mentioned these four indications, He said: ﴿yet they dispute about Allah﴾. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, demonstrated the proofs of His perfect knowledge in His saying: ﴿He knows what every female bears﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8], and demonstrated the proofs of perfect power in this verse.

Then He said: ﴿yet they dispute about Allah﴾, meaning: these disbelievers, despite the manifestation of these proofs, dispute about Allah. This may have several meanings:
One: that it is a refutation of the disbeliever who said: "Tell us about our Lord: is He of brass or of iron?"
Second: that it is a refutation of their disputation in denying resurrection and rejecting the gathering and raising of the dead.
Third: that it is a refutation of them in demanding all sorts of miracles.

And the fourth: that the intended meaning is a rebuttal of them regarding their demand for a punishment of annihilation (ʿadhāb al-istiʾṣāl).

Regarding this waw there are two views:

The first: that it is the waw of circumstance (li-l-ḥāl), and the meaning is: "He strikes with the thunderbolt whom He wills while they are disputing about Allah," and that is because Arbad, when he disputed about Allah, was burned by the thunderbolt.

The second: that it is the waw of resumption (wāw al-istiʾnāf), as if the Exalted, when He had completed the mention of these proofs, said after that: ﴿while they dispute about Allah﴾.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and He is severe in might﴾. Concerning the word al-miḥāl (might/power) there are several views:

Ibn Qutaybah said: the mīm is extra, and it is from al-ḥawl (power), and similar to it is the mīm of makān (place).

Al-Azharī said: this is an error, for when a word is of the pattern fiʿāl whose first letter is a kasra-vowelled mīm, it is original (aṣliyyah), like mihād, midās, and midād. They differed regarding what it is derived from, in several ways:

The first: it is said it is from their saying: "Maḥala fulān bi-fulān" when he informed on him to the ruler and exposed him to destruction, and "tamaḥḥala li-kadhā" when he exerted effort in employing a stratagem and strove in it. So the meaning is: He, glory be to Him, is severe in plotting against His enemies, destroying them by a way they do not anticipate.

The second: that al-miḥāl is an expression for severity, and from it the difficult year is called "sanat al-maḥl" (the year of drought), and "māḥaltu fulānan miḥālan," meaning: I contended with him, which of us is more severe. Abū Muslim said: miḥāl is fiʿāl from al-maḥl, which is severity, and the form fiʿāl applies to requital and counter-action, so the meaning is: He, the Exalted, is severe in overpowering. Regarding this the commentators have various expressions: Mujāhid and Qatādah said: "severe in strength"; Abū ʿUbaydah said: "severe in punishment"; al-Ḥasan said: "severe in retribution"; Ibn ʿAbbās said: "severe in power (ḥawl)."

The third: Ibn ʿArafah said: it is said "māḥala ʿan amrihi," meaning he disputed concerning his affair; so His saying ﴿severe in might﴾ means severe in disputation.

The fourth: it has been narrated from some of them: ﴿severe in might﴾ means severe in enmity (ḥiqd). They said: this is not valid, because enmity is not possible with respect to Allah, the Exalted. However, we have mentioned in this book that such expressions, when they occur with respect to Allah the Exalted, refer to the ultimate ends of the attributes and not their initial origins. So what is meant by enmity here is that He, the Exalted, intends to bring harm to him while concealing that intention from him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 12–13 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and who produces the heavy clouds.﴾ ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about Allah, and He is mighty in power.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, made His servants fear by sending down what cannot be turned back, He followed it with mention of these signs. They contain three matters, because they are indications of Allah's power and wisdom, and because they resemble blessings and kindness in some respects and resemble punishment and subjugation in other respects.

Page 20

Know also that He, the Exalted, mentions here four matters.

The first: the lightning, which is His saying: ﴿He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope.﴾ On this there are several issues.

First issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said, concerning the grammatical status (i'rab) of His saying ﴿as a fear and a hope﴾, there are several views:
The first: They cannot be objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for them, because they are not the act of the agent of the verb being explained, except on the assumption that a word has been omitted, i.e. "the desire of fear and hope," or in the sense of "causing fear and causing hope."
The second: They may be in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the lightning, as if it were itself fear and hope, the sense being "possessing fear and possessing hope," or in the sense of "causing fear and causing hope."
The third: That they are circumstantial states of the addressees, i.e. "fearful and hopeful."

Second issue: Concerning the lightning being fear and hope, there are several views:
The first: At the flashing of lightning, one fears the occurrence of thunderbolts and hopes for the descent of rain. Al-Mutanabbi said:
A youth like the dark cloud, who fears and hopes: he hopes for the rain from it and fears its thunderbolts.
The second: One who has harm from rain, such as a traveler, fears it, while dates and raisins are stored in his saddlebag; and one who has benefit from it hopes for it.
The third: Everything that occurs in this world is good for some people and bad for others. Likewise rain is good for one who needs it at its proper time, and bad for one whom it harms, either because of place or because of time.

Third issue: Know that the occurrence of lightning is a wondrous proof of Allah's power. Its explanation is that the cloud is undoubtedly a body composed of moist watery parts, and of airy and fiery parts. Undoubtedly the watery parts predominate in it, and water is a cold and moist body, while fire is a dry body. The appearance of an opposite from a complete opposite is contrary to reason, so there must be a choosing Creator who brings forth opposite from opposite.

If it is said: Why is it not possible to say that wind is enclosed within the body of the cloud, cold settles on its exterior so that its outer surface freezes, and then that wind tears it apart violently, so that from that violent tearing a fierce motion arises, and the fierce motion causes heat, which is the lightning?

The answer: All that you have mentioned is contrary to reason, and its explanation is in several respects:
The first: If the matter were as you say, it would necessarily follow that wherever lightning occurs, thunder—the sound produced by the tearing of the cloud—must occur as well. It is known that this is not the case, for strong lightning often occurs without any thunder.
The second: The heat produced by the strength of motion is opposed to the watery nature that causes cold. When this strong accident occurs, how does fire arise? Rather, we say: great fires are extinguished by pouring water on them, and the cloud is entirely water, so how can a weak fiery flame arise in it?
The third: According to your own doctrine, pure fire has no color at all. Suppose that fiery nature was produced through the strength of friction among the parts of the cloud; yet from where did that red color come? Thus it is established that the cause you mentioned is weak, and that the arising of fire within the body of the cloud, while it is pure water, is possible only by the power of the Powerful, the Wise.

* * *

The second type of the indications mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and He produces the heavy clouds.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Sahab" (cloud) is a collective noun whose singular is "sahabah," and "thiqal" is the plural of "thaqilah," because you say "sahabah thaqilah" and "sahab thiqal," just as you say "imra'ah karimah" and "nisa' kiram." It means laden with water.

Know that this too is one of the proofs of power and wisdom, because these watery parts either came into existence in the atmosphere of the air, or rose up from the surface of the earth. If the former, then their coming into being must be by the act of a wise, powerful originator, which is what is sought. If the latter, namely that those parts rose from the earth and, when they reached the cold layer of the air, grew cold and heavy and so returned to the earth, we say: this is false. The reason is that rains vary: sometimes the drops are large, sometimes small, sometimes close together, sometimes far apart; sometimes rain lasts a long time, sometimes briefly. The variation of rains in these attributes, while the nature of the earth is one and the nature of the sun that heats the vapors is one, necessarily requires the specification of a choosing agent. Moreover, experience has shown that supplication and humble entreaty have a great effect in the descent of rain, which is why the prayer for rain (salat al-istisqa') was legislated. Thus we know that the one who effects it is the power of the Agent, not nature and inherent property.

The third type of the indications mentioned in this verse is the thunder, which is His saying: ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him.﴾ On this there are several views.

The first view: The thunder is the name of an angel among the angels, and this audible sound is the sound of that angel glorifying and declaring God's oneness (tahlil). This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "The Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ about thunder, what is it? He said: 'It is an angel among the angels, entrusted with the clouds, with rods of fire with which he drives the clouds wherever Allah wills.' They said: 'What is the sound that we hear?' He said: 'His driving of the clouds.'" And from al-Hasan that it is a creation of Allah's creation, not an angel. According to this view, thunder is the angel entrusted with the clouds, and its sound is glorification of Allah the Exalted, and that sound is also called thunder. This is confirmed by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when he heard thunder he would say: "Glory be to the One whom it glorifies." And from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Allah produces the heavy clouds, and they speak the finest speech and laugh the finest laughter; their speech is the thunder and their laughter is the lightning."

Know that this view is not far-fetched, because according to the People of the Sunnah, bodily structure is not a condition for the occurrence of life. Therefore it is not far from Allah the Exalted to create life, knowledge, power, and speech in the parts of the cloud, so that this audible sound is an act of His. And how is that deemed unlikely when we see that the salamander arises in fire, frogs arise in cold water, and a great worm sometimes arises in ancient snows? Moreover, if the glorification of mountains in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, was not far-fetched, nor the glorification of pebbles in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, how is the glorification of clouds deemed unlikely? On this view, this thing called thunder is either an angel or not an angel, and there are two opinions on it:
One: that it is not an angel, because He joined the angels to it by saying: "and the angels, out of awe of Him," and the thing joined to is distinct from what it is joined to.
The second: that it is not far-fetched that it is of the kind of the angels, and its being mentioned separately is for the sake of honor, as in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98], and in His saying: ﴿and when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7].

The second view: The thunder is the name of this specific sound, and nevertheless the thunder glorifies Allah, the Glorified, because glorification (tasbih), sanctification (taqdis), and what is similar to them are nothing but the existence of an utterance indicating the occurrence of declaring Allah free of imperfection and sanctifying Him. Since the occurrence of this sound is a proof of the existence of a being exalted above deficiency and contingency, that is in reality glorification, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

Page 22

The third view: The meaning of the thunder being glorifying is that whoever hears the thunder glorifies Allah the Exalted, and for this reason this glorification is attributed to it.

The fourth view: From the sayings of the Sufis: the thunder is the swooning of the angels, the lightning is the sighs of their hearts, and the rain is their weeping.

If it is said: What is the reality of thunder?
We reply: We have fully discussed this in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, in His saying: ﴿therein are darknesses, and thunder, and lightning﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].

As for His saying: ﴿and the angels, out of awe of Him﴾, know that among the exegetes there are those who say: by these angels is meant the helpers of the thunder, for He, glorified is He, has appointed helpers for it. The meaning of His saying ﴿and the angels, out of awe of Him﴾ is: and the angels glorify out of fear and dread of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They fear Allah, not as the fear of the son of Adam; for one of them does not know who is on his right and who is on his left, and food, drink, or anything does not preoccupy him from the worship of Allah."

Know that the scholarly philosophers (muhaqqiqun min al-hukama') mention that these higher effects are accomplished only by spiritual celestial powers. So for the cloud there is a spirit from the celestial spirits that manages it; and likewise concerning the winds and all other higher effects. This is exactly what we related: that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies Allah. Thus what the exegetes expressed in this phrasing is what the investigating scholars cited from the philosophers. How then is it fitting for a sensible person to deny it?

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 14:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him is the call of truth. And those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches out his hands toward water so that it may reach his mouth, but it will not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is but in error.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾ means: to Allah belongs the call of truth. In this there are two discussions.

**The first discussion: the views of the exegetes, which are several.**

First: what Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: ﴿The call of truth﴾ is the saying "There is no god but Allah."

Second: the saying of al-Hasan: Indeed Allah is the Truth, so His call is the truth, as if he is alluding to the fact that turning to Him in supplication is the truth.

Third: that His worship is the truth and sincerity.

Know that the truth (al-haqq) is that which exists, and what exists is of two kinds. One kind accepts non-existence, and it is a truth that could become falsehood. The other kind does not accept non-existence, so it is impossible for it to become falsehood, and this is the true Truth. Since the Necessarily Existent in Himself exists and does not accept non-existence, He is the most worthy of existents to be the truth, He Himself. And the most worthy of beliefs and the most worthy of remembrances to be true is the belief in His existence and the mention of His being. Thus it has been established that His existence is the truth among existents, belief in His existence is the truth among beliefs, and mentioning Him with praise, divinity and perfection is the truth among remembrances. Therefore He said: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾.

**The second discussion:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: ﴿The call of truth﴾ has two possible readings.

One: the call is attributed to the truth which is the opposite of falsehood, just as the word is attributed to it in the phrase [the word of truth]. The purpose is to indicate that this call is distinguished by being true and by being free of signs of its being false. This is from the category of attributing a thing to its quality.

The second: it is attributed to the Truth which is Allah, may He be glorified, meaning: the call of the Called One who is the Truth, who hears and responds. And from al-Hasan: the Truth is Allah, and every call to Him is the call of the Truth.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And those they call upon besides Him﴾, meaning the gods whom the disbelievers call upon besides Allah ﴿do not respond to them with anything﴾ of what they request, except with a response like that of one who stretches out his hands toward water. Water is inanimate; it does not perceive the outstretching of his hands, nor his thirst and need for it, and it cannot answer his call and reach his mouth. Likewise, what they call upon is inanimate: it does not sense their supplication, cannot respond to them, and cannot benefit them. It has also been said that they were compared, in the futility of their supplication to their gods, to one who wants to scoop water with his hands in order to drink it, so he stretches them out with fingers spread, but his palms do not reach that water and he does not attain his aim of drinking. It is also read as [tad'ūna] with the letter *tā'* (you call), and [kabāsiṭi kaffayhi] with tanwīn (as an indefinite noun).

Then He said: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is but in error﴾, meaning: it is only in loss, with no benefit in it. For if they call upon Allah, He does not respond to them, and if they call upon the gods, they cannot respond to them.
