Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or by compulsion, and their shadows [too] in the mornings and the evenings.﴾

Know that concerning the meaning of this prostration there are two opinions.

The first opinion: that what is meant by it is prostration in the sense of placing the forehead upon the ground. On this view there are two aspects.

The first: although the expression is general, what is meant by it is particular, namely the believers. Some of the believers prostrate to Allah willingly, with ease and vigour, while among the Muslims there are those who prostrate to Allah by compulsion, because that is difficult for them, although they force themselves to perform that obedience whether they wish or not.

The second: the expression is general and what is meant by it is also general. On this view there is a difficulty in the verse, because not everyone in the heavens and the earth prostrates to Allah; rather the angels prostrate to Allah, and the believers among the jinn and humankind prostrate to Allah, the Exalted, whereas the disbelievers do not prostrate.

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: what is meant by His saying ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is: it is obligatory upon everyone in the heavens and the earth to prostrate to Allah, so the obligation is expressed in terms of occurrence and actuality.

The second: that what is meant by prostration is veneration and acknowledgment of servitude, and everyone in the heavens and everyone on the earth acknowledges the servitude of Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25].

As for the second opinion regarding the interpretation of the verse, it is that prostration is an expression for submission, subjection, and not refusing; and everyone in the heavens and the earth is prostrating to Allah in this sense, because His power and will take effect over all. The clarification of this statement is that whatever is other than Him is contingent in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and the contingent in its essence is that whose quiddity is equally receptive to non-existence and existence. Whoever is like this, the preponderance of its existence over its non-existence, or the reverse, is impossible except through the influence of an existent and an effecting agent. Thus the existence of everything other than the Truth, glorified is He, is by His bringing it into being, and the non-existence of everything other than Him is by His annihilating it. His influence therefore takes effect upon all contingent things at both ends, of bringing into being and of annihilation, and that is prostration, which is humility, submission and compliance. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Nay, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are obedient to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116], and His saying: ﴿And to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 83].

As for His saying, ﴿willingly and by compulsion﴾, what is meant is: some occurrences are those toward which the nature inclines, such as life and wealth, and some are those from which the nature recoils, such as death, poverty, blindness, grief, disability and all kinds of disliked things; and all of them come about by His decree, His measure, His ordaining and His bringing into being, and no one has the power to refuse or resist.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿and their shadows [too] in the mornings and the evenings﴾, and concerning this there are two opinions.

The first opinion: the exegetes said: every person, whether believer or disbeliever, his shadow prostrates to Allah. Mujahid said: the shadow of the believer prostrates to Allah willingly, and he is obedient; the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates to Allah by compulsion, and he is unwilling. Al-Zajjaj said: it has come in the tafsir that the disbeliever prostrates to other than Allah, while his shadow prostrates to Allah. At this point Ibn al-Anbari said: it is not far-fetched that Allah, exalted, should create for shadows minds and understandings by which they prostrate and humble themselves, just as Allah gave the mountains understandings so that they occupied themselves with glorifying Allah, the Exalted, and so that the effect of manifestation appeared in them, as He said: ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾ [al-A'raf: 143].

The second opinion: that what is meant by the prostration of shadows is their inclining from side to side, and their lengthening due to the descent of the sun and their shortening due to the sun's rising; thus they are submissive and compliant in their lengthening, their shortening, and their inclining from side to side. The mornings and the evenings were singled out for mention only because shadows become greatest and most numerous at these two times.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah." Say: "Have you then taken, apart from Him, protectors who have no power to benefit or harm themselves?" Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal? Or have they set up for Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them?" Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained that everything in the heavens and the earth prostrates to Him, meaning that it is subservient to Him, He returned to refuting the idol-worshippers, and said: ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah."﴾ Since this answer is one that the one questioned acknowledges and confesses and does not deny, He commanded him (ﷺ) to be the one who mentions this answer, as a reminder that they do not deny it at all. Having explained that He, glorified is He, is the Lord of all beings, He said: Say to them: then why have you taken, apart from Allah, protectors, which are inanimate objects, and which possess no power to benefit or harm themselves? And since they are incapable of securing benefit for themselves or warding off harm from themselves, it is all the more so that they are incapable of securing benefit for others or warding off harm from others. If they are not able to do that, then worshipping them is pure futility and folly. And having mentioned this clear argument, He explained that the one ignorant of such an argument is like the blind, and the one who knows it is like the seeing; ignorance of such an argument is like the darknesses, and knowledge of it is like the light. Just as everyone knows by necessity that the blind is not equal to the seeing, and darkness is not equal to light, so too everyone knows by necessity that the one ignorant of this argument is not equal to the one who knows it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and 'Amr, from 'Asim, read ﴿يَسْتَوِي الظُّلُماتُ والنُّورُ﴾ with the ya' (yastawi), because the verb is placed before a collective noun (ism al-jam'); the rest read it with the ta' (tastawi), and Abu 'Ubaydah preferred this reading. Then He emphasised this explanation, saying: ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ meaning: these things which they claim to be partners of Allah have no creation resembling the creation of Allah, such that they could say that they share with Allah in being creators, and so it would be necessary that they share with Him in divinity. Rather, these polytheists know by necessity that these idols have never produced any act at all, neither creation nor effect. And if the matter is so, then their judgement that they are partners of Allah in divinity is pure folly and ignorance. There are several issues in this verse.

First issue: Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) have used this verse in the question of the creation of acts, in several respects:

The first: the Mu'tazilah claimed that animals create movements and stillnesses like the movements and stillnesses which Allah, exalted is He, creates. On this supposition, they have made for Allah partners who created like His creation. And it is well known that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this verse only in the context of blame and denunciation, so this verse indicates that a servant does not create the act of himself. The judge (al-Qadi) said: We, although we say that the servant acts and brings into being, do not use the unqualified expression that he creates. Even if we used it, we would not say that he creates like the creation of Allah, because one of us acts by the power of Allah, and acts in order to bring about benefit and avert harm, whereas Allah, exalted is He, is exempt from all of that. Thus it is established that, on the supposition that the servant is a creator, his creation would still not be like the creation of Allah, exalted is He. Furthermore, this objection applies to the Mujbirah (determinists), because they say: whatever is the creation of Allah, exalted is He, is also the acquisition (kasb) of the servant and his act; and this is the very essence of shirk, because the God and the servant, in the creation of those acts, are like two partners, neither of whom has any property without the other having a right in it. Furthermore, He, exalted is He, only mentioned this statement as a reproach to the disbelievers and a censure of their way; and if the act of the servant were a creation of Allah, exalted is He, this censure would have no benefit, because the disbelievers could say on this supposition: since Allah, glorified and exalted is He, created this disbelief in us, why does He blame us for it, and not attribute to us ignorance and negligence, when it has come about in us neither by our act nor by our choice?

The answer to the first question: the word "khalq" (creation) either means bringing into existence from non-existence, or it means determining (taqdir). On either meaning, if the servant is an originator, then he must himself be originated. As for his saying: even though the servant is a creator, his creation is not like the creation of Allah.

We say: "khalq" means bringing about, forming, and bringing into existence from non-existence. And it is well known that when the movement occurring by the power of the servant is like the movement occurring by the power of Allah, exalted is He, then one of the two created things is like the second created thing. At that point it is correct to say that this, which is the creation of the servant, is like what is created by Allah, exalted is He. Indeed, there is no doubt that difference exists in all other respects; but the existence of difference in all other respects does not detract from the existence of likeness from this one aspect, and this degree suffices for the argument. As for his saying: this is binding on the Mujbirah, since they say the act of the servant is created by Allah, exalted is He, we say: this is not binding, because this verse indicates that the creation of the servant may not be a like of the creation of Allah, exalted is He, and we do not affirm for the servant any creation at all; so how would that be binding on us? As for his saying: if the act of the servant were a creation of Allah, exalted is He, it would not be fitting to blame the disbelievers on this view.

We say: its outcome returns to the point that, since praise and blame occur, the servant must be independent in the act; and this is refuted, because He, exalted is He, blamed Abu Lahab for his disbelief, although He knew of him that he would die in disbelief; and we have already mentioned that contrary to what is known is impossible to occur. This is the explanation of this aspect in this verse.

The second aspect of relying on this verse is His saying: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾. There is no doubt that the act of the servant is a thing, so it is necessary that its creator is Allah; and their objection to it has already been mentioned.

The third aspect of relying on this verse is His saying: ﴿and He is the One, the Subduer﴾. It cannot be said of Him that He is one in every sense; and since the preceding mention was of creatorship, it is necessary that what is meant is that He is One in creatorship, the Subduer over everything other than Him; and in that case it is also evidence for the correctness of our statement.

* * *

Second issue: Jahm claimed that the name "thing" (shay') does not apply to Allah, exalted is He.

Know that this dispute is only about the word: whether this name applies to Him or not. He claimed that this name does not apply to Allah, exalted is He, and he argued for it by saying: if He were a thing, it would necessarily follow that He is a creator of Himself, because of His saying: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾; and since that is impossible, it follows that the name "thing" does not apply to Him. It cannot be said: this is a general expression to which specification has entered; because a general expression that has been specified is only good when the specified part is smaller and baser than the remainder, as when one says: I ate this pomegranate, although some seeds fell from it and he did not eat them. Here, however, the essence of Allah, exalted is He, is the highest and most noble of existents; so how is it possible to mention a general word which encompasses Him, while the ruling is specific in His case?

The second argument: he relied on His saying: ﴿There is nothing like His likeness, anything﴾, and the meaning is: there is nothing like the likeness of His likeness. It is well known that every reality is like the likeness of its own self; so the Creator, exalted is He, is like the likeness of His own self; yet He, exalted is He, has pointed out that the likeness of His likeness is not a thing. This is an explicit statement that He, exalted is He, is not named by the name "thing."

The third argument: His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. This verse indicates that Allah may not be called upon except by the most beautiful names; and the word "things" encompasses the basest of existents, so this word does not suggest a good meaning; therefore it is necessary that this word is not among the most beautiful names, and so it is necessary that it is not permissible to call upon Allah, exalted is He, by this word. The Ashab (Ash'aris) relied, for applying this name to Him, exalted is He, on His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah is witness between me and you."﴾ [al-An'am: 19].

The opponent answered concerning this that His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ is a question left without an answer, and His saying: ﴿Say: "Allah is witness between me and you"﴾ is an independent, newly begun statement that has no connection to what precedes it.

* * *

Third issue: The Mu'tazilah relied on this verse for the claim that He, exalted is He, is knowing by His essence, not by a knowledge, and powerful by His essence, not by a power. They said: because if knowledge, power and life were to occur to Allah, exalted is He, these attributes would either be brought about by the creation of Allah or not by His creation; the first is invalid, otherwise an infinite regress would follow; and the second is invalid, because His saying: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾ encompasses the essence and the attributes. We have ruled that specification enters it with regard to the essence of Allah, exalted is He, so it is necessary that it remain in what is other than the essence according to the original sense, namely that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of everything other than His essence, exalted is He. So if Allah had knowledge and power, it would necessarily follow that He is the Creator of them both, and that is impossible. Furthermore, they relied on this verse for the createdness of the Qur'an. They said: the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of all things, and the Qur'an is not Allah, exalted is He; so it is necessary that it be created and that it fall under this generality.

The answer: at most, the form is general; but we specify it with regard to the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, by means of rational proofs.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 13, verses 17–19 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a foaming scum. And from what they heat in the fire, seeking an ornament or a utensil, there is a similar scum. Thus God strikes [the parable of] truth and falsehood. As for the scum, it passes away as worthless debris; but what benefits people remains on the earth. Thus God strikes the parables.﴾ ﴿For those who respond to their Lord there is the best [reward]. But those who do not respond to Him, even if they had everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom. For them is a wretched reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and what an evil resting place it is.﴾ ﴿Is one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only people of understanding take heed.﴾

Know that when He, exalted be He, had likened the believer and the disbeliever, and faith and disbelief, to the sighted and the blind, and to darkness and light, He struck another parable for faith and disbelief, saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure.﴾ It is in the nature of water to settle in valleys that lie lower than the mountains and hills, in proportion to the width and narrowness of those valleys. And it is in the nature of water, when it exceeds the capacity of the valleys, to spread over the ground. And it is in the nature of the foam that water carries, which floats on top and swells above it, to disperse at the edges and perish, whether that foam is the whiteness resembling boiling, or the light bodies that are held by the water. Then, having mentioned this foam, which appears only when the flow of water becomes strong, He mentioned the foam that appears only through fire. This is because each of the seven bodies (metals), when melted in fire to make an ornament or another utensil among the goods needed for the household's affairs, separates from it a kind of scum and dross, which is of no benefit but is lost and perishes, and the pure remains. The summary is this: when a valley flows, foam floats on it, and that foam perishes while the water remains; and when the seven bodies are melted for making ornaments or for making other goods, dross and scum separate from them, which perish, and that essence which benefits remains. Likewise here: He sent down from the sky of greatness, majesty and benevolence water, which is the Qur'an. The valleys are the hearts of the servants. He likened the hearts to valleys because the lights of the sciences of the Qur'an settle in them, just as the waters descending from the sky settle in valleys. And just as each valley receives of the rainwater what suits its width or narrowness, so too each heart receives of the lights of the Qur'anic sciences what suits that heart in its purity or impurity, and in the strength or weakness of its understanding. And just as the water is topped by the scum of the melted seven bodies, mixed with dross, and then that scum and dross go away and are lost while the essence of the water and the essence of the seven bodies remain, so too here: the clarifications of the Qur'an are mixed with doubts and misgivings, but in the end these pass away and are lost, and knowledge, religion, wisdom and unveiling remain in the outcome. This is the explanation of this parable and the aspect in which the parable applies to what it illustrates. Most of the exegetes remained silent about explaining the manner of the figurative comparison.

The first issue: among the verbal discussions in this verse, there are investigations concerning the word *al-awdiyah* (valleys).

The first investigation: *al-awdiyah* is the plural of *wadi* (valley). Regarding the meaning of *wadi* there are two views.

The first view: it refers to the low-lying open land below the mountains and hills through which the torrent flows. This is the view of the majority of the lexicographers.

The second view: al-Suhrawardi said: water is called a *wadi* when it flows. He said: from this, the flowing moisture (*wady*) was named *wady* because of its emergence and flow. On this view, *wadi* is a name for flowing water, like *masil* (a channel of flow). The first view is the well-known one, but on this assumption His saying ﴿valleys flow﴾ is a metaphor, so the sense is: the waters of the valleys flowed, but the genitive-noun was omitted and the genitive-attribute (the "valleys") was put in its place.

The second investigation: Abu Ali al-Farisi, may God have mercy on him, said: *al-awdiyah* is the plural of *wadi*, and we do not know of any active-participle pattern (*fa'il*) pluralized on the pattern *af'ilah*. He said: this is probably because the active-participle form (*fa'il*) and the *fa'il* form (*fa'il*) are interchangeable for one and the same thing, like *'alim* and *'alim* (knower), *shahid* and *shahid* (witness), *nasir* and *nasir* (helper). Then the pattern *fa'il* is pluralized as *af'al*, like *sahib* and *as'hab* (companion), and *ta'ir* and *at'ar* (bird); and the pattern *fa'il* (in the sense of *fa'il*) is pluralized as *af'ilah*, like *jarib* and *ajribah* (a sack). Then, since the aforementioned correspondence arose between *fa'il* and *fa'il*, the *fa'il* is inevitably pluralized in the plural of *fa'il*, so one says *wadi*, *awdiyah*; and the *fa'il* is pluralized in the plural of *fa'il*, so one says *yatim*, *aytam* (orphan) and *sharif*, *ashraf* (noble). This is what Abu Ali al-Farisi said. Others said: the parallel of *wadi* and *awdiyah* is *nadi* and *andiyah*, for gatherings.

The third investigation: the word *awdiyah* is mentioned in indefinite form, because rain does not come except alternately among the tracts of land, so some valleys of the earth flow while others do not. As for His saying ﴿according to their measure (*bi-qadarihā*)﴾, there are two investigations.

The first: al-Wahidi said: *al-qadr* and *al-qadar* both mean the extent of a thing. One says: what is the *qadr* of these dirhams, and what is their *qadar* and *miqdar*? That is, what do they amount to in weight? Whatever equals them in weight is their *qadr*.

The second: ﴿valleys flow according to their measure﴾ means, of water. If the valley is small, little water flows; if the valley is wide, much water flows.

As for His saying ﴿and the torrent carries a foam, swelling (*rabiyan*)﴾, there are two investigations.

The first: al-Farra' said: one says *azbada al-wadi* (the valley foamed), with the verbal noun *izbad*, and *zabad* is the noun. As for His saying ﴿swelling (*rabiyan*)﴾, al-Zajjaj said: floating high above the water. Others said: increasing because of its swelling; one says *raba yarbu* when it increases.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And from what they heat in the fire, seeking an ornament or a utensil, there is a similar scum﴾: know that when He had struck the parable with the foam produced by water, He followed it with a parable from the foam produced by fire. In this there are investigations.

The first: Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, on the authority of Asim, read ﴿yuqidun (they heat)﴾ with the *ya'* (third person). Abu Ubayda preferred this, because of His saying ﴿that benefits people﴾, and also because there is no addressee here. The others read it with *ta'* (second person) as an address. On this reading there are two possibilities. The first: it is an address to those mentioned in His saying ﴿Say: Have you taken protectors apart from Him?﴾ (13:16). The second: it may be a general address intended for all, as if He had said: "And from what you heat in the fire, O you who heat."

The second: heating (*al-iqad*) over a thing is of two kinds. One: that thing is not in the fire, like His saying ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, over the clay﴾ (28:38). The second: one heats over a thing, and that thing is in the fire; for whoever wants to melt the seven bodies puts them in the fire. For this reason He said here ﴿from what they heat in the fire﴾.

The third: in His saying ﴿seeking an ornament﴾, the scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: what is heated for seeking an ornament is gold and silver; what is heated for seeking utensils is iron, copper and lead, and tin is made into vessels and things that are used. *Al-mata'* is everything with which one enjoys oneself. His saying ﴿a similar scum﴾ means a scum like the scum of the water that the torrent carries.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿Thus God strikes [the parable of] truth and falsehood.﴾ The meaning: thus God strikes the parables for truth and falsehood. Then He said: ﴿As for the scum, it passes away as worthless debris, but what benefits people﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-juta'* is throwing away and casting off; one says *ja al-wadi ghuthaahu yajfuhu juta'an* when it casts away its refuse. *Al-juta'* is a noun for what is gathered from it, its parts pressed one upon another. The position of *juta'an* is the accusative of circumstance (*hal*, a state-clause). The meaning: the scum rises on the surface of the water, swells and puffs up, but in the end it dwindles away, and the pure essence of the water and of the seven bodies remains. Likewise, doubts and illusions may grow and become great, but in the end they become void, dwindle and vanish, and the truth remains manifest, unmixed with any doubt. In the reading of Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj it is *judalan* (?) [the text reads *juffalan*], and it is reported from Abu Hatim: Ru'ba's reading should not be recited, because he used to eat mice.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿For those who respond to their Lord there is the best (*al-husna*)﴾, there are two possibilities.

The first: the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿Thus God strikes the parables﴾, and then a new sentence begins with His saying ﴿For those who respond to their Lord, the best﴾. Its position is nominative, as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the nominal sentence) and *lilladhina* is its predicate (*khabar*, the comment). Its sense is: for them is the good quality and the good state.

The second: it is connected to what precedes it. The sense: as if He had said: the one that remains is the parable of the one who responds, and the one that passes away as worthless debris is the parable of the one who does not respond. Then He explained the aspect in which it is a parable: for the one who responds there is the best, which is Paradise; and for the one who does not respond there are kinds of regret and punishment. There is another possibility: the sense is "Thus God strikes the parables for those who responded to their Lord with the good response," so *al-husna* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*).

Know that He, exalted be He, mentioned here the states of the blessed and the states of the wretched. As for the states of the blessed, it is His saying ﴿For those who respond to their Lord, the best﴾. The meaning is that those who answered Him in what He called them to, namely monotheism, justice, prophethood, the sending of messengers, and adherence to the laws revealed upon the tongue of His messenger, for them is the best. Ibn Abbas said: this is Paradise. The scholars of meanings said: *al-husna* is the greatest benefit in beauty, a pure benefit free from any admixture of harm, lasting and unceasing, accompanied by honour and reverence. He did not mention the increase here, because He mentioned it in another surah, namely His saying ﴿For those who did good is the best, and more﴾ (Yunus 10:26). As for the states of the wretched, it is His saying ﴿But those who did not respond to Him﴾, and for them are four kinds of torment and punishment.

The first kind is His saying ﴿Even if they had everything on earth together and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom (*iftada*)﴾. *Iftida'* is making one of two things a substitute for the other. The object of *iftadaw bihi* is omitted; its sense: they would ransom themselves with it, that is, they would make it the ransom for their souls from punishment. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to *ma* in His saying ﴿what is on the earth﴾.

Know that this meaning is true, because what is loved in itself by every human being is his own self, and everything else he loves only because it is a means to the benefits of his self. So when the soul is in harm, pain and hardship, and he owns what equals the whole world of bodies and spirits, he will consent to make it a ransom for his soul; for what is loved only incidentally must necessarily be a ransom for what is loved in itself.

The second kind of the punishment that God prepared for them is His saying ﴿For them is a wretched reckoning (*su' al-hisab*)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is because their disbelief nullified their deeds. I say: here there are two states. Whatever occupies you with God, His worship and His love, is the blessed, noble, sublime, holy state; and whatever occupies you with other than God is the harmful, injurious, base state. There is no doubt that these two states admit of more and less, of greater and lesser. And there is no doubt that persistence in deeds suited to these states makes their strength and firmness; for it is established in rational principles that the multiplication of acts produces firmly rooted dispositions. And there is no doubt that since the multiplication of acts produces those firmly rooted dispositions, and each one of those acts, even the glance, the momentary thought, the passing recollection, and the weak turning of attention, produces some effect in establishing that state in the soul, this is the reckoning. On reflection on these discussions, it becomes clear to a person that His saying is true: ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ (Az-Zalzalah 99:7–8).

[Page 29]

When this is established, the happy ones are those who responded to their Lord by turning away from all that is other than God and turning wholeheartedly to the worship of God Most High. Therefore, without doubt, they attained al-husna (the best reward).

As for the wretched, they are those who did not respond to their Lord. For this reason, they must suffer evil reckoning (su' al-hisab). The meaning of evil reckoning is that they loved this world and turned away from their Master. When they died, they remained deprived of their beloved, which is this world, and remained deprived of the honor of serving the presence of their Master.

The third type is God's words: ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾. This is because they were heedless of gaining felicity through serving the presence of their Master, and were devoted to the pleasures of this world. When they died, they were separated from their beloved, so they burn with grief at the separation, and they have nothing else that could compensate for this calamity. Therefore He said: ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾. Then God described this refuge, saying: ﴿And it is an evil resting-place﴾, and there is no doubt that the matter is as He said.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ This refers to the example mentioned earlier, which is that one who knows a thing is like one who sees, and one who is ignorant of it is like the blind. The two are not alike, because the blind man, when he walks without a guide, will apparently fall into a well or into dangers, and perhaps he will ruin the useful goods that were on his path. As for the seeing man, he is safe from destruction and from causing destruction.

Then He said: ﴿Only those of understanding take heed﴾. The meaning is that none benefit from these examples except the possessors of understanding (ulu al-albab), who seek the meaning of every form, take the kernel from every husk, and pass from the outward of every discourse to its inner secret and its essence.

The second: one heats over a thing, and that thing is in the fire; for whoever wants to melt the seven bodies puts them in the fire. For this reason He said here ﴿from what they heat in the fire﴾.

The position of *juta'an* is the accusative of circumstance (*hal*, a state-clause). The meaning: the scum rises on the surface of the water, swells and puffs up, but in the end it dwindles away, and the pure essence of the water and of the seven bodies remains. Likewise, doubts and illusions may grow and become great, but in the end they become void, dwindle and vanish, and the truth remains manifest, unmixed with any doubt. As for His saying ﴿For those who respond to their Lord there is the best (*al-husna*)﴾, there are two possibilities.

The first: the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿Thus God strikes the parables﴾, and then a new sentence begins with His saying ﴿For those who respond to their Lord, the best﴾. Its position is nominative, as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the nominal sentence) and *lilladhina* is its predicate (*khabar*, the comment). Its sense is: for them is the good quality and the good state.

The second: it is connected to what precedes it. The sense: as if He had said: the one that remains is the parable of the one who responds, and the one that passes away as worthless debris is the parable of the one who does not respond. Then He explained the aspect in which it is a parable: for the one who responds there is the best, which is Paradise; and for the one who does not respond there are kinds of regret and punishment. There is another possibility: the sense is "Thus God strikes the parables for those who responded to their Lord with the good response," so *al-husna* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*).

Know that He, exalted be He, mentioned here the states of the blessed and the states of the wretched. As for the states of the blessed, it is His saying ﴿For those who respond to their Lord, the best﴾. The meaning is that those who answered Him in what He called them to, namely monotheism, justice, prophethood, the sending of messengers, and adherence to the laws revealed upon the tongue of His messenger, for them is the best. Ibn Abbas said: this is Paradise. The scholars of meanings said: *al-husna* is the greatest benefit in beauty, a pure benefit free from any admixture of harm, lasting and unceasing, accompanied by honour and reverence. He did not mention the increase here, because He mentioned it in another surah, namely His saying ﴿For those who did good is the best, and more﴾ (Yunus 10:26). As for the states of the wretched, it is His saying ﴿But those who did not respond to Him﴾, and for them are four kinds of torment and punishment.

The first kind is His saying ﴿Even if they had everything on earth together and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom (*iftada*)﴾. *Iftida'* is making one of two things a substitute for the other. The object of *iftadaw bihi* is omitted; its sense: they would ransom themselves with it, that is, they would make it the ransom for their souls from punishment. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to *ma* in His saying ﴿what is on the earth﴾.

Know that this meaning is true, because what is loved in itself by every human being is his own self, and everything else he loves only because it is a means to the benefits of his self. So when the soul is in harm, pain and hardship, and he owns what equals the whole world of bodies and spirits, he will consent to make it a ransom for his soul; for what is loved only incidentally must necessarily be a ransom for what is loved in itself.

I say: here there are two states. Whatever occupies you with God, His worship and His love, is the blessed, noble, sublime, holy state; and whatever occupies you with other than God is the harmful, injurious, base state. There is no doubt that these two states admit of more and less, of greater and lesser. And there is no doubt that persistence in deeds suited to these states makes their strength and firmness; for it is established in rational principles that the multiplication of acts produces firmly rooted dispositions. And there is no doubt that since the multiplication of acts produces those firmly rooted dispositions, and each one of those acts, even the glance, the momentary thought, the passing recollection, and the weak turning of attention, produces some effect in establishing that state in the soul, this is the reckoning. When this is established, the happy ones are those who responded to their Lord by turning away from all that is other than God and turning wholeheartedly to the worship of God Most High. Therefore, without doubt, they attained al-husna (the best reward).

As for the wretched, they are those who did not respond to their Lord. For this reason, they must suffer evil reckoning (su' al-hisab). The meaning of evil reckoning is that they loved this world and turned away from their Master. When they died, they remained deprived of their beloved, which is this world, and remained deprived of the honor of serving the presence of their Master.

The third type is God's words: ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾. This is because they were heedless of gaining felicity through serving the presence of their Master, and were devoted to the pleasures of this world. When they died, they were separated from their beloved, so they burn with grief at the separation, and they have nothing else that could compensate for this calamity. Therefore He said: ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾. Then God described this refuge, saying: ﴿And it is an evil resting-place﴾, and there is no doubt that the matter is as He said.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ This refers to the example mentioned earlier, which is that one who knows a thing is like one who sees, and one who is ignorant of it is like the blind. The two are not alike, because the blind man, when he walks without a guide, will apparently fall into a well or into dangers, and perhaps he will ruin the useful goods that were on his path. As for the seeing man, he is safe from destruction and from causing destruction.

Then He said: ﴿Only those of understanding take heed﴾. The meaning is that none benefit from these examples except the possessors of understanding (ulu al-albab), who seek the meaning of every form, take the kernel from every husk, and pass from the outward of every discourse to its inner secret and its essence.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 20–24 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the pledge﴾ ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord and dread an evil reckoning﴾ ﴿And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, and establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good — for them is the good outcome of the abode﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring; and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode!"﴾.

Know that this verse: is it connected to what precedes it or not? There are two opinions on this.

The first opinion: that it is connected to what precedes it. On this basis there are two possibilities:

The first: that the words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ may be a description of "those of understanding" (ulu al-albab).

The second: that this may be a description of His words ﴿Is one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth [like one who is blind]?﴾.

The second opinion: that the words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ are a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿for them is the good outcome of the abode﴾, like His words ﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾ up to His words ﴿for them is the curse﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 25].

Know that this verse, from its beginning to its end, is one single sentence of condition and consequence (shart and jaza'). Its condition contains a number of qualifications, and its consequence also contains qualifications. As for the qualifications considered in the condition, they are nine:

The first qualification: His words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾. On this there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it means the covenant He made with them when they were in the loins of Adam, and He made them bear witness against themselves: ﴿"Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172].

The second: that by the covenant of Allah is meant every matter for which evidence has been established as sound, and this is of two kinds:

One of them: things for which Allah has established decisive rational proofs, which do not admit abrogation (naskh) or change.

The other: things for which Allah has established revealed (sam'i) proofs and explained those rulings to them. The sum of it is that under His words ﴿fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ enters everything for which evidence has been established. The term "covenant" may correctly be applied to a proof (hujjah); indeed, the truth is that there is no covenant more binding than proof. The evidence for this is that one who swears to something is obliged to fulfil it only when its obligation has been established by evidence, not merely by the oath itself; therefore he may sometimes be obliged to reproach his own soul if that is good for him. So there is no covenant more binding than Allah's obligating a person to that by rational proof or by revealed proof. A servant does not fulfil the covenant except by performing all of those things, just as one who swears to many things is not truthful in his oath unless he does all of them. It includes performing all the commanded acts and refraining from all the forbidden acts; it includes fulfilling contracts in transactions; it includes rendering trusts. This view is the chosen and correct interpretation of the verse.

* * *

The second qualification: His words ﴿and do not break the pledge﴾. On this there are several opinions:

The first opinion — the view of the majority — is that this phrase is close in meaning to fulfilling the covenant, for fulfilling the covenant is close to not breaking the pledge and the covenant. This is like someone saying: when its existence became necessary, its non-existence must be impossible. These two concepts are distinct but mutually entailing; likewise, fulfilling the covenant necessarily entails not breaking the pledge.

Know that fulfilling the covenant is among the highest levels of felicity. He, peace be upon him, said: "There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness, and no religion for one who has no covenant." The verses concerning this matter in the Qur'an are numerous.

The second opinion: the pledge (mithaq) is what a responsible person binds upon himself. The sense is: His words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ refer to what Allah obligated the servant with from the outset, and His words ﴿and do not break the pledge﴾ refer to what the servant has committed himself to of kinds of obedience by his own choice, such as vowing acts of obedience and good deeds.

The third opinion: by fulfilling the covenant is meant the covenant of lordship and servanthood, and by the pledge is meant the covenants mentioned in the Torah, the Gospel and the rest of the divine books concerning the obligation to believe in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ upon his appearance.

Know that fulfilling the covenant is something praised by reason and by the sacred laws. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever makes a covenant with Allah and then betrays it has a characteristic of hypocrisy." And from him, peace be upon him: "There are three whom I will oppose on the Day of Resurrection, and whomever I oppose I will prevail against: a man who gave a covenant and then betrayed it; a man who hired a worker, took full work from him, and withheld his wage; and a man who sold a free person, enslaved the free person and consumed his price." It is also related that: "There was a covenant between Mu'awiyah and the king of the Romans, and he wished to go to them and break the covenant. Then a man on a horse appeared, saying: 'Fulfilment of covenant, not betrayal! I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: whoever has between himself and a people a covenant, let him not dissolve it nor tie it until its term has ended, and let him inform them openly.'" He said: "Who is this?" They said: "'Amr ibn 'Uyaynah." So Mu'awiyah turned back.

* * *

The third qualification: ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾. Here there is a question: fulfilling the covenant and not breaking the pledge already include the obligation to perform all the commanded acts and to avoid all the forbidden acts, so what is the benefit of mentioning these qualifications after them?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: it was mentioned lest someone suppose that this applies only to what is between him and Allah, so the matters between him and the servants were singled out for mention. The second: it is for emphasis.

Having understood this, we say: they have mentioned several interpretations of it:

The first: that what is meant is the joining of kinship ties (silat al-rahim). He, peace be upon him, said: "Three will come on the Day of Resurrection having a sharpness to them: the womb (rahim) will say, 'O Lord, I was severed'; the trust will say, 'O Lord, I was abandoned'; and the blessing will say, 'O Lord, I was ungratefully rejected.'"

The second opinion: that what is meant is joining with Muhammad ﷺ, supporting him, and aiding him in jihad.

The third opinion: the observance of all the obligatory rights of servants, which includes joining kinship ties and the relationship established through the brotherhood of faith, as He said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10]. This joining includes supporting them by conveying good things and warding off calamities as far as possible, visiting the sick, attending funerals, spreading the greeting of peace among people, smiling in their faces, and withholding harm from them. It also includes every living creature, even the cat and the hen. It is related from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, may Allah have mercy on him, that a group entered upon him in Mecca, and he said: "Where are you from?" They said: "From Khurasan." He said: "Fear Allah and be wherever you wish, and know that if a servant does the utmost good, yet has a hen and mistreats it, he is not among the doers of good."

I say: the sum of the matter is that His words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the pledge﴾ point to the exalting of Allah's command, and His words ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ point to compassion toward the creation of Allah.

* * *

The fourth qualification: His words ﴿and fear their Lord﴾. The meaning: even if he performs everything within his capacity in exalting Allah's command and in compassion toward Allah's creation, it is still necessary that fear of Allah and dread of Him dominate his heart. This fear is of two kinds:

One of them: that he fears that some excess, deficiency or flaw may occur in his acts of worship and obedience, such that it would invalidate the worship or diminish its reward.

The second, which is the fear of majesty: because when the servant stands before a sovereign who is awe-inspiring and dominating, even though he is in the state of obedience, the awe of majesty, exaltation and greatness does not leave his heart.

The fifth qualification: His words ﴿and dread an evil reckoning﴾. Know that the fourth qualification refers to fear of Allah, while this fifth qualification refers to fear and dread of an evil reckoning. This indicates that by fear of Allah is meant what we have mentioned: the fear of majesty, awe and greatness; otherwise there would be repetition.

* * *

The sixth qualification: His exalted words ﴿And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾. This includes patience in performing acts of worship, patience under the burden of illnesses, harms, distresses and sorrows, patience in abstaining from desires, and in sum patience in refraining from sins and in performing acts of obedience. Then a person may undertake patience for several reasons:

One: that he is patient so that it may be said how perfect his patience is and how strong his endurance of calamities.

Second: that he is patient so that he will not be blamed for impatience.

Third: that he is patient so that the enemies will not gloat.

Fourth: that he is patient because he knows there is no benefit in impatience. When a person is patient for one of these reasons, that does not count as part of the perfection of the soul and the felicity of the heart. But if he endures affliction because he knows that this affliction is a portion decreed by the Allotter, the All-Knowing, who is exempt from defect, falsehood and folly — and that this portion must contain profound wisdom and a preponderant benefit — and he is content with it, because it is the disposal of the owner over his property, and there is no objection to the owner disposing of his property; or he is patient because he has become wholly absorbed in beholding the One who tests, so that his absorption in the manifestation of the light of the One who tests makes him oblivious to the pain of the affliction — this is the highest station of the sincere (siddiqun). These three aspects are those in which it is truly said of him that he was patient seeking the countenance of his Lord, meaning that he was patient solely for the sake of His reward and the seeking of Allah's pleasure.

Know that His words ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ contain a subtle point: that when a lover is struck by his beloved, the lover may look at that striker and rejoice in it. So His words ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ are to be understood in this figurative sense: just as the lover accepts that blow out of delight in gazing upon the face of his beloved, so the servant endures affliction and trial and is content with it,

because of his absorption in knowing the light of the Truth. This is a subtle and delicate point.

The seventh qualification: His words ﴿and establish the prayer﴾.

Know that although prayer and zakat are included in the first general statement, Allah mentioned them separately to draw attention to their being more noble than the other acts of worship. The establishing of prayer has already been explained earlier in this book, and it is not precluded that voluntary prayers are also included in it.

* * *

The eighth qualification: His exalted words ﴿and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. On this there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Hasan said: what is meant is the obligatory zakat. If one is not suspected of withholding zakat, it is preferable to pay it secretly; but if one is suspected of withholding zakat, it is preferable to pay it openly. It was also said that "secretly" means paying it oneself, and "openly" means paying it to the imam. Others said: rather, what is meant is obligatory zakat and voluntary charity given in the manner of a supererogatory act; so His words ﴿secretly﴾ refer to voluntary charity, and His words ﴿and openly﴾ refer to obligatory zakat.

The second issue: the Mu'tazilites said: He encouraged spending from everything that is provision (rizq), and this indicates that there is no provision except what is lawful; for if what is unlawful were provision, He would have encouraged spending unlawful wealth, and that is not permissible.

The ninth qualification: His words ﴿and repel evil with good﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: that when they commit a sin, they repel it and push it away by repentance, as it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "When you commit an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will wipe it out."

*Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 20–24 (part 2 of 2):*

The second view: the meaning is that they do not meet evil with evil, but meet evil with good, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by it with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. It is related from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him both: "The one who maintains ties is not the one who returns the favour of being kept ties with. Rather, the one who maintains ties is the one whose ties were cut, yet he maintained them and showed kindness to the one who did not maintain ties with him. The forbearing person is not the one who is wronged and then shows forbearance, only to be provoked when a people provoke him. Rather, the forbearing person is the one who has power and then pardons." And from al-Hasan: "They are those who, when they are deprived, give, and when they are wronged, pardon." It is also narrated that Shaqiq ibn Ibrahim al-Balkhi entered upon Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak in disguise. He asked: "Where are you from?" He said: "From Balkh." He said: "Do you know Shaqiq?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What is the way of his companions?" He said: "When they are denied, they are patient, and when they are given, they are thankful." Abdullah said: "The way of our dogs is like this." He said: "Then how should it be?" He said: "The perfect ones are those who, when they are denied, are thankful, and when they are given, they prefer others."

* * *

Know that the totality of these nine conditions is what is mentioned in the conditional clause. As for the conditions mentioned in the consequent clause, they are four.

The first condition: His saying ﴿for them is the ultimate abode (ʿUqbā al-Dār)﴾, that is, the final outcome of the abode, which is Paradise, because it is the one that Allah intended to be the outcome of the world and the return of its people. Al-Wahidi said: "ʿUqbā is like ʿāqiba (outcome)." It may be a verbal noun, like shūrā, qurbā and rujʿā. Something like this also comes in the pattern fa'lā, as in najwā and daʿwā, and in fi'lā, as in dhikrā and ḍīzā. It may also be a noun, and here it is a verbal noun annexed to the agent. The meaning is: for them, their deeds will have as their outcome the abode, which is Paradise.

The second condition: His saying ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter﴾, and in it there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: "Gardens of Eden is an apposition (badal) to ʿuqbā. The discussion of Gardens of Eden we have covered in detail at His saying: ﴿and good dwellings in Gardens of Eden﴾ [al-Tawba: 72], and there we mentioned the view of the exegetes and the view of the lexicographers."

The second issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr recited [yudkhalūnahā] with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ, in the passive form. The rest recited with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the khāʾ, attributing the entering to them.

The third condition: His saying ﴿and whoever is righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿUlayya recited [ṣaluḥa] with a ḍamma on the lām. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The fatḥa is more eloquent."

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: the position of "man" is nominative, because of its being coordinated with the wāw in His saying ﴿they will enter them﴾. It may also be accusative, as you say: "They have entered and Zayd," meaning "along with Zayd."

The third issue: Regarding His saying ﴿and whoever is righteous﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It means whoever believed in what they believed in, even if he did not do deeds like theirs." Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah the Exalted has made clear that lineage does not benefit when it is not accompanied by righteous deeds. Rather, the fathers, spouses and offspring will not enter Paradise except through righteous deeds." Al-Wahidi said: "The correct view is what Ibn ʿAbbas said, because Allah the Exalted made among the reward of the obedient servant his joy at the presence of his family with him in Paradise. This indicates that they enter it as an honour for the obedient one who performs righteous deeds. If they entered it by their own righteous deeds, there would be no honour in that for the obedient one, nor any benefit in the promise of it, since everyone who is righteous in his deeds enters Paradise."

Know that this argument is weak, because the intended purpose is to give the obedient one glad tidings of everything that increases his joy and delight. When Allah gives the responsible person the good news that when he enters Paradise, his fathers, spouses and children will be present with him, there is no doubt that his joy increases greatly and his delight is strengthened by it. It is said that among the greatest causes of their joy is that they gather together and recall their conditions in the world, then thank Allah for being delivered from it and for achieving Paradise. For this reason, Allah the Exalted, in describing the people of Paradise, said that they say: ﴿Would that my people knew, of what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured﴾ [Ya Sin: 26–27].

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿and their spouses﴾ contains nothing that indicates a distinction between one wife and another. Perhaps the preferable reading is "whoever dies leaving her or she dies leaving him." And what is narrated from Sawda: "When the Messenger (ﷺ) intended to divorce her, she said: 'Leave me, O Messenger of Allah, that I may be raised in the company of your wives,'" serves as an indication of what we have mentioned.

The fourth condition: His saying ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently. How excellent is the ultimate abode﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "For them is a tent of hollow pearl, its length a farsakh and its width a farsakh, with a thousand doors whose frames are of gold. The angels will enter upon them from every door, saying to them: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾," meaning in obedience to Allah's command. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "From every door of the doors of righteousness, such as the door of prayer, the door of zakat, and the door of patience, and they will say: 'How excellently Allah has given you the outcome after the first abode.'"

Know that if we take the entering of the angels to be in the first sense, it is a lofty rank. This is because Allah the Exalted informed us about these obedient ones that they enter the everlasting Garden and gather with their fathers, spouses and offspring in the best manner. Then the angels, despite the sublimity of their ranks, enter upon them for the sake of greeting and honour. When they enter upon them, they honour them with greeting and peace, and give them glad tidings by their saying: ﴿How excellent is the ultimate abode﴾. There is no doubt that this differs from what the theologians say, that reward is a pure and everlasting benefit accompanied by majesty and veneration. It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he used to come to the graves of the martyrs at the beginning of every year and say: "Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently. How excellent is the ultimate abode." The four Caliphs used to do the same.

As for if we take it in the second sense, the interpretation of the verse is that the angels are groups, among them spiritual beings (rūḥāniyyūn) and cherubic beings (karūbiyyūn). When the servant trains his soul with various kinds of spiritual discipline, such as patience, gratitude, watchfulness (murāqaba) and self-examination (muḥāsaba), and each of these stations has a sacred essence (jawhar quddusī) and a lofty spirit (rūḥ ʿulwī) that is specially connected with that quality, then at death, when those sacred essences shine forth, there are manifested in them from every spirit of the heavenly spirits what corresponds to them of the particular quality proper to them. Thus there overflows upon them from the angels of patience special psychic perfections that appear only in the station of patience, and from the angels of gratitude spiritual perfections that are revealed only from the station of gratitude. The same is true of all the stations.

* * *

The second issue: Some scholars have used this verse to argue that the angel is superior to the human being. They said: Glory be to Him, He concluded the ranks of human felicity with the angels entering upon them as a greeting, honour and veneration. Thus they were, by this, of higher rank than humans. If they were of lower rank than humans, their entering upon them for the sake of peace and greeting would not have been a cause of raising their ranks and the nobility of their stations. Do you not see that if someone returns from his journey to his house, and it is said in praise of his high station that the emir, the vizier, the judge and the mufti visit him, this indicates that the rank of that visited person is lower and inferior to the ranks of the visitors? So it is the same here.

The third issue: al-Zajjaj said: Here there is an omitted element, its estimated form being: "The angels enter upon them from every door and say, 'Peace be upon you.'" So the saying was left implicit, because there is an indication of it in the discourse. As for His saying ﴿for what you endured patiently, how excellent is the ultimate abode﴾, there are two possibilities:

One: It is connected to "peace," and the meaning is: this safety has come to you only through your patience in acts of obedience and your abstaining from forbidden things.

The second: It is connected to an omitted element, and the estimate is: these honours that you see and these good things that you witness have come about only through that patience.

But if he endures affliction because he knows that this affliction is a portion decreed by the Allotter, the All-Knowing, who is exempt from defect, falsehood and folly — and that this portion must contain profound wisdom and a preponderant benefit — and he is content with it, because it is the disposal of the owner over his property, and there is no objection to the owner disposing of his property; or he is patient because he has become wholly absorbed in beholding the One who tests, so that his absorption in the manifestation of the light of the One who tests makes him oblivious to the pain of the affliction — this is the highest station of the sincere (siddiqun). These three aspects are those in which it is truly said of him that he was patient seeking the countenance of his Lord, meaning that he was patient solely for the sake of His reward and the seeking of Allah's pleasure.

Know that His words ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ contain a subtle point: that when a lover is struck by his beloved, the lover may look at that striker and rejoice in it. So His words ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ are to be understood in this figurative sense: just as the lover accepts that blow out of delight in gazing upon the face of his beloved, so the servant endures affliction and trial and is content with it,

because of his absorption in knowing the light of the Truth. This is a subtle and delicate point.

The seventh qualification: His words ﴿and establish the prayer﴾.

Know that although prayer and zakat are included in the first general statement, Allah mentioned them separately to draw attention to their being more noble than the other acts of worship. The establishing of prayer has already been explained earlier in this book, and it is not precluded that voluntary prayers are also included in it.

* * *

The eighth qualification: His exalted words ﴿and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. On this there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Hasan said: what is meant is the obligatory zakat. If one is not suspected of withholding zakat, it is preferable to pay it secretly; but if one is suspected of withholding zakat, it is preferable to pay it openly. It was also said that "secretly" means paying it oneself, and "openly" means paying it to the imam. Others said: rather, what is meant is obligatory zakat and voluntary charity given in the manner of a supererogatory act; so His words ﴿secretly﴾ refer to voluntary charity, and His words ﴿and openly﴾ refer to obligatory zakat.

The second issue: the Mu'tazilites said: He encouraged spending from everything that is provision (rizq), and this indicates that there is no provision except what is lawful; for if what is unlawful were provision, He would have encouraged spending unlawful wealth, and that is not permissible.

The ninth qualification: His words ﴿and repel evil with good﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: that when they commit a sin, they repel it and push it away by repentance, as it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "When you commit an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will wipe it out."
