So there is no covenant more binding than Allah's obligating a person to that by rational proof or by revealed proof. A servant does not fulfil the covenant except by performing all of those things, just as one who swears to many things is not truthful in his oath unless he does all of them. It includes performing all the commanded acts and refraining from all the forbidden acts; it includes fulfilling contracts in transactions; it includes rendering trusts. This view is the chosen and correct interpretation of the verse.

* * *

The second qualification: His words ﴿and do not break the pledge﴾. On this there are several opinions:

The first opinion — the view of the majority — is that this phrase is close in meaning to fulfilling the covenant, for fulfilling the covenant is close to not breaking the pledge and the covenant. This is like someone saying: when its existence became necessary, its non-existence must be impossible. These two concepts are distinct but mutually entailing; likewise, fulfilling the covenant necessarily entails not breaking the pledge.

Know that fulfilling the covenant is among the highest levels of felicity. He, peace be upon him, said: "There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness, and no religion for one who has no covenant." The verses concerning this matter in the Qur'an are numerous.

The second opinion: the pledge (mithaq) is what a responsible person binds upon himself. The sense is: His words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ refer to what Allah obligated the servant with from the outset, and His words ﴿and do not break the pledge﴾ refer to what the servant has committed himself to of kinds of obedience by his own choice, such as vowing acts of obedience and good deeds.

The third opinion: by fulfilling the covenant is meant the covenant of lordship and servanthood, and by the pledge is meant the covenants mentioned in the Torah, the Gospel and the rest of the divine books concerning the obligation to believe in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ upon his appearance.

Know that fulfilling the covenant is something praised by reason and by the sacred laws. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever makes a covenant with Allah and then betrays it has a characteristic of hypocrisy." And from him, peace be upon him: "There are three whom I will oppose on the Day of Resurrection, and whomever I oppose I will prevail against: a man who gave a covenant and then betrayed it; a man who hired a worker, took full work from him, and withheld his wage; and a man who sold a free person, enslaved the free person and consumed his price." It is also related that: "There was a covenant between Mu'awiyah and the king of the Romans, and he wished to go to them and break the covenant. Then a man on a horse appeared, saying: 'Fulfilment of covenant, not betrayal! I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: whoever has between himself and a people a covenant, let him not dissolve it nor tie it until its term has ended, and let him inform them openly.'" He said: "Who is this?" They said: "'Amr ibn 'Uyaynah." So Mu'awiyah turned back.

* * *

The third qualification: ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾. Here there is a question: fulfilling the covenant and not breaking the pledge already include the obligation to perform all the commanded acts and to avoid all the forbidden acts, so what is the benefit of mentioning these qualifications after them?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: it was mentioned lest someone suppose that this applies only to what is between him and Allah, so the matters between him and the servants were singled out for mention. The second: it is for emphasis.

Having understood this, we say: they have mentioned several interpretations of it:

The first: that what is meant is the joining of kinship ties (silat al-rahim). He, peace be upon him, said: "Three will come on the Day of Resurrection having a sharpness to them: the womb (rahim) will say, 'O Lord, I was severed'; the trust will say, 'O Lord, I was abandoned'; and the blessing will say, 'O Lord, I was ungratefully rejected.'"

The second opinion: that what is meant is joining with Muhammad ﷺ, supporting him, and aiding him in jihad.

The third opinion: the observance of all the obligatory rights of servants, which includes joining kinship ties and the relationship established through the brotherhood of faith, as He said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10]. This joining includes supporting them by conveying good things and warding off calamities as far as possible, visiting the sick, attending funerals, spreading the greeting of peace among people, smiling in their faces, and withholding harm from them. It also includes every living creature, even the cat and the hen. It is related from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, may Allah have mercy on him, that a group entered upon him in Mecca, and he said: "Where are you from?" They said: "From Khurasan." He said: "Fear Allah and be wherever you wish, and know that if a servant does the utmost good, yet has a hen and mistreats it, he is not among the doers of good."

I say: the sum of the matter is that His words ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the pledge﴾ point to the exalting of Allah's command, and His words ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ point to compassion toward the creation of Allah.

* * *

The fourth qualification: His words ﴿and fear their Lord﴾. The meaning: even if he performs everything within his capacity in exalting Allah's command and in compassion toward Allah's creation, it is still necessary that fear of Allah and dread of Him dominate his heart. This fear is of two kinds:

One of them: that he fears that some excess, deficiency or flaw may occur in his acts of worship and obedience, such that it would invalidate the worship or diminish its reward.

The second, which is the fear of majesty: because when the servant stands before a sovereign who is awe-inspiring and dominating, even though he is in the state of obedience, the awe of majesty, exaltation and greatness does not leave his heart.

The fifth qualification: His words ﴿and dread an evil reckoning﴾. Know that the fourth qualification refers to fear of Allah, while this fifth qualification refers to fear and dread of an evil reckoning. This indicates that by fear of Allah is meant what we have mentioned: the fear of majesty, awe and greatness; otherwise there would be repetition.

* * *

The sixth qualification: His exalted words ﴿And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾. This includes patience in performing acts of worship, patience under the burden of illnesses, harms, distresses and sorrows, patience in abstaining from desires, and in sum patience in refraining from sins and in performing acts of obedience. Then a person may undertake patience for several reasons:

One: that he is patient so that it may be said how perfect his patience is and how strong his endurance of calamities.

Second: that he is patient so that he will not be blamed for impatience.

Third: that he is patient so that the enemies will not gloat.

Fourth: that he is patient because he knows there is no benefit in impatience. When a person is patient for one of these reasons, that does not count as part of the perfection of the soul and the felicity of the heart. But if he endures affliction because he knows that this affliction is a portion decreed by the Allotter, the All-Knowing, who is exempt from defect, falsehood and folly — and that this portion must contain profound wisdom and a preponderant benefit — and he is content with it, because it is the disposal of the owner over his property, and there is no objection to the owner disposing of his property; or he is patient because he has become wholly absorbed in beholding the One who tests, so that his absorption in the manifestation of the light of the One who tests makes him oblivious to the pain of the affliction — this is the highest station of the sincere (siddiqun). These three aspects are those in which it is truly said of him that he was patient seeking the countenance of his Lord, meaning that he was patient solely for the sake of His reward and the seeking of Allah's pleasure.

Know that His words ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ contain a subtle point: that when a lover is struck by his beloved, the lover may look at that striker and rejoice in it. So His words ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ are to be understood in this figurative sense: just as the lover accepts that blow out of delight in gazing upon the face of his beloved, so the servant endures affliction and trial and is content with it,

because of his absorption in knowing the light of the Truth. This is a subtle and delicate point.

The seventh qualification: His words ﴿and establish the prayer﴾.

Know that although prayer and zakat are included in the first general statement, Allah mentioned them separately to draw attention to their being more noble than the other acts of worship. The establishing of prayer has already been explained earlier in this book, and it is not precluded that voluntary prayers are also included in it.

* * *

The eighth qualification: His exalted words ﴿and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. On this there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Hasan said: what is meant is the obligatory zakat. If one is not suspected of withholding zakat, it is preferable to pay it secretly; but if one is suspected of withholding zakat, it is preferable to pay it openly. It was also said that "secretly" means paying it oneself, and "openly" means paying it to the imam. Others said: rather, what is meant is obligatory zakat and voluntary charity given in the manner of a supererogatory act; so His words ﴿secretly﴾ refer to voluntary charity, and His words ﴿and openly﴾ refer to obligatory zakat.

The second issue: the Mu'tazilites said: He encouraged spending from everything that is provision (rizq), and this indicates that there is no provision except what is lawful; for if what is unlawful were provision, He would have encouraged spending unlawful wealth, and that is not permissible.

The ninth qualification: His words ﴿and repel evil with good﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: that when they commit a sin, they repel it and push it away by repentance, as it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "When you commit an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will wipe it out."

[p. 36 marker from source: صفحة ٣٦ was not present in the original text as a marker; see note below]

*Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 20–24 (part 2 of 2):*

The second view: the meaning is that they do not meet evil with evil, but meet evil with good, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by it with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. It is related from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him both: "The one who maintains ties is not the one who returns the favour of being kept ties with. Rather, the one who maintains ties is the one whose ties were cut, yet he maintained them and showed kindness to the one who did not maintain ties with him. The forbearing person is not the one who is wronged and then shows forbearance, only to be provoked when a people provoke him. Rather, the forbearing person is the one who has power and then pardons." And from al-Hasan: "They are those who, when they are deprived, give, and when they are wronged, pardon." It is also narrated that Shaqiq ibn Ibrahim al-Balkhi entered upon Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak in disguise. He asked: "Where are you from?" He said: "From Balkh." He said: "Do you know Shaqiq?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What is the way of his companions?" He said: "When they are denied, they are patient, and when they are given, they are thankful." Abdullah said: "The way of our dogs is like this." He said: "Then how should it be?" He said: "The perfect ones are those who, when they are denied, are thankful, and when they are given, they prefer others."

* * *

Know that the totality of these nine conditions is what is mentioned in the conditional clause. As for the conditions mentioned in the consequent clause, they are four.

The first condition: His saying ﴿for them is the ultimate abode (ʿUqbā al-Dār)﴾, that is, the final outcome of the abode, which is Paradise, because it is the one that Allah intended to be the outcome of the world and the return of its people. Al-Wahidi said: "ʿUqbā is like ʿāqiba (outcome)." It may be a verbal noun, like shūrā, qurbā and rujʿā. Something like this also comes in the pattern fa'lā, as in najwā and daʿwā, and in fi'lā, as in dhikrā and ḍīzā. It may also be a noun, and here it is a verbal noun annexed to the agent. The meaning is: for them, their deeds will have as their outcome the abode, which is Paradise.

The second condition: His saying ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter﴾, and in it there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: "Gardens of Eden is an apposition (badal) to ʿuqbā. The discussion of Gardens of Eden we have covered in detail at His saying: ﴿and good dwellings in Gardens of Eden﴾ [al-Tawba: 72], and there we mentioned the view of the exegetes and the view of the lexicographers."

The second issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr recited [yudkhalūnahā] with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ, in the passive form. The rest recited with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the khāʾ, attributing the entering to them.

The third condition: His saying ﴿and whoever is righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿUlayya recited [ṣaluḥa] with a ḍamma on the lām. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The fatḥa is more eloquent."

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: the position of "man" is nominative, because of its being coordinated with the wāw in His saying ﴿they will enter them﴾. It may also be accusative, as you say: "They have entered and Zayd," meaning "along with Zayd."

The third issue: Regarding His saying ﴿and whoever is righteous﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It means whoever believed in what they believed in, even if he did not do deeds like theirs." Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah the Exalted has made clear that lineage does not benefit when it is not accompanied by righteous deeds. Rather, the fathers, spouses and offspring will not enter Paradise except through righteous deeds." Al-Wahidi said: "The correct view is what Ibn ʿAbbas said, because Allah the Exalted made among the reward of the obedient servant his joy at the presence of his family with him in Paradise. This indicates that they enter it as an honour for the obedient one who performs righteous deeds. If they entered it by their own righteous deeds, there would be no honour in that for the obedient one, nor any benefit in the promise of it, since everyone who is righteous in his deeds enters Paradise."

Know that this argument is weak, because the intended purpose is to give the obedient one glad tidings of everything that increases his joy and delight. When Allah gives the responsible person the good news that when he enters Paradise, his fathers, spouses and children will be present with him, there is no doubt that his joy increases greatly and his delight is strengthened by it. It is said that among the greatest causes of their joy is that they gather together and recall their conditions in the world, then thank Allah for being delivered from it and for achieving Paradise. For this reason, Allah the Exalted, in describing the people of Paradise, said that they say: ﴿Would that my people knew, of what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured﴾ [Ya Sin: 26–27].

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿and their spouses﴾ contains nothing that indicates a distinction between one wife and another. Perhaps the preferable reading is "whoever dies leaving her or she dies leaving him." And what is narrated from Sawda: "When the Messenger (ﷺ) intended to divorce her, she said: 'Leave me, O Messenger of Allah, that I may be raised in the company of your wives,'" serves as an indication of what we have mentioned.

The fourth condition: His saying ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently. How excellent is the ultimate abode﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "For them is a tent of hollow pearl, its length a farsakh and its width a farsakh, with a thousand doors whose frames are of gold. The angels will enter upon them from every door, saying to them: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾," meaning in obedience to Allah's command. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "From every door of the doors of righteousness, such as the door of prayer, the door of zakat, and the door of patience, and they will say: 'How excellently Allah has given you the outcome after the first abode.'"

Know that if we take the entering of the angels to be in the first sense, it is a lofty rank. This is because Allah the Exalted informed us about these obedient ones that they enter the everlasting Garden and gather with their fathers, spouses and offspring in the best manner. Then the angels, despite the sublimity of their ranks, enter upon them for the sake of greeting and honour. When they enter upon them, they honour them with greeting and peace, and give them glad tidings by their saying: ﴿How excellent is the ultimate abode﴾. There is no doubt that this differs from what the theologians say, that reward is a pure and everlasting benefit accompanied by majesty and veneration. It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he used to come to the graves of the martyrs at the beginning of every year and say: "Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently. How excellent is the ultimate abode." The four Caliphs used to do the same.

As for if we take it in the second sense, the interpretation of the verse is that the angels are groups, among them spiritual beings (rūḥāniyyūn) and cherubic beings (karūbiyyūn). When the servant trains his soul with various kinds of spiritual discipline, such as patience, gratitude, watchfulness (murāqaba) and self-examination (muḥāsaba), and each of these stations has a sacred essence (jawhar quddusī) and a lofty spirit (rūḥ ʿulwī) that is specially connected with that quality, then at death, when those sacred essences shine forth, there are manifested in them from every spirit of the heavenly spirits what corresponds to them of the particular quality proper to them. Thus there overflows upon them from the angels of patience special psychic perfections that appear only in the station of patience, and from the angels of gratitude spiritual perfections that are revealed only from the station of gratitude. The same is true of all the stations.

* * *

The second issue: Some scholars have used this verse to argue that the angel is superior to the human being. They said: Glory be to Him, He concluded the ranks of human felicity with the angels entering upon them as a greeting, honour and veneration. Thus they were, by this, of higher rank than humans. If they were of lower rank than humans, their entering upon them for the sake of peace and greeting would not have been a cause of raising their ranks and the nobility of their stations. Do you not see that if someone returns from his journey to his house, and it is said in praise of his high station that the emir, the vizier, the judge and the mufti visit him, this indicates that the rank of that visited person is lower and inferior to the ranks of the visitors? So it is the same here.

The third issue: al-Zajjaj said: Here there is an omitted element, its estimated form being: "The angels enter upon them from every door and say, 'Peace be upon you.'" So the saying was left implicit, because there is an indication of it in the discourse. As for His saying ﴿for what you endured patiently, how excellent is the ultimate abode﴾, there are two possibilities:

One: It is connected to "peace," and the meaning is: this safety has come to you only through your patience in acts of obedience and your abstaining from forbidden things.

The second: It is connected to an omitted element, and the estimate is: these honours that you see and these good things that you witness have come about only through that patience.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 25:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth - for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾

Know that when the Exalted mentioned the attributes of the blessed and what follows from them of noble and exalted states, He followed them with mention of the state of the wretched and what follows for them of disgraceful and hateful conditions. He followed promise with threat and reward with punishment, so that the explanation would be complete. He said: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation﴾. We have already explained that the covenant of Allah (ʿahd) is what He has obligated His servants to by means of rational and revealed proofs, because these are more binding than any pact or oath. Oaths only confer firmness through proofs indicating that they require fulfilment in accordance with what they entail. The meaning of breaking these covenants is that a person does not consider the proofs at all, so that he cannot act upon what they require; or that he considers them, knows their soundness, then obstinately does not act by his knowledge; or that he considers a doubt and thereby believes what is contrary to the truth.

[p. 38]

As for His saying: ﴿after its confirmation﴾, the meaning is: after Allah had established those proofs and made them firm, because nothing is stronger than what Allah has indicated to be obligatory, in that its performance benefits and its neglect harms.

If it is said: if a covenant (ʿahd) exists only together with a confirmation (mīthāq), what is the benefit of Him stipulating it by His saying ﴿after its confirmation﴾?

We say: there is no impediment to the meaning of "covenant" being what Allah has imposed upon the servant, and the meaning of "confirmation" (mīthāq) being the emphasizing proofs, because He may confirm the covenant to you by other proofs, whether those confirming proofs are rational or revealed.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾. This is in contrast to His saying: ﴿those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾. So He made severance, the opposite of that joining, one of their attributes. The meaning is severing everything that Allah has obligated to be joined, and it includes joining with the Messenger through loyalty and support, joining with the believers, joining the ties of kinship, and joining all others who have a right. Then He said: ﴿and cause corruption on the earth﴾, and that corruption is calling to other than the religion of Allah; it may also be by wrongdoing against lives and property and by ruining lands. Then after mentioning these attributes, the Exalted said: ﴿for them is the curse﴾. The curse from Allah is removal from the good of this world and the Hereafter to their opposites, of punishment and vengeance. ﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾, because the intended meaning is Hell, and there is nothing in it except what displeases those who arrive at it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it. And they rejoice in the worldly life, but the worldly life, in the Hereafter, is but a brief enjoyment.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, passed judgment on those who broke the covenant of Allah regarding accepting monotheism and prophethood, by saying that they are cursed in this world and punished in the Hereafter, it was as if it were said: "If they were enemies of Allah, He would not have opened to them the doors of blessings and pleasures in this world." So Allah, may He be exalted, answered this objection with this verse, namely that He extends provision to some and restricts it for others, and this has no connection to disbelief or faith. Thus a disbeliever may be found with abundance while a believer is found with restriction, and the reverse. Therefore the world is a place of trial.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of qadr (قَدْر) in the language is: cutting a thing so that it equals another without excess or deficiency. And the exegetes said: the meaning of [yaqdir] here is "restricts," and similar to it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], meaning restricted, and its meaning is that He gives him according to what suffices him, so that nothing beyond it remains.

As for His saying: ﴿And they rejoice in the worldly life﴾, it refers to those for whom Allah extended their provision, and He, may He be exalted, made clear that this does not necessitate rejoicing, because the hasty worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is like the small and trifling in comparison with that which has no end.

Page 39

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance,"﴾ ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, it is in the remembrance of Allah that hearts find rest.﴾

Know that the disbelievers said, "O Muhammad, if you are a messenger, then bring us a sign and a clear, overpowering miracle, like the miracles of Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both."

He answered this question with His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance."﴾ The explanation of how this answer is to be understood is given in several aspects:

The first: It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: Allah has sent down to him clear signs and overpowering miracles, but misguidance and guidance are from Allah. He has led you astray from those overpowering, dazzling signs, and He has guided other peoples to them, so that through them they recognised the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) in his claim to prophethood. Since this is so, there is no benefit in multiplying signs and miracles.

The second: It is a statement that comes in the manner of expressing wonder at their words. This is because the dazzling, abundant signs that appeared upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were too many to remain ambiguous to a sensible person. So when they asked for further signs after these, this was a matter for wonder and disapproval. It is as if it were said to them: How great is your obstinacy! "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whoever He wills," meaning whoever has your disposition of firm resolve and stubborn adherence to disbelief, there is no path for you to be guided, even if every sign were sent down; "and guides" whoever is of a disposition opposite to yours.

The third: When they asked for all the other signs and miracles, it was as if it were said to them: There is no benefit in the appearance of signs and miracles, for misguidance and guidance are from Allah. If many signs come but guidance does not come, then no benefit is obtained from them. But if only one sign comes and guidance comes from Allah, then benefit is obtained from it. So do not occupy yourselves with seeking signs, but humbly implore Allah for guidance.

The fourth: Abu Ali al-Jubba'i said: The meaning is that Allah leaves astray whom He wills from His mercy and reward, as a punishment for his disbelief. Therefore you are not among those whom Allah, exalted is He, responds to in what they ask, since you deserve punishment, namely being led astray from reward. "And guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance," that is, He guides to His Paradise whoever repents and believes. He said: This shows that guidance is reward, inasmuch as He follows it with His saying "whoever turns back in repentance," that is, repents. The guidance that He bestows upon the believer is the reward, because he deserves it for his faith. This indicates that He, exalted is He, only leads astray from reward through punishment, not from religion through disbelief, contrary to what those who differ from us have held. This is the end of the words of Abu Ali. As for His saying "anāba" (turns back), it means he came to the truth; its real sense is that he entered into the portion of good.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 28:**

[Page 40 marker omitted: the page number is not part of the text.]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God. Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is joy and a good place of return.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Those who believe﴾ is a substitute (badal, an apposition that replaces the previous noun) for His saying ﴿who turns back (to Him)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means that when they hear the Qur'an, their hearts become humbly submissive and at rest.

If it is asked: Did He not say in surah al-Anfal: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned﴾ [al-Anfal: 2]? Trembling is the opposite of being at rest. How then does He describe them here as being at rest?

The answer has several aspects.

The first: when they recall the punishments and do not feel secure from committing acts of disobedience, He describes them then as trembling. When they are reminded of His promise of reward and mercy, their hearts become calm at that. Neither of the two conditions contradicts the other, because trembling comes from remembering punishment and rest comes from remembering reward. Trembling occurs when they reflect on acts of disobedience, and rest occurs when they are occupied with acts of obedience.

The second: the meaning is that their knowledge that the Qur'an is miraculous (mu'jiz) brings them rest concerning the fact that Muhammad (ﷺ) is truly a prophet from God. As for their doubt about whether they have performed the acts of obedience in complete and perfect form, that brings trembling into their hearts.

The third: their hearts are at rest that God is truthful in His promise and His threat, and that Muhammad (ﷺ) is truthful in everything he reports from Him. However, trembling and fear arise in their hearts as to whether they have performed the obedience that merits reward or not, and whether they have guarded against the disobedience that merits punishment or not.

Know that for us, in His saying ﴿Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾, there are subtle and obscure investigations, and they are of several aspects.

The first aspect: existent things are of three kinds. There is that which acts but is not acted upon, that which is acted upon but does not act, and that which both acts upon something and is acted upon by something. The one that acts without being acted upon is God, glorified and exalted. The one that is acted upon without acting is the body (jism), for it is a substance receptive to different attributes and contrary effects, and it has no property except receptivity alone. As for the existent that acts at one time and is acted upon at another, these are the spiritual existents (al-mawjudat al-ruhaniyya). This is because, when they turn toward the Divine Presence (al-hadra al-ilahiyya), they become receptive to the effects that overflow from God's will, power, bringing into being, and creation. When they turn toward the world of bodies, they yearn to act upon them, because the world of spirits governs the world of bodies.

Once you know this, the heart, whenever it turns to contemplating the world of bodies, experiences agitation, anxiety, and a strong inclination to gain control over them and to act upon them. But when the heart turns to contemplating the Divine Presence, there arise in it the lights of divine self-sufficiency (al-samadiyya) and divine illuminations. Then it is still. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.﴾

The second aspect: whenever the heart reaches something, it seeks to move from it to another state that is more noble than it, because there is no happiness in the world of bodies except that above it there is another level of pleasure and delight. But when the heart and the intellect arrive at finding happiness in the divine knowledges and the lights of self-sufficiency, they remain and settle, and it is absolutely impossible for them to move away from it, because there is no higher and more perfect level of happiness beyond it. For this meaning He said: ﴿Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.﴾

The third aspect in explaining this phrase: when a single particle of the elixir (iksir) falls upon a copper body, it turns into gold that endures through the passing of ages and times, and it withstands the melting caused by fire. So, if the elixir of God's majesty falls into the heart, it is even more fitting that it transforms it into a pure, luminous, enduring substance that does not accept change or alteration. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.﴾

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds - for them is joy (ṭūbā) and a good return﴾. And in this there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the explanation of the word "ṭūbā" there are three opinions:

The first opinion: that it is the name of a tree in Paradise. It has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Ṭūbā is a tree in Paradise, which Allah planted with His own hand; it produces ornaments and garments, and its branches can be seen from beyond the wall of Paradise." Abu Bakr al-Asamm (may Allah be pleased with him) related that the root of this tree is in the house of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in the house of every believer there is a branch of it.

The second opinion, which is the view of the lexicographers: that ṭūbā is a verbal noun from ṭāba (to be good), like bushrā and zulfā, and the meaning of "ṭūbā laka" is: you have attained what is good. Then they differed in several ways:

It has been said: joy and coolness of the eye for them; from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with both of them).

It has been said: the blessings they enjoy; from ʿIkrima.

It has been said: envy-worthy good fortune for them; from al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It has been said: goodness for them; from Qatāda.

It has been said: good and honour for them; from Abu Bakr al-Asamm.

It has been said: the good life for them; from al-Zajjāj.

Know that the meanings are close, and the difference is nearly only in wording. The sum is that it is an intensive expression for attaining good things, and it includes all pleasures; its explanation is that the best of things in every matter is attained by them.

The third opinion: that this word is not Arabic. Then they differed: some of them said: ṭūbā is the name of Paradise in Ethiopian (Ḥabashī), and it was said: the name of Paradise in Hindi, and it was said: the garden in Hindi. This opinion is weak, because the Qur'an contains only Arabic, especially since the derivation of this word from the Arabic language is evident.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshāf said: ﴿Those who believe﴾ is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and ﴿ṭūbā lahum﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The meaning of "ṭūbā laka" is: you have attained good. Its position (maḥall) is either accusative or nominative, as in your saying: ṭayyiban laka and ṭayyibun laka, and salāman laka and salāmun laka. The reading in His words ﴿and a good return﴾ with the nominative and accusative indicates its position. And Makwazah al-Aʿrābī read "ṭībā lahum".

As for His words ﴿and a good return﴾, the intended meaning is the goodness of the place of return and abode. All of this is a promise from Allah of the greatest bliss, as an encouragement to His obedience and a warning against disobedience.

**The Words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away, that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾**

Know that the *kaf* in "*kadhalika*" ("thus") is for comparison (*tashbih*). It has been said that the aspect of comparison is: "We have sent you just as We sent the prophets before you, to a community before which other communities had passed away." This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

It has also been said: "Just as We sent messengers to communities and gave them scriptures to be recited to them, so too have We given you this Book, and you recite it to them. So what have they proposed other than it?"

The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's Qur'an commentary) said: "*Kadhalika arsalnaka*" means: in the manner of that sending, "We have sent you," meaning We have sent you with a sending that has a rank and excellence over all other sendings. Then he explained how He sent him, saying: ﴿in a community before which other communities had passed away﴾, that is, We have sent you to a community that was preceded by other communities. So it is the last of the communities, and you are the last of the prophets.

As for His words: ﴿that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you﴾, the meaning is: that you may recite to them the Great Book which We have revealed to you. ﴿While they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, that is, the state of these people is that they disbelieve in the Most Merciful, whose mercy encompasses everything, and whatever blessing they have is from Him. They have rejected His blessing in sending someone like you to them and in sending down this inimitable Qur'an upon them.

﴿Say: He is my Lord﴾, the One, exalted above partners. ﴿There is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust﴾ in my being given victory over you. ﴿And to Him is my return﴾, so that He may help me to endure and struggle against you.

It has been said: the words ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ were revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, who used to say: "As for Allah, we know Him; but as for the Most Merciful, we do not know Him, except the one of al-Yamama," meaning Musaylima the Liar. Then the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra: 110]. This is like His words:

[p. 42]

﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60].

It has also been said: "When he (ﷺ) made the treaty with the Quraysh at Hudaybiyyah, he wrote: 'This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed upon.' The polytheists said: 'If you are the Messenger of Allah, we would not have fought you, so we have wronged you. But write: "This is what Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah has agreed upon."' So he wrote that. And when he wrote in the document 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate,' they said: 'As for the Most Merciful, we do not know Him.' They used to write 'In Your name, O Allah.' So he (ﷺ) said: 'Write what you wish.'"

Know that His words ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, if we interpret them according to these two reports, mean that they disbelieved in applying this name to Allah, the Exalted, not that they disbelieved in Allah, the Exalted. Others said: rather, they disbelieved in Allah, either by denying Him or by ascribing partners to Him. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this view is more fitting to the apparent meaning, because His words ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ require that they disbelieved in Allah, and that is what is understood from "the Most Merciful," and not the name itself is what is understood from it. It is like when someone says, "They disbelieved in Muhammad and denied him," where what is understood is the person himself, not merely his name.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 31:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if only a Qur'an had by it the mountains been set in motion, or the earth been split asunder, or the dead been made to speak. Rather, the command belongs entirely to Allah. Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would have guided all of mankind? And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done, or it will settle near their home until the promise of Allah comes. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾.

Know that it has been narrated: "The people of Makkah sat in the courtyard of Makkah, and the Messenger (ﷺ) came to them and presented Islam to them. Abdullah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi said to him: 'Set the mountains of Makkah in motion for us so that the place becomes spacious for us, and make rivers in it for us so that we may plant in them, or bring back to life for us some of our dead so that we may ask them whether what you say is true or false, for Isa used to revive the dead, or subject the wind to us so that we may ride it and travel through the lands, for the wind was subjected to Sulayman. You are not less honoured before your Lord than Sulayman.'" So there was revealed His saying: ﴿And if only a Qur'an had by it the mountains been set in motion﴾, meaning, from their places, ﴿or the earth been split asunder﴾, meaning, cleft so that it is made into rivers and springs, ﴿or the dead been made to speak﴾, that would have been this Qur'an which We have sent down to you.

The answer (jawab) of "law" (lau, "if") has been omitted because it is known. Al-Zajjaj said: the omitted element is that: "And if only a Qur'an had by it the mountains been set in motion," and so on, they still would not have believed in it, like His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them﴾ [al-An'am: 111].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, the command belongs entirely to Allah﴾, meaning: if He wills He does, and if He wills He does not, and no one has the right to impose a judgment upon Him regarding His actions and His rulings.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would have guided all of mankind?﴾ On this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Concerning His saying ﴿have not ... despaired﴾, there are two opinions:

**The first opinion:** It means "have they not known." On this interpretation there are two views:

**The first view:** *yaʼs* (يَيْأس, "despair") means "to know" in the dialect of al-Nakha'. This is the view of most exegetes, such as Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah. They argued for it with the words of the poet:

*Have not the peoples despaired that I am his son, though you be far from the land of the tribe?*

And Abu Ubaydah recited:

*I say to them in the ravine when they capture me: "Have you not despaired that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?"*

That is, "have you not known?" Al-Kisa'i said: I have not found the Arabs saying *yaʼistu* with the meaning of *ʻalimtu* ("I knew") absolutely.

**The second view:** It has been narrated that Ali and Ibn Abbas used to recite: ﴿Did not those who believe *yaʼs*﴾ (أفلم يأس الذين آمنوا). It was said to Ibn Abbas: "[Is it] *afalam yayʼas*?" He said: "I think the scribe wrote it while drowsy. In the script it was *yaʼs*, and the scribe added one tooth-stroke, so it became *yayʼas*, and so it was read *yayʼas*." This view is very far-fetched, because it implies that the Qur'an is a place for alteration and misreading, and that removes it from being a proof. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "This view, by Allah, is nothing but a calumny beyond doubt."

**The second opinion:** Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "or have those who believe despaired of the faith of these people, since, if Allah willed, He would have guided all of mankind?" Its explanation is that knowledge that a thing will not occur necessitates despair of its occurrence, and the connection (mulazamah) necessitates the beauty of metaphor (majaz). For this reason it is good to use the word "despair" to mean "knowledge."

**The second issue:** Our companions argued with His saying: ﴿if Allah willed, He would have guided all of mankind﴾. The word *law* ("if") indicates the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, did not will the guidance of all of mankind. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school) at times interpret this will as the will of compulsion (*mashiʼat al-ilja'*), and at times they interpret the guidance as guidance to the path of Paradise. Among them are those who take the speech according to its apparent meaning and say: He, exalted is He, did not will the guidance of all of mankind, because He did not will the guidance of children and the insane, so He is not one who wills the guidance of all of mankind. The discussion of this issue has preceded many times.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done, or it will settle near their home﴾, on it there are two issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ has two opinions:

**The first opinion:** It has been said: He intended by it all the disbelievers, because the severe calamities that befell some of the disbelievers, such as killing and captivity, caused grief to enter the hearts of all of them. And it has been said: He intended some of the disbelievers, a specific group, and the *alif* and *lam* in the word "disbelievers" refer to the previously known group, namely that specific group.

**The second issue:** The verse has two interpretations:

**The first:** ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done﴾, meaning, for their disbelief and evil deeds, a calamity, a great affliction, that strikes them, through what Allah brings upon them at every time of the various trials and calamities in their souls, their children and their wealth, ﴿or it will settle near their home﴾, so that they are alarmed and disturbed, and its sparks fly toward them and its evils reach them, ﴿until the promise of Allah comes﴾, which is their death or the Resurrection.

**The second opinion:** "And the disbelievers of Makkah will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of enmity and denial." This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept sending expeditions (*sarayā*), which raided around Makkah, seized from them and struck their livestock. Or, "you, O Muhammad, will settle near their homes with your army, as he settled at al-Hudaybiyah, until the promise of Allah comes," which is the conquest of Makkah, and Allah had promised him that.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) and to remove grief from him. The Qadi ('Abd al-Jabbar) said: This indicates the falsity of the view of those who permit that Allah breaks His promise regarding His appointment. And although this verse is addressed concerning the disbelievers, the consideration is with the generality of the wording and not with the specificity of the cause, since by its generality it encompasses every threat that came concerning the sinners.

Our answer: breaking a promise is one thing, and specifying a general ruling is another. We do not say that Allah breaks His promise, but we specify the general threats by the verses that indicate pardon.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 32–34:

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And messengers before you were mocked, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them. So how was My punishment?﴾ ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who have no such attributes]? Yet they have set up partners to Allah. Say: "Name them. Or will you inform Him of something He does not know on earth, or of mere outward speech?" Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved, and they were barred from the way. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is harder, and they have no protector from Allah.﴾

Know that when the people demanded all the other miracles from the Messenger (ﷺ) in a spirit of mockery and derision, and that was distressing to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was pained by those words, Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse as consolation for him and to make him patient with the foolishness of his people. He said to him: the peoples of all the prophets mocked them, just as your people mock you. ﴿So I gave the disbelievers respite﴾, meaning: I lengthened their term by delaying the punishment. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment of them?﴾

Know that I will take vengeance upon these disbelievers just as I took vengeance upon those earlier ones. Al-imla' (respite) means granting time and leaving them for a period of time in ease and security, like an animal that is given free rein to graze. This is a threat to them and an answer to their demand for signs from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a spirit of mockery. Then He, may He be exalted, presented to the polytheists what functions as an argument and what serves as a rebuke to them and a wonder at their minds. He said: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [...]﴾. The meaning is: He, may He be exalted, is capable of all possible things, knows all knowable things, both particulars and universals. Since this is so, He knows the states of all souls, and is able to bring about what they seek, namely the attainment of benefits and the repelling of harms, and the conveying to them of reward for every act of obedience and the conveying to them of punishment for every sin. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿standing over every soul in what it has earned﴾. And there is none who does this except the Truth, glorified is He. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18].

[Page 45]
Know that this statement must have an answer, and they differed about it in several ways.

The first view: the implied sense is: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ like one who does not have this attribute? That being the idols, which neither benefit nor harm. This answer is implied in His saying: ﴿and they have set up partners to Allah﴾. The meaning is: Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned like their partners which neither harm nor benefit? A parallel is His saying: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22], and its answer did not come, because it is implied in His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22]. So likewise here. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is permissible to supply what would be the predicate of the subject, or to make ﴿and they set up﴾ coordinated with it. The meaning is: Is He who is with this attribute (not made Him unique, nor glorified Him), and they have set up partners for Him?

The second view: This is what al-Sayyid, the author of Hall al-'Aqd, mentioned. He said: We make the waw in His saying ﴿and they set up﴾ the waw of circumstance (al-hal), and we imply for the subject a predicate such that the subject together with it forms a sentence confirming the possibility of what accompanies it of circumstance. The meaning is: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ existing, while the circumstance is that they set up partners for Him. Then the apparent noun, namely His saying ﴿for Allah﴾, was placed in the position of the pronoun, to establish divinity and make it explicit. This is like when you say: "A generous one who gives people and enriches them exists, yet withholds from one like me."

Know that when He, may He be exalted, established this argument, He added to the argument, and said: [Say: "Name them."] This is said only of a matter that is so despicable, reaching such baseness, that it is not mentioned and no name is given to it. In that case one says: "Name it if you wish," meaning: it is too base to be named and mentioned. But if you wish to give it a name, then do so. It is as if He had said: name them "gods," as a threat. The meaning is: whether you name them by this name or do not name them by it, they are so base that a reasonable person should not deign to turn to them. Then He added to the argument and said: ﴿Or will you inform Him of something He does not know on earth?﴾ The meaning is: Are you able to inform Him and make Him know something you know and He does not know? He specified "on earth" in the denial of a partner in it, even though there is no partner at all, because they claimed that He had partners on earth but not elsewhere. ﴿Or of mere outward speech﴾: meaning, you disguise with the utterance of a saying that has no reality. This is like His saying: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30].

Then, after this argument, He, may He be exalted, explained the badness of their way, and said, in order to belittle what they were upon: ﴿Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of "rather" here is as if He were saying: leave off mentioning what we were discussing; their scheming was made attractive to them. This is because, when He mentioned the proofs against their claim, it is as if He were saying: leave off mentioning the proof, for there is no benefit in it, since their disbelief and their scheming were made attractive to them, so they do not benefit from mention of these proofs. Al-Qadi said: There is no doubt that He mentioned that only in order to blame them for it. Since that is so, it is impossible that the one who made it attractive be Allah. Rather, it must be either the devils of mankind or the devils of the jinn.

Know that this interpretation is weak for several reasons.

The first: if the one who made it attractive were one of the devils of the jinn or of mankind, then if the one who makes attractive in the heart of that devil is another devil, it leads to an infinite regress; and if it is Allah, then the question is resolved.

The second: it is said that hearts cannot be controlled except by Allah.

The third: we have shown that the preponderance of the motive comes only from Allah, may He be exalted, and when it arises, the act becomes necessary.

As for His saying: ﴿and they were barred from the way﴾: know that 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-suddu" with a damma on the sad, and in Ha Mim (Ghafir: 37) ﴿wa-ṣuddda 'ani as-sabil﴾ in the passive form whose subject is unnamed, meaning that the disbelievers were barred by others. According to the people of the Sunnah, Allah barred them. The Mu'tazilah have two views on this: it was said that it was Satan; it was said that it was themselves, and some of them to others, as one says "so-and-so is amazed," even if there is none other than him. This is the view of Abu Muslim and others. And "wa-saddu" with a fatha on the sad in both surahs means that the disbelievers barred themselves from the way of Allah, that is, turned away; it was also said: they diverted others. It is both intransitive and transitive. The argument for the first reading is that it matches what precedes it in building the verb in the passive. The argument for the second reading is His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ Know that our companions held to this verse for several reasons.

The first of them is His saying: ﴿Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾, and we have shown by proof that this one who makes attractive is Allah.

The second: His saying ﴿and they were barred﴾ with a damma on the sad, and we have shown that this one who bars is Allah.

The third: His saying ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, which is explicit regarding the point and clear that the one who makes attractive and the one who bars is none but Allah.

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾. He informed about them that they will fall into the punishment of the Hereafter, and the informing of Allah cannot change. If change is impossible in this report, then it is impossible for faith to proceed from them. We have summarized all these points in this book many times.

Al-Qadi said: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, meaning: from the reward of Paradise, because of his disbelief. His saying ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ indicates that reward is not attained except by obedience specifically, so whoever turns away from it does not find a way to it. It was said: what is meant is whoever He judges to be astray and names as astray. It was said: what is meant is whoever Allah leaves astray from faith, by making him find it so. Then he said: the first view is stronger.

Know that the first view is very weak, because the discussion came only to explain their faith and disbelief in this world, and no mention of their going to Paradise occurred at all. So turning the discourse from what was mentioned to what was not mentioned is far-fetched. Moreover, even granting that the matter is as they have stated, when He, may He be exalted, informed that they do not enter Paradise, the purpose is already achieved, because opposing Allah's knowledge and His report is impossible and cannot occur.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, informed about them with those mentioned matters, He made clear that He had gathered for them both the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, which is harder, and that there is no repeller for them from it, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. As for the punishment of this world, it is by killing, fighting, cursing, blame, and humiliation. Do calamities and illnesses enter into this or not? They differed about it. Some said: they do enter into it. Others said: they are not a punishment, because everyone who is struck by a calamity is commanded to be patient with it, and if it were a punishment, that would not be required. So the meaning of the verse according to this view is: killing, captivity, the seizure of wealth, and cursing. He said ﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ because it is greater, if you wish, by reason of its strength and severity; if you wish, by reason of the multiplicity of its kinds; if you wish, by reason that nothing of the causes of ease is mixed with it; and if you wish, by reason of its permanence and non-cessation. Then He explained with His saying ﴿and they have no protector from Allah﴾, meaning that no one shields them from the punishment of Allah that has descended upon them. Al-Wahidi said: Most of the readers paused on the qaf without affirming a yā' in His saying ﴿wāqin﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿wa-man yuḍlili llāhu fa-mā lahu min hād﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿wālin﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 1]. This is the proper form, because in continuous recitation you say: "hādin," "wālin," "wāqin," and you delete the yā' because it is sukūn and meets the tanwin. When you pause, the tanwin is dropped in pausal position in the nominative and genitive, and the yā' had already been dropped, so the pause meets the vowel which is a kasra on a non-agent, and you drop it as you drop the other vowels on which you pause, so it becomes "hād," "wāl," "wāq." Ibn Kathir used to pause with the yā' in "hādī," "wālī," "wāqī." Its basis is what Sibawayh related, that some Arabs who are trusted say "hādhā dāʿī," and they pause with the yā'.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 32–34:

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And messengers before you were mocked, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them. So how was My punishment?﴾ ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who have no such attributes]? Yet they have set up partners to Allah. Say: "Name them. Or will you inform Him of something He does not know on earth, or of mere outward speech?" Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved, and they were barred from the way. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is harder, and they have no protector from Allah.﴾

Know that when the people demanded all the other miracles from the Messenger (ﷺ) in a spirit of mockery and derision, and that was distressing to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was pained by those words, Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse as consolation for him and to make him patient with the foolishness of his people. He said to him: the peoples of all the prophets mocked them, just as your people mock you. ﴿So I gave the disbelievers respite﴾, meaning: I lengthened their term by delaying the punishment. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment of them?﴾

Know that I will take vengeance upon these disbelievers just as I took vengeance upon those earlier ones. Al-imla' (respite) means granting time and leaving them for a period of time in ease and security, like an animal that is given free rein to graze. This is a threat to them and an answer to their demand for signs from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a spirit of mockery. Then He, may He be exalted, presented to the polytheists what functions as an argument and what serves as a rebuke to them and a wonder at their minds. He said: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [...]﴾. The meaning is: He, may He be exalted, is capable of all possible things, knows all knowable things, both particulars and universals. Since this is so, He knows the states of all souls, and is able to bring about what they seek, namely the attainment of benefits and the repelling of harms, and the conveying to them of reward for every act of obedience and the conveying to them of punishment for every sin. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿standing over every soul in what it has earned﴾. And there is none who does this except the Truth, glorified is He. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18].

[Page 45]
Know that this statement must have an answer, and they differed about it in several ways.

The first view: the implied sense is: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ like one who does not have this attribute? That being the idols, which neither benefit nor harm. This answer is implied in His saying: ﴿and they have set up partners to Allah﴾. The meaning is: Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned like their partners which neither harm nor benefit? A parallel is His saying: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22], and its answer did not come, because it is implied in His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22]. So likewise here. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is permissible to supply what would be the predicate of the subject, or to make ﴿and they set up﴾ coordinated with it. The meaning is: Is He who is with this attribute (not made Him unique, nor glorified Him), and they have set up partners for Him?

The second view: This is what al-Sayyid, the author of Hall al-'Aqd, mentioned. He said: We make the waw in His saying ﴿and they set up﴾ the waw of circumstance (al-hal), and we imply for the subject a predicate such that the subject together with it forms a sentence confirming the possibility of what accompanies it of circumstance. The meaning is: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ existing, while the circumstance is that they set up partners for Him. Then the apparent noun, namely His saying ﴿for Allah﴾, was placed in the position of the pronoun, to establish divinity and make it explicit. This is like when you say: "A generous one who gives people and enriches them exists, yet withholds from one like me."

Know that when He, may He be exalted, established this argument, He added to the argument, and said: [Say: "Name them."] This is said only of a matter that is so despicable, reaching such baseness, that it is not mentioned and no name is given to it. In that case one says: "Name it if you wish," meaning: it is too base to be named and mentioned. But if you wish to give it a name, then do so. It is as if He had said: name them "gods," as a threat. The meaning is: whether you name them by this name or do not name them by it, they are so base that a reasonable person should not deign to turn to them. Then He added to the argument and said: ﴿Or will you inform Him of something He does not know on earth?﴾ The meaning is: Are you able to inform Him and make Him know something you know and He does not know? He specified "on earth" in the denial of a partner in it, even though there is no partner at all, because they claimed that He had partners on earth but not elsewhere. ﴿Or of mere outward speech﴾: meaning, you disguise with the utterance of a saying that has no reality. This is like His saying: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30].

Then, after this argument, He, may He be exalted, explained the badness of their way, and said, in order to belittle what they were upon: ﴿Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of "rather" here is as if He were saying: leave off mentioning what we were discussing; their scheming was made attractive to them. This is because, when He mentioned the proofs against their claim, it is as if He were saying: leave off mentioning the proof, for there is no benefit in it, since their disbelief and their scheming were made attractive to them, so they do not benefit from mention of these proofs. Al-Qadi said: There is no doubt that He mentioned that only in order to blame them for it. Since that is so, it is impossible that the one who made it attractive be Allah. Rather, it must be either the devils of mankind or the devils of the jinn.

Know that this interpretation is weak for several reasons.

The first: if the one who made it attractive were one of the devils of the jinn or of mankind, then if the one who makes attractive in the heart of that devil is another devil, it leads to an infinite regress; and if it is Allah, then the question is resolved.

The second: it is said that hearts cannot be controlled except by Allah.

The third: we have shown that the preponderance of the motive comes only from Allah, may He be exalted, and when it arises, the act becomes necessary.

As for His saying: ﴿and they were barred from the way﴾: know that 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-suddu" with a damma on the sad, and in Ha Mim (Ghafir: 37) ﴿wa-ṣuddda 'ani as-sabil﴾ in the passive form whose subject is unnamed, meaning that the disbelievers were barred by others. According to the people of the Sunnah, Allah barred them. The Mu'tazilah have two views on this: it was said that it was Satan; it was said that it was themselves, and some of them to others, as one says "so-and-so is amazed," even if there is none other than him. This is the view of Abu Muslim and others. It is both intransitive and transitive. The argument for the first reading is that it matches what precedes it in building the verb in the passive. The argument for the second reading is His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ Know that our companions held to this verse for several reasons.

The first of them is His saying: ﴿Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾, and we have shown by proof that this one who makes attractive is Allah.

The second: His saying ﴿and they were barred﴾ with a damma on the sad, and we have shown that this one who bars is Allah.

The third: His saying ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, which is explicit regarding the point and clear that the one who makes attractive and the one who bars is none but Allah.

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾. He informed about them that they will fall into the punishment of the Hereafter, and the informing of Allah cannot change. If change is impossible in this report, then it is impossible for faith to proceed from them. We have summarized all these points in this book many times.

Al-Qadi said: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, meaning: from the reward of Paradise, because of his disbelief. His saying ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ indicates that reward is not attained except by obedience specifically, so whoever turns away from it does not find a way to it. It was said: what is meant is whoever He judges to be astray and names as astray. It was said: what is meant is whoever Allah leaves astray from faith, by making him find it so. Then he said: the first view is stronger.

Know that the first view is very weak, because the discussion came only to explain their faith and disbelief in this world, and no mention of their going to Paradise occurred at all. So turning the discourse from what was mentioned to what was not mentioned is far-fetched. Moreover, even granting that the matter is as they have stated, when He, may He be exalted, informed that they do not enter Paradise, the purpose is already achieved, because opposing Allah's knowledge and His report is impossible and cannot occur.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, informed about them with those mentioned matters, He made clear that He had gathered for them both the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, which is harder, and that there is no repeller for them from it, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. As for the punishment of this world, it is by killing, fighting, cursing, blame, and humiliation. Do calamities and illnesses enter into this or not? They differed about it. Some said: they do enter into it. Others said: they are not a punishment, because everyone who is struck by a calamity is commanded to be patient with it, and if it were a punishment, that would not be required. So the meaning of the verse according to this view is: killing, captivity, the seizure of wealth, and cursing. He said ﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ because it is greater, if you wish, by reason of its strength and severity; if you wish, by reason of the multiplicity of its kinds; if you wish, by reason that nothing of the causes of ease is mixed with it; and if you wish, by reason of its permanence and non-cessation. Then He explained with His saying ﴿and they have no protector from Allah﴾, meaning that no one shields them from the punishment of Allah that has descended upon them. Al-Wahidi said: Most of the readers paused on the qaf without affirming a yā' in His saying ﴿wāqin﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿wa-man yuḍlili llāhu fa-mā lahu min hād﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿wālin﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 1]. This is the proper form, because in continuous recitation you say: "hādin," "wālin," "wāqin," and you delete the yā' because it is sukūn and meets the tanwin. When you pause, the tanwin is dropped in pausal position in the nominative and genitive, and the yā' had already been dropped, so the pause meets the vowel which is a kasra on a non-agent, and you drop it as you drop the other vowels on which you pause, so it becomes "hād," "wāl," "wāq." Ibn Kathir used to pause with the yā' in "hādī," "wālī," "wāqī." Its basis is what Sibawayh related, that some Arabs who are trusted say "hādhā dāʿī," and they pause with the yā'.
