Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 35:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its fruit is everlasting and so is its shade. That is the final outcome of those who have been righteous, and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire.﴾

On this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, He followed it with mention of the reward of the righteous. As for His words ﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: Sibawayh said: "Mathalu al-Jannah" (the likeness of the Garden) is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "In what We have related to you is the likeness of the Garden."

The second: al-Zajjaj said: "Mathalu al-Jannah" means "a garden whose description is such and such."

The third: "Mathalu al-Jannah" is the subject, and its predicate is "beneath it rivers flow," just as you say: "The description of Zayd is that he is a noun."

The fourth: The predicate is His words ﴿its fruit is everlasting﴾, because it is the thing that departs from custom. It is as if He said: "The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised is that beneath it rivers flow," just as you know from the condition of your own gardens, except that this one's fruit is everlasting.

The second issue: Know that Allah the Exalted described the Garden with three attributes:

The first of them: beneath it rivers flow.

The second: its fruit is everlasting. The meaning is that the gardens of this world do not last in their leaves, their fruit, and their benefits. As for the gardens of the Hereafter, their fruits are everlasting and not cut off.

The third: its shade is also everlasting. The intended meaning is that there is no heat, no cold, no sun, no moon, and no darkness there. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾ [al-Insan: 13]. Then, when Allah the Exalted described the Garden with these three attributes, He made clear that this is the final outcome of those who have been righteous, meaning: the final end of the people of piety is the Garden, and the final end of the disbelievers is the Fire. The summary of the speech from this verse is that the reward of the righteous is pure benefits, free of impurities, described with the attribute of permanence.

Know that His words ﴿its fruit is everlasting﴾ contain three issues:

The first issue: It indicates that the fruit of the Garden does not perish, as is related from Jahm and his followers.

The second issue: It indicates that the movements of the people of the Garden do not end in a permanent state of rest, as Abu al-Hudhayl and his followers say.

The third issue: al-Qadi said: This verse indicates that the Garden has not yet been created, for if it were created, it would necessarily perish and its fruit would be cut off, due to His saying: ﴿Everyone upon it is perishing﴾ [al-Rahman: 26], and ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. But its fruit is not cut off, due to His saying: ﴿its fruit is everlasting﴾. Therefore it is necessary that the Garden is not created. Then he said: We do not deny that there presently exist in the heavens many gardens which the angels enjoy, and those among the prophets and martyrs and others who are considered alive, as has been related concerning that. However, what we hold is that the Garden of Eternity in particular is created only after the resurrection.

The answer: Their proof is composed of two verses:

One of them is His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾, and the other is His saying: ﴿its fruit is everlasting and so is its shade﴾. So when we introduce specification (takhsis) into one of these two general statements, their proof collapses. We specify one of these two general statements by the proofs indicating that the Garden is created, namely His saying, Exalted is He:

Page 48
﴿A Garden whose breadth is as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

The Almighty said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book rejoice at what has been sent down to you, and among the factions are those who deny part of it. Say, "I have only been commanded to worship God and not to associate anything with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return."﴾

Know that concerning what is meant by "the Book" there are two views.

The first: it is the Qur'an. The meaning is that the people of the Qur'an rejoice in what was sent down to Muhammad of the kinds of monotheism (tawhid), justice, prophethood, resurrection, legal rulings, and narratives. "Among the factions" refers to the groups of Jews, Christians, and the rest of the disbelievers who deny part of it. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

If it is asked: "The factions deny the whole Qur'an," we say: the factions do not deny everything in the Qur'an, because it contains the affirmation of God Most High, the affirmation of His knowledge, power, and wisdom, and the stories of the prophets, and the factions did not deny all of these things.

The second view: the Book means the Torah and the Gospel. On this interpretation, there are two opinions regarding the verse.

The first: Ibn Abbas said, "Those to whom We gave the Book are those among the People of the Book who believed in the Messenger (ﷺ), such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Ka'b, and their companions, and those Christians who embraced Islam. They were eighty men: forty in Najran, eight in Yemen, and thirty-two in the land of Abyssinia. They rejoiced at the Qur'an because they believed in it and affirmed it. 'The factions' are the rest of the People of the Book and all the polytheists." The qadi (judge) said: "This view is better than the first, because there is no doubt that those who were given the Qur'an rejoice in the Qur'an. But if we take it in this way, the benefit becomes apparent. It may also be said that the rejoicing of those who were given the Qur'an increases because of the many sciences and great benefits they saw in it. For this reason God Most High related their rejoicing in it."

The second: "Those to whom We gave the Book" are the Jews, who were given the Torah, and the Christians, who were given the Gospel. They rejoice at what has been sent down in this Qur'an because it confirms what they have. "Among the factions" are the rest of the disbelievers who deny part of it. This is the view of Mujahid. The qadi said: "This is not sound, because His saying ﴿rejoice at what has been sent down to you﴾ encompasses everything that was sent down to him, and it is known that they do not rejoice at everything that was sent down to him." It may be answered: His saying ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾ does not imply generality, as is shown by the permissibility of prefixing the words "all" (kull) and "part" (ba'd) to it. If the word "ma" (what) were for generality, prefixing "all" to it would be redundant and prefixing "part" to it would be deficient.

Then, when God Most High had explained this, He gathered in a few words everything a person needs to know regarding the origin and the return. He said: ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship God and not to associate anything with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return.﴾ This statement comprises everything for which obligation has come, and in it there are several benefits:

First: the word "innama" (only) is for restriction, and its meaning is "I have only been commanded to worship God Most High." This indicates that there is no obligation, command, or prohibition except through this.

Second: worship is the utmost degree of glorification, and this indicates that a person is obligated to it.

Third: worshipping God Most High is not possible except after knowing Him, and there is no way to know Him except through evidence. This indicates that a person is obligated to reflect and reason in order to know the essence of the Creator, His attributes, and what is necessary, possible, and impossible for Him.

Fourth: worshipping God is obligatory, and this refutes the view of those who deny obligation (legal responsibility) and refutes the pure doctrine of compulsion (jabr).

Fifth: His saying ﴿and not associate anything with Him﴾ indicates the negation of partners, equals, and opposites entirely. It includes refuting the view of everyone who affirms a deity other than God Most High, whether they claim that deity is the sun, the moon, the stars, idols, images, or the exalted spirits, or Yazdan and Ahriman as the Magians say, or light and darkness as the Dualists say.

Sixth: His saying ﴿To Him I call﴾ means that just as it was obligatory for him to perform these acts of worship, so it is obligatory for him to call to the worship of God Most High. This is an indication of his prophethood.

Seventh: His saying ﴿and to Him is my return﴾ is an indication of the gathering, the scattering, the resurrection, and the Day of Judgment. When a person reflects on these few words and comprehends them, he will know that they contain all the essential matters of religion.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 37:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment.﴾ ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against Allah no protector or defender.﴾

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that He, Exalted is He, likened His sending down of it as an Arabic judgment to what He sent down to the prophets before, meaning: just as We sent down the Books to the prophets in their tongues, so likewise have I sent down the Qur'an to you. The pronoun in His saying ﴿We have sent it down﴾ refers to "what" in His saying ﴿They rejoice in what has been sent down to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

The second issue: His saying ﴿We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾ has several interpretations:

The first: a wisdom in Arabic, translated into the language of the Arabs.

The second: the Qur'an comprises all the categories of obligations, so judgment is not possible except through the Qur'an. Since the Qur'an is the cause of judgment, the judgment itself was made to be the Qur'an, by way of emphasis (mubalaghah).

The third: He, Exalted is He, passed judgment on all the accountable people to accept the Qur'an and act by it, and since He passed judgment on creation regarding the obligation of accepting it, He made it a judgment.

Know that His saying ﴿an Arabic judgment﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: We sent it down in the state of being an Arabic judgment.

The third issue: The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that the Qur'an is created (muhdath), from several aspects:

The first: that He, Exalted is He, described it as being "sent down" (munazzal), and that is only fitting for something created (muhdath).

The second: that He described it as being "Arabic" (arabi), and the Arabic is that which came about by the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and whatever is so is created.

The third: that the verse indicates that it was an Arabic judgment only because Allah, Exalted is He, made it so and described it with this attribute, and whatever is so is created.

The answer: all these aspects indicate that what is composed of letters and sounds is created, and there is no dispute about this. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: It is related that the polytheists used to invite him to the religion of his forefathers, so Allah, Exalted is He, threatened him for following them in those ways, such as praying toward their qibla after Allah had turned him away from it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the address is with the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his community (ummah). It was also said: rather, the purpose of it is to urge the Messenger, peace be upon him, to uphold the right of the message and to warn him against deviating from it, and this also contains a warning to all accountable people, for whoever is of higher rank, when he is warned with this warning, then they are more deserving of it and more fitting for it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 38–39 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and made for them wives and offspring. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah. For every term is a decree.﴾ ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms [what He wills], and with Him is the Mother of the Book.﴾

Know that the people used to raise various kinds of doubts in denying his prophethood.

The first doubt was their saying: ﴿What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. Allah mentioned this doubt in another surah.

The second doubt: their saying that a messenger whom Allah sends to creation must necessarily be of the kind of the angels, as Allah related about them in His saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7], and His saying: ﴿Why was not an angel sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8].

Allah answered this here with His saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and made for them wives and offspring.﴾ Meaning: the prophets who were before him were of the kind of humankind, not of the kind of the angels. If that was permissible concerning them, why is it not permissible likewise concerning him?

The third doubt: they reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for having many wives, and said: "If he were a messenger from Allah he would not be occupied with matters of women, but would turn away from them and be occupied with worship and asceticism." Allah answered this with His saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and made for them wives and offspring.﴾ In sum, this statement may serve as an answer to the previous doubt and may also serve as an answer to this doubt, for Solomon, peace be upon him, had three hundred free wives and seven hundred concubines, and David had a hundred wives.

The fourth doubt: they said, "If he were a messenger from Allah, whatever miracle we asked of him he would bring it and would not hesitate; and since the matter is not so, we know that he is not a messenger." Allah answered this with His saying: ﴿And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah.﴾ Its explanation: a single miracle is sufficient to remove excuse and pretext, and to manifest the proof and the clear evidence. As for what exceeds it, it is entrusted to the will of Allah, the Exalted: if He wills, He manifests it, and if He wills, He does not manifest it, and no one has any objection to Him in that.

The fifth doubt: that he, peace be upon him, used to warn them of the descent of punishment and of the manifestation of victory for him and his people. Then that promised matter would be delayed, and when they did not witness those matters, they used them as an argument to discredit his prophethood, and said, "If he were a truthful prophet, his lie would not have become manifest."

Allah answered this with His saying: ﴿For every term is a decree﴾, meaning: the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the manifestation of conquest and victory for the friends of Allah, Allah has decreed that they occur at specific, determined times, and every event has a determined time. And "For every term is a decree": before the arrival of that time, that event does not occur; so the delay of those promises does not indicate that he is a liar.

The sixth doubt: they said, "If he were right in claiming prophethood, he would not have abrogated the rulings whose establishment in the earlier laws Allah had explicitly affirmed, such as the Torah and the Gospel. But he abrogated them and altered them, like the change of the qibla and the abrogation of most rulings of the Torah and the Gospel. Therefore he must not be a true prophet."

Allah, glorified and exalted, answered this with His saying: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms [what He wills], and with Him is the Mother of the Book.﴾ It is also possible that His saying, "For every term is a decree," serves as a preface to establishing this answer. This is because we observe that He creates an animal of wondrous form and marvelous nature from a drop of semen, then keeps it for a specific period, then causes it to die and scatters its parts and portions. Since it is not impossible for Him to give life first and then cause death second, how can it be impossible for Him to legislate a ruling at some times and then abrogate it at other times? So the intended meaning of "For every term is a decree" is what we have mentioned. Then, when He had established that premise, He said: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms [what He wills], and with Him is the Mother of the Book.﴾ The meaning: He brings into existence at one time and annihilates at another, gives life at one time and causes death at another, enriches at one time and impoverishes at another. Likewise, it is not far-fetched that He legislates a ruling at one time and then abrogates it at another, according to what the divine will requires, according to the people of the Sunnah, or according to what the consideration of benefits requires, according to the Mu'tazilah. This is the completion of the verification in the interpretation of this verse. Then here there are issues:

* * *

The first issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For every term is a decree﴾ — concerning it there are opinions:

The first: that for everything there is a predetermined time. The signs they asked for have a specific time which Allah has decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet, so it does not change from that decree because of their corrupt whims. Had Allah given them what they sought, there would have been the greatest corruption in it.

The second: that for every event there is a specific time at which Allah has decreed its occurrence, such as life and death, wealth and poverty, happiness and misery, and it absolutely does not change from that time.

The third: that this is an inversion, and the meaning is: for every revealed book from heaven there is a term in which it is sent down, i.e., for every book there is a time in which it is acted upon. The time for acting upon the Torah and the Gospel has ended, and the time for acting upon the Qur'an has come and arrived.

The fourth: for every specific term there is a book with the guardian angels. For a human being there are states, the first of which is a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then he becomes a youth, then an elder. The same is said concerning all states, of faith and disbelief, happiness and misery, beauty and ugliness.

The fifth: every specific time includes a hidden benefit and a good that no one knows but Allah, the Exalted. So when that time comes, that event occurs, and it is not permissible for it to occur at any other time.

Know that this verse is explicit that everything is by the decree and measure of Allah, and that affairs are bound to their appointed times; because His saying, "For every term is a decree," means that beneath every term there is a specific event. It is impossible that this determination is due to a property of the time itself, for that is absurd, since the substances occurring in successive times are equal. Therefore it must be that the particularization of each time with the event that occurs in it is by the act and choice of Allah, the Exalted. This indicates that all is from Allah, the Exalted, and it is parallel to His saying, peace be upon him: "The pen has dried with what is to be until the Day of Resurrection."

The second issue: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read [wa-yuthbitu] with the thaa unvowelled (sakin) and the baa light, from athbata yuthbitu, while the rest read with a fatha on the thaa and a shadda on the baa, from at-tathbit. The argument of the one who lightened it is that the opposite of effacement (mahw) is affirmation (ithbat), not tathbit; and also that the doubling indicates intensification, while the aim of effacement is not intensification, so likewise what is in opposition to it. The one who doubled it argued with His saying: ﴿and firmer in establishing [them]﴾ [an-Nisa': 66], and His saying: ﴿So make firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 12].

The third issue: mahw is the disappearance of the trace of writing; it is said: "mahahu yamhuhu mahwan" when he removes its trace. As for His saying, "and confirms," the grammarians said: the intended meaning is "and confirms it," but the first verb's transitivity was sufficient, so the second did not need to be transitive, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard [them]﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35].

* * *

The fourth issue: concerning this verse there are two views:

The first view: that it is general over everything, as the apparent wording requires. They said: Allah effaces from provision and increases it, and likewise regarding term of life, happiness and misery, faith and disbelief. This is the position of 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, and those who held this view used to supplicate and humbly beseech Allah to make them among the happy and not the wretched. This interpretation was narrated by Jabir from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second view: that this verse is specific to some of the wretched and not others. On this presentation, there are several aspects:

The first: the meaning of effacement and confirmation is: abrogation of a previous ruling and establishing another ruling in its place.

The second: that He, exalted is He, effaces from the register of the guardian angels what is neither good nor evil, for they are commanded to record every word and deed, and He confirms other than that. Abu Bakr al-Asamm criticized this, saying: He, exalted is He, described the Book by His saying: ﴿It leaves out nothing, small or great, but it has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and He also said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [az-Zalzalah: 7–8]. The Qadi answered him: that it does not leave out any small or great sin, and permissible acts are neither small nor great sins. Al-Asamm could respond to this answer by saying: by your technical convention you have restricted "small" to the minor sin and "great" to the major sin, and this is merely the terminology of the theologians. As for the original linguistic usage, "small" and "great" encompass every act and accident, for if it is trivial it is small, and if it is other than that it is great. On this presentation, His saying, ﴿It leaves out nothing, small or great, but it has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], also encompasses permissible acts.

The third: that He, exalted is He, intended by effacement that whoever sins, that sin is recorded in his register; when he repents of it, it is effaced from his register.

The fourth: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills﴾ refers to the one whose term has come, and He leaves the one whose term has not come and confirms him.

The fifth: that He, exalted is He, confirms at the beginning of the year the ruling of that year; when the year passes, it is effaced, and another book is confirmed for the future.

The sixth: He effaces the light of the moon and confirms the light of the sun.

The seventh: He effaces this world and confirms the Hereafter.

The eighth: that in matters of provision, trials and calamities, He records them in the Book, then removes them by supplication and charity, and in this there is an exhortation to devote oneself to Allah, exalted is He.

The ninth: the changing states of the servant: what has passed of them is the effacement, and what has occurred and is present is the confirmation.

The tenth: He removes what He wills and confirms what He wills of His ruling; He does not make any of His creatures aware of His unseen; He alone is the sole decider as He wills, and He is independent in bringing into existence, annihilating, giving life, causing death, enriching and impoverishing, such that none of His creatures is aware of those unseen matters.

Know that this subject is a vast field.

If someone says: Do you not claim that the measures are pre-decreed, with which the pen has dried, and that the matter is not something newly begun? How then does effacement and confirmation accord with this meaning?

We say: that effacement and confirmation are themselves also among the things with which the pen has dried; so He effaces only what was already decreed in His knowledge and decree to be effaced.

The fifth issue: The Rafidah said: al-bada' (a change of mind) is permissible for Allah, the Exalted, meaning that He believes something and then it becomes apparent to Him that the matter is contrary to what He had believed. They held fast to His saying: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾.

Know that this is false, for the knowledge of Allah is one of the necessary attributes of His essence, and whatever is so, the entry of change and alteration into it is impossible.

The sixth issue: As for ﴿the Mother of the Book﴾, the intended meaning is the origin of the Book. The Arabs call whatever functions as the origin of a thing its "mother," such as "the mother of the head" for the brain, and "Mother of Towns" for Makkah, and every city is a "mother" to the villages around it. Likewise, the Mother of the Book is that which is the origin of all books. Concerning it there are two views:

The first view: that the Mother of the Book is the Preserved Tablet, and all the events of the upper world and the lower world are recorded in it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah was and there was nothing with Him; then He created the Tablet and recorded in it the states of all creation until the Hour." The theologians said: the wisdom in it is that He, exalted is He, might show the angels that He knows all the known things in detail. On this premise, then, with Allah there are two books:

The first of them: the Book that the angels write down concerning creation, and this Book is the place of erasure and affirmation.

The second Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the guarded tablet on which all things are recorded), which contains the determination of all states, both celestial and terrestrial, and it is the enduring one. Abu al-Darda' narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in three hours left of the night, looks into the Book which no one else looks into, and He erases what He wills and affirms what He wills." The sages have remarkable words and obscure secrets concerning the interpretation of these two Books.

The second opinion: the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab) is the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. For He, exalted is He, has knowledge of all the known things, of existents and non-existents, even though they change. Yet His knowledge of them remains, free from change. So what is meant by the Mother of the Book is that. And Allah knows best.

If someone says: Do you not claim that the measures are pre-decreed, with which the pen has dried, and that the matter is not something newly begun? How then does effacement and confirmation accord with this meaning?

We say: that effacement and confirmation are themselves also among the things with which the pen has dried; so He effaces only what was already decreed in His knowledge and decree to be effaced.

The fifth issue: The Rafidah said: al-bada' (a change of mind) is permissible for Allah, the Exalted, meaning that He believes something and then it becomes apparent to Him that the matter is contrary to what He had believed. They held fast to His saying: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾.

Know that this is false, for the knowledge of Allah is one of the necessary attributes of His essence, and whatever is so, the entry of change and alteration into it is impossible.

The sixth issue: As for ﴿the Mother of the Book﴾, the intended meaning is the origin of the Book. The Arabs call whatever functions as the origin of a thing its "mother," such as "the mother of the head" for the brain, and "Mother of Towns" for Makkah, and every city is a "mother" to the villages around it. Likewise, the Mother of the Book is that which is the origin of all books. Concerning it there are two views:

The first view: that the Mother of the Book is the Preserved Tablet, and all the events of the upper world and the lower world are recorded in it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah was and there was nothing with Him; then He created the Tablet and recorded in it the states of all creation until the Hour." The theologians said: the wisdom in it is that He, exalted is He, might show the angels that He knows all the known things in detail. On this premise, then, with Allah there are two books:

The first of them: the Book that the angels write down concerning creation, and this Book is the place of erasure and affirmation.

The second Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the guarded tablet on which all things are recorded), which contains the determination of all states, both celestial and terrestrial, and it is the enduring one. Abu al-Darda' narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in three hours left of the night, looks into the Book which no one else looks into, and He erases what He wills and affirms what He wills." The sages have remarkable words and obscure secrets concerning the interpretation of these two Books.

The second opinion: the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab) is the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. For He, exalted is He, has knowledge of all the known things, of existents and non-existents, even though they change. Yet His knowledge of them remains, free from change. So what is meant by the Mother of the Book is that. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whether We show you part of what We promise them, or We take you (in death) before that, your duty is only to convey (the message), and upon Us is the reckoning.﴾

Know that the meaning is: ﴿And whether We show you part of what We promise them﴾ of the punishment, ﴿or We take you (in death)﴾ before that. The meaning is: whether We show you that, or We cause you to die before its appearing, what is obligatory upon you is to convey the commands of Allah the Exalted and to discharge His trust and His message, and upon Us is the reckoning. And al-balagh (conveyance) is a noun placed in the position of al-tabligh (the act of conveying), like al-siraj (the lamp) and al-ada' (the discharge).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verses 41–42:

[Page 54]

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Have they not seen that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts? And Allah judges; there is none to repel His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿And those before them had already plotted, but to Allah belongs all plotting. He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will come to know to whom belongs the final abode.﴾

Know that when Exalted Allah promised His Messenger that He would show him some of what they had been promised, or would take him (in death) before that, He explained in this verse that the effects of the fulfilment of those promises and their signs had already appeared and grown strong. As for His saying, ﴿Have they not seen that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾, there are several views on it.

The first view: the meaning is that We come to the land of the disbelievers, reducing it from its outskirts. This is because the Muslims were taking control of the outskirts of Makkah and seizing them from the disbelievers by force and compulsion. The diminishing of the circumstances of the disbelievers and the increasing strength of the Muslims is among the strongest signs and indications that Allah fulfils His promise. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts? Are they then the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:44], and His saying: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾ [Fussilat 41:53].

The second view, which is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), is that His saying ﴿reducing it from its outskirts﴾ means the death of its nobles, its elders and its scholars, and the passing away of its righteous and good people. Al-Wahidi said: although the wording admits this view, the view most fitting to this place is the first. It may be said that this view too is not fitting to this place. Its explanation is that it may be said: Have they not seen what occurs in the world of changes: ruin after prosperity, death after life, humiliation after honour, and decline after perfection? If these changes are observed and perceived, what then secures them from Allah turning the matter against these disbelievers, making them humiliated after they were honoured, and making them subdued after they were dominant? On this view the connection of this statement with what precedes it is sound. It was also said: ﴿reducing it from its outskirts﴾ refers to the death of its people and the ruin of their abodes and lands. So how are these disbelievers secure from the occurrence among them of such events?

Then Exalted Allah said, emphasising this meaning: ﴿And Allah judges; there is none to repel His judgment.﴾ Its meaning: there is no one who turns back His judgment. The mu'aqqib (one who reverses) is the one who reverses it by rejection and nullification. From this, the holder of a right is called mu'aqqib, because he follows up his debtor (ya'qibuhu) with demand and request.

If it is asked: what is the grammatical position of His saying, ﴿there is none to repel His judgment﴾?

We say: it is a clause in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal), as if it were said: Allah judges, His judgment being executed, free from any opposer, obstructer or contender.

Then He said: ﴿and He is swift in reckoning.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He means swift in retribution. That is, His reckoning for requital, whether with good or evil, is swift and near, and no repeller can ward it off.

As for His saying: ﴿And those before them had already plotted﴾, it means that the disbelievers of past nations plotted against their messengers and prophets, such as Namrud, who plotted against Ibrahim, Fir'awn, who plotted against Musa, and the Jews, who plotted against 'Isa.

Then He said: ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: its meaning is that the plotting of all the plotters belongs to Him and comes from Him, that is, it occurs by His creation and His will, because it is established that Allah Exalted is the Creator of all the actions of the servants. Moreover, that plotting harms only by Allah's permission and takes effect only by His decree. It contains consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and security for him from their plotting, as if it were said to him: since the occurrence of plotting is from Allah, and its effect on the one plotted against is likewise from Allah, it is necessary that fear should be of none but Allah Exalted, and that hope should be in none but Allah Exalted. Some people held that the meaning is: to Allah belongs the recompense of the plotting, because when they plotted against the believers, Allah Exalted explained that He would repay them for their plotting. Al-Wahidi said: the first of the two views is more evident, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾, meaning that the earnings of all servants are known to Allah Exalted, and what is contrary to what is known is impossible to occur. If that is so, then whatever Allah knows will occur is necessarily going to occur, and whatever Allah knows will not occur is impossible to occur. If that is so, then the servant has no power over doing and not doing, and so everything is from Allah Exalted.

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that holds that human beings create their own actions) said: if the first verse supports your position, then the second verse, His saying ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾, supports our position, because kasb (acquisition, earning) is an act that involves averting harm or bringing benefit. If the occurrence of the act were by the creation of Allah Exalted, the servant's power would have no effect in it, and so it would necessarily follow that the servant has no kasb.

Its answer: our view is that the combined power together with the motive necessitates the act, and on this assumption the kasb is attributed to the servant. Then He Exalted emphasised this threat, saying: ﴿and the disbelievers will come to know to whom belongs the final abode.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "wa-sa-ya'lamu al-kafir" in the singular, and the rest read it in the plural. The author of al-Kashshaf (Al-Kashshaf) said: it was recited as "al-kuffar" (the disbelievers), "al-kafirun" (the disbelievers, masculine plural), "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved), and "al-kufr" (disbelief), meaning its people. Jinah ibn Hubaysh recited "wa-sa-yu'lamu al-kafir," from a'lamahu, meaning he will be informed.

The second issue: by "the disbeliever" is meant the category, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr 103:2]. The meaning is: although they are ignorant of the outcomes, they will come to know to whom the praiseworthy end belongs, and this is like a warning and a threat.

The second view, which is the view of 'Ata': it means the mocking ones, who were five, and the dividers (al-muqtasimin), who were twenty-eight.

The third view, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas: it means Abu Jahl. The first view is the correct one.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 13, verse 43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related of the people that they denied his being a messenger from Allah. Then He, exalted is He, argued against them with two matters.

The first: the testimony of Allah to his prophethood. What is meant by that testimony is that He, exalted is He, manifested the miracles (mu'jizat) that indicate he was truthful in his claim to the message. This is the highest rank of testimony, because testimony (shahadah) is a statement that conveys a strong probability that the matter is so, whereas the miracle is a specific act that necessitates certainty that he is a messenger from Allah, exalted is He. Thus the manifestation of the miracle is the greatest rank of testimony.

The second: His saying, ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾. Regarding it there are two readings.

The first: the well-known reading, ﴿wa-man 'indahu﴾ (وَمَن عِنْدَهُ), meaning "and the one who has with Him the knowledge of the Book."

The second: [wa-min 'indihi 'ilmu al-kitab] (وَمِن عِنْدِهِ عِلْمُ الكِتابِ), where the particle "min" (مِن) here denotes the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), i.e., "and from Allah there came the knowledge of the Book." As for the first reading, there are several opinions regarding the interpretation of the verse:

The first opinion: What is meant is the testimony of the People of the Book from among those who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), namely: Abdullah ibn Salam, Salman al-Farisi, and Tamim al-Dari. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he would refute this interpretation, saying: "The surah is Meccan, so it is not permissible that it refer to Ibn Salam and his companions, for they believed in Medina after the Hijrah." This objection was answered by saying: "Although this surah is Meccan, this verse is Medinan. Moreover, establishing prophethood by the word of one or two people, who are not infallible from lying, is not permissible, and this objection stands."

The second opinion: By "the Book" is meant the Qur'an, that is, the Book I have brought you is an overpowering miracle and a dazzling proof. However, knowledge that it is a miracle is attained only by one who knows what is in this Book of eloquence and rhetorical excellence, and its containing of the unseen and of many sciences. Whoever knows this Book in this way knows that it is a miracle. Thus His saying, ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ means "and whoever has knowledge of the Qur'an." This is the view of al-Asamm.

The third opinion: By "whoever has knowledge of the Book" is meant the one who has acquired knowledge of the Torah and the Gospel. That is, anyone who is knowledgeable in these two books knows that they contain good tidings of the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ). So if that scholar is fair and does not lie, he is a witness that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a true messenger from Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth opinion: ﴿whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ is Allah, exalted is He. This is the view of al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Zajjaj. Al-Hasan said: "No, by Allah, He means none other than Allah." The meaning is: "Sufficient is the One who deserves worship, and the One who alone knows the knowledge of what is in the Preserved Tablet, as a witness between me and you." Al-Zajjaj said: "The more likely is that Allah, exalted is He, does not call upon any other to witness the validity of His judgment." This view is problematic, because coordinating an attribute with the thing it describes (ʿatf al-sifah 'ala al-mawsuf), although generally permissible, is contrary to the basic rule. One does not say "Zayd and the jurist testified to this," but rather "Zayd the jurist testified to it." As for his statement that Allah, exalted is He, does not call upon another to witness the truth of His judgment, this is far-fetched, because since Allah, exalted is He, may swear by His own words to affirm the truth of His speech, saying ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾ (al-Tin: 1), then what impediment is there in what al-Zajjaj has mentioned?

As for the second reading, which is [wa-min 'indihi 'ilmu al-kitab] with "min" as the preposition, the meaning is: "and from Him comes the knowledge of the Book," because no one knows the Book except through His bounty, His grace, and His teaching. Then, according to this reading, there are also two readings: [wa-min 'indihi 'ilmu al-kitab], and the meaning of "knowledge" is that which is the opposite of ignorance, i.e., this knowledge has come only from Allah.

The third reading: [wa-min 'indihi 'ulima al-kitab] (وَمِن عِنْدِهِ عُلِمَ الكِتابُ), with the ʿayn vowelled with a damma, the lam with a kasra, and the mim with a fatha, in the passive voice (ma lam yusamm fa'iluhu, i.e., the form whose subject is not named). The meaning is: when He commanded His Prophet to argue against them with the testimony of Allah, exalted is He, on the matter we have mentioned, and since the testimony of Allah to his prophethood has no meaning except the manifestation of the Qur'an in accordance with his claim, and since it cannot be known that the Qur'an is a miracle except after comprehending what is in the Qur'an and its secrets, He, exalted is He, made clear that this knowledge is not attained except from Allah. The meaning is that the realization that the Qur'an is a miracle is not attained unless Allah, exalted is He, honours that servant by teaching him the knowledge of the Qur'an. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best what is correct.

The exegesis of this surah was completed on Sunday, the eighteenth of Sha'ban, in the year six hundred and one. I ask of everyone who looks into this book of mine and benefits from it that he single out my son Muhammad with mercy and forgiveness, and that he remember me in supplication. And I say, in elegy for that son, these verses:

I see the landmarks of this transient world mixed with fears and sorrows.

Its good things are like frightening dreams, and its evil among creatures is constant and near.
